title: Application-Layer Protocols
summary: The bytes behind the protocols you use every day: HTTP/1.1 framing and cookies, HTTP/2 frames and HPACK, QUIC packets, the DNS wire format and DNSSEC, email and its authentication, NTP, SSH and gRPC, and peer-to-peer systems from BitTorrent to WebRTC.

lessons.title: HTTP/1.1 messages and body boundaries
lessons.summary: HTTP/1.1 framing follows ordered rules; a TCP read is not an HTTP message.
lessons.body:
HTTP/1.1 is a text protocol over an ordered TCP byte stream. TCP exposes bytes without application-message boundaries, so the receiver must determine where each message ends. Incorrect framing can hang a client, truncate content or create a security hole. HTTP semantics are shared across versions in RFC 9110; RFC 9112 specifies the HTTP/1.1 wire format.

## Anatomy of a request

The start line and header field lines end with **CRLF** (`\r\n`, bytes `0D 0A`). A blank line separates the headers from the body.

```
GET /search?q=tcp HTTP/1.1\r\n
Host: example.com\r\n
User-Agent: curl/8.5.0\r\n
Accept: */*\r\n
\r\n
```

- The **request line** is method, request target and version, separated by single spaces.
- **Header fields** are `Name: value`. Names are case-insensitive, so `content-length` and `Content-Length` are the same field.
- `Host` is **mandatory** in HTTP/1.1. A server must answer `400 Bad Request` if it is missing. It is what lets one IP address serve thousands of virtual hosts.
- A GET usually has no body, so the message ends at the blank line.

The response has the same shape, with a **status line** instead:

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n
Content-Type: text/html\r\n
Content-Length: 1256\r\n
\r\n
<1256 bytes of body>
```

A TCP read returns whatever bytes have arrived: half a header, or the end of one response plus the start of the next. The receiver therefore needs rules that say where a message ends.

A quick inspection tool can send `Connection: close` and read until the server closes the connection. EOF alone still does not prove the response is valid or complete. Without that header, HTTP/1.1 uses **persistent connections** by default, so a read-until-close loop can sit waiting after the response has fully arrived, until a timeout or the server closes. That is exactly why message framing matters.

## Where does the body end?

RFC 9112 gives the receiver an ordered list of rules. Simplified:

1. Responses to `HEAD`, all `1xx`, `204 No Content` and `304 Not Modified` responses **never have a message body**, whatever the headers say. An informational response may precede a final response; a `101` switches protocols.
2. A successful `2xx` response to `CONNECT` starts a tunnel after the headers; ignore framing fields for its length.
3. `Transfer-Encoding` overrides `Content-Length`. Senders must not send both. Reject ambiguous requests; a forwarding intermediary that processes such a message must remove `Content-Length`.
4. If transfer coding ends in `chunked`, decode chunks. If it ends in another coding, a response is close-delimited; a request must receive `400` and the connection must close.
5. With no transfer coding, a valid `Content-Length` gives the exact byte count. Invalid or conflicting lengths are framing errors; identical repeated values have a specified normalisation exception.
6. Otherwise, a **request** has no body and a **response** is close-delimited. Complete header validation and the RFC’s error rules are still required.

Close-delimited responses are supported for compatibility and are fragile: an apparently clean connection close cannot distinguish a complete body from a prematurely ended one without additional information. HTTP/1.0 also supported Content-Length.

> [!note] Why HEAD responses carry Content-Length
> A server should send the fields it would send for GET, but may omit fields calculated only while generating content. If it sends Content-Length on HEAD, that value must describe the content an equivalent GET would send. No body follows; waiting for those bytes can block until a timeout or close.

## Key takeaways
- HTTP/1.1 framing follows ordered rules; a TCP read is not an HTTP message.
- HEAD responses carry no body, even when Content-Length describes an equivalent GET.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9112](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112)
- [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)

questions.prompt: You hand-write an HTTP/1.1 client that sends a `GET` without `Connection: close`, then loops on `recv()` until it returns no data. The response arrives quickly but your program hangs for a long time. Assume the response has a valid Content-Length and the server leaves the connection open. Why?

options.text: The server is waiting for you to send a request body
options.explanation: A GET with no `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding` has no body, so the server is not waiting for one. It has already responded.

options.text: You forgot the `Host` header, so the server never replies
options.explanation: A conforming server must reject a request missing the Host header with 400. That is not the described complete response followed by a blocked read; no universal response timing is guaranteed.

options.text: TCP buffers the last segment until the window fills
options.explanation: The complete response bytes have already arrived. TCP is a byte stream; it does not require an application to wait for a whole receive window to fill before returning data.

options.text: The framed response is complete, but a persistent connection remains open, so another recv can block
options.explanation: Correct. The server sent a complete, framed response and is waiting for your next request. You should use `Content-Length` or chunked framing to know when the response ends, not connection close.

questions.workedExample: HTTP/1.1 permits persistence by default. After sending Content-Length: 1256 and 1,256 bytes, the server can wait for another request while a read-until-close client blocks. An eventual server close or client timeout may end the wait. HTTP/1.0 also supported Content-Length and some implementations used keep-alive; EOF was never a universal integrity check. Parse the response framing, or request close for this limited inspection pattern.

questions.prompt: A reverse proxy forwards a `HEAD /big.iso` response from the origin with header `Content-Length: 4700000000`. A hand-written client then waits to read 4.7 GB of body. What is the correct behaviour?

options.text: The response has no body; the client must know it sent HEAD and stop at the blank line
options.explanation: Correct. Responses to HEAD (and all 1xx, 204 and 304 responses) never have a body, regardless of framing headers. The client must remember which method it sent.

options.text: The client should read 4.7 GB because Content-Length is authoritative
options.explanation: Content-Length is overridden by the rule that HEAD responses never carry a body; it describes what a GET would return.

options.text: The proxy is wrong to forward Content-Length on a HEAD response
options.explanation: Content-Length is permitted on HEAD if it equals the content length an equivalent GET would send. It need not be present; the value can describe an encoded representation rather than a raw file size.

options.text: The client should switch to reading until the connection closes
options.explanation: Close-delimited reading would hang on a persistent connection and is unnecessary: the message already ended at the blank line.

questions.workedExample: RFC 9112 applies the HEAD/bodyless-status rule first, so this message ends at the header terminator. The length does not make a HEAD body appear. For other responses, successful CONNECT creates a tunnel; transfer coding and framing-error rules precede ordinary valid Content-Length. The parser therefore needs the request method as well as the response headers.

lessons.title: Streaming bodies with chunked encoding
lessons.summary: Chunk sizes are hexadecimal byte counts; their CRLF delimiters are framing rather than content.
lessons.body:
## Chunked transfer encoding

`Content-Length` must be known *before* the first body byte is sent. That is a problem for anything generated on the fly: a streamed template, a database export, a proxied upstream, a long-poll. Without a length, the server could only signal the end by closing the connection, losing persistence.

**Chunked encoding** solves this. The body is sent as a sequence of chunks, each prefixed by its size in **hexadecimal**, and a zero-size chunk marks the end:

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n
Transfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n
\r\n
7\r\n
Mozilla\r\n
11\r\n
Developer Network\r\n
0\r\n
\r\n
```

`11` is hexadecimal: one sixteen plus one, so that chunk is 17 bytes ("Developer Network"). The decoded body is `MozillaDeveloper Network`, 7 + 17 = 24 bytes. The CRLF after each chunk's data is framing, not content, so it is not counted. Reading `11` as decimal eleven would cut the chunk short and desynchronise the parser.

The key idea is that the receiver reads **exactly the number of bytes the size line announced**, then expects one CRLF. It never searches the data for line breaks, so a chunk may itself contain `\r\n` bytes without ending early.

A deliberately restricted decoder for an already-buffered, bounded message with **no extensions or trailers**. It rejects those unsupported forms and returns any following bytes separately. Production receivers must handle the full grammar and incremental input.

```python
import re

def read_chunked(buf):
    if len(buf) > 1_000_000:
        raise ValueError("demo limit")
    parts = []
    while True:
        # Remove the next size line.
        line, sep, buf = buf.partition(
            b"\r\n")
        if not sep or not re.fullmatch(
                rb"[0-9A-Fa-f]+", line):
            raise ValueError("bad size")
        # Sizes are hex, not decimal.
        size = int(line, 16)
        if size == 0:
            if not buf.startswith(b"\r\n"):
                raise ValueError(
                    "bad terminator")
            # Keep any next-message bytes.
            return b"".join(parts), buf[2:]
        if (len(buf) < size + 2
                or buf[size:size + 2]
                != b"\r\n"):
            raise ValueError("bad chunk")
        # Save data; skip its trailing CRLF.
        parts.append(buf[:size])
        buf = buf[size + 2:]
```

Details worth knowing:

- **Trailer fields.** After the `0` chunk, the sender may add header fields before the final blank line, for example a checksum computed while streaming. Native gRPC over HTTP/2 relies on trailers to send its status. Many HTTP/1.1 clients and browsers ignore them.
- **Chunk extensions** (`7;name=value`) can carry per-chunk metadata. A conforming receiver ignores unrecognised extensions after parsing their syntax and imposing suitable limits.
- Chunks have nothing to do with TCP segments. A 7-byte chunk may arrive split across two `recv` calls, and ten chunks may arrive in one. A real parser is a finite-state machine fed arbitrary slices.
- HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 **forbid** `Transfer-Encoding`. Both have length-delimited DATA frames. HTTP/2 signals message completion with END_STREAM; HTTP/3 uses the end of its underlying QUIC stream, not a DATA-frame END_STREAM flag.

## Key takeaways
- Chunk sizes are hexadecimal byte counts; their CRLF delimiters are framing rather than content.
- A restricted buffered decoder demonstrates the rules but is not a production incremental parser.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9112](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112)
- [RFC 9114](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114)

questions.prompt:
A chunked response body arrives as:

```
4
Wiki

6
pedia 

E
in 

chunks.

0


```

A colleague's decoder splits the body on every `
` and treats the pieces as alternating size lines and data. It decodes the first two chunks correctly. What goes wrong at the third chunk (`E`, which is hexadecimal for 14)?

options.text: Nothing; CRLF always separates a size line from its data, so splitting on it is safe
options.explanation: CRLF bytes can also appear *inside* chunk data. The third chunk's 14 bytes include `\r\n\r\n`, so splitting on CRLF breaks that chunk into pieces.

options.text: It reads `E` as a decimal number and rejects the size line
options.explanation: The described bug is splitting on line breaks, not parsing the size. Even with the hex size read correctly, a line-splitting decoder ignores the announced length.

options.text: It takes only `in ` as the chunk's data, then treats the following pieces (an empty line, `chunks.`) as size lines and loses its place
options.explanation: Correct. The 14 announced bytes are `in `, CRLF, CRLF and `chunks.`. Splitting on CRLF ends the data after 3 bytes, and the decoder then tries to read later pieces as hexadecimal sizes, so it rejects the message or desynchronises.

options.text: It adds the size lines `4`, `6` and `E` to the decoded body
options.explanation: The colleague's decoder recognises size lines; the failure comes from treating every CRLF as a boundary, including CRLFs that are part of the data.

questions.workedExample:
1. A chunked decoder must read each size line as **hexadecimal**: `4`, `6` and `E` (14).
2. It must then read exactly that many bytes, whatever they contain, and expect one CRLF after them.
3. The third chunk's 14 bytes are `in ` (3), `\r\n\r\n` (4) and `chunks.` (7). Those CRLFs are **data**.
4. A decoder that splits on CRLF stops the third chunk after `in `, then meets an empty piece and `chunks.` where it expects size lines. It either rejects the message or misframes everything after it.
5. A size-driven decoder gets the 24-byte body `Wikipedia in \r\n\r\nchunks.` and is never confused by data CRLFs.

The lesson rule in one line: chunk boundaries come from the announced sizes, not from line breaks.

questions.prompt: Which of these are good reasons for an HTTP/1.1 server sending a response with content to use `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` rather than `Content-Length`? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is streaming a CSV export whose total size is not known when the first row is ready
options.explanation: Correct. Content-Length must be sent before the body; chunked lets the server start sending immediately.

options.text: It wants to keep the connection persistent without buffering the whole response
options.explanation: Correct. Without a length, the only other way to end the body is closing the connection, which loses persistence.

options.text: It wants to append a checksum header computed over the body after sending it
options.explanation: Correct. Trailers after the final `0` chunk can carry values computed during streaming (though many clients ignore them).

options.text: It is speaking HTTP/2 and wants to stream
options.explanation: HTTP/2 forbids `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`. DATA frames carry their own lengths and END_STREAM flag, so streaming needs no extra encoding.

options.text: Chunked encoding compresses the body
options.explanation: Chunking only delimits the body; it adds a few bytes of overhead per chunk. Compression is `Content-Encoding: gzip` (or `br`).

questions.workedExample:
Ask what problem chunking solves: **framing a body of unknown length on a persistent connection**.

- Unknown size (CSV export): yes.
- Persistence without buffering: yes, that is the core reason.
- Trailers: yes, a feature of chunked framing.
- HTTP/2: no, it has binary framing and bans the header.
- Compression: no, that is Content-Encoding, a different layer.

lessons.title: Request smuggling and parser disagreement
lessons.summary: Different framing decisions at successive HTTP hops can leave attacker bytes for the next request.
lessons.body:
## Request smuggling: when framing disagrees

What if a request has **both** `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`? RFC 9112 gives transfer coding precedence, recommends treating the combination as an error, and requires connection closure after responding if a server elects to process such a request. But when a front-end proxy and a back-end server pick *different* rules, an attacker can hide one request inside another. This is **HTTP request smuggling**.

The classic **CL.TE** variant below assumes vulnerable hops: the front end trusts Content-Length, the back end parses chunks and improperly keeps the connection reusable. Lines use CRLF, but the final `SMUGGLED` bytes have **no trailing CRLF**. This is a boundary illustration, not a complete valid second request.

```
POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example
Content-Length: 13
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

SMUGGLED
```

The attacker chose `Content-Length: 13` by counting every byte after the blank line, CRLFs included: `0` and its CRLF (3 bytes), the empty line's CRLF (2) and the 8 letters of `SMUGGLED`. A chunked parser stops after the first 5 of those bytes. The two hops therefore disagree by 8 bytes:

1. The front end reads 13 body bytes (`0\r\n\r\nSMUGGLED`) and forwards everything as one request.
2. The back end decodes chunked: the `0` chunk ends the body after 5 bytes.
3. `SMUGGLED` is left in the back end's buffer on the shared, persistent connection. It becomes the **start of the next request**, which may belong to a different user.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Two clerks counting pages differently
> A front desk accepts a bundle labelled "13 pages" and passes it to the back office as one customer's file. The back-office clerk ignores the label and stops at the sheet marked "END", which the customer slipped in after page 5. The last 8 pages stay on the clerk's desk and get stapled to the next customer's file.
>
> **How it maps:** The front desk is a proxy trusting `Content-Length`; the back office is a server using chunked framing, where the `0` chunk is the "END" sheet. The leftover pages are the bytes that become the start of the next request on the shared connection.
>
> **Where it stops:** A clerk might notice odd pages; a parser just carries on, and the attacker can shape the leftover bytes into the start of a request that merges with another user's. Conforming servers avoid the situation altogether by rejecting the ambiguous message or closing the connection.

Attackers use this to poison caches, bypass front-end access controls and hijack other users' requests. Defences:

- Reject requests with both framing fields, invalid transfer-coding syntax, repeated chunked coding or a final coding other than chunked. Whitespace permitted by the grammar is not inherently malformed.
- Make every hop use the same parser rules, and close the connection after any framing error.
- Using HTTP/2 end to end removes this HTTP/1.1 delimiter disagreement, but does not excuse validation of header fields and length consistency. Translation to HTTP/1.1 needs particular care.

## Key takeaways
- Different framing decisions at successive HTTP hops can leave attacker bytes for the next request.
- Reject ambiguous framing and close after errors; protocol translation still needs validation.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9112](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112)
- [Original request-smuggling research and examples](https://portswigger.net/web-security/request-smuggling)

questions.prompt:
A front-end proxy uses `Content-Length` and ignores `Transfer-Encoding`; the back end honours chunked. An attacker sends:

```
POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example
Content-Length: 13
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

SMUGGLED
```

(Header/size lines end in CRLF; the final 8 SMUGGLED bytes have no trailing CRLF.) Assume the vulnerable back end accepts both fields, uses chunked, and improperly reuses the connection. What does the back end do?

options.text: Rejects the whole thing because chunked bodies cannot follow Content-Length
options.explanation: Rejecting this ambiguity and closing is the recommended defence. The specified vulnerable back end instead processes chunks and leaves the connection reusable; a conforming server that processes both fields must close after its response.

options.text: Ends the first request's body at the `0` chunk and treats `SMUGGLED` as the start of the next request on the connection
options.explanation: Correct. The back end sees an empty chunked body (5 bytes). The leftover 8 bytes become the start of whatever request comes next on the shared connection, possibly another user's.

options.text: Reads a 13-byte body and sees one request
options.explanation: That is the front end's view. The back end uses chunked framing, so it disagrees about where the body ends.

options.text: Waits forever for more chunks
options.explanation: The `0` chunk and final CRLF terminate a chunked body cleanly, so the back end does not wait.

questions.workedExample:
Count the body bytes after the blank line:

```
0\r\n          3 bytes
\r\n            2 bytes
SMUGGLED       8 bytes
               = 13
```

1. Front end: Content-Length 13, so all 13 bytes belong to this request. It forwards them.
2. Back end: chunked. Reads `0\r\n` (last chunk) then `\r\n` (end of trailers). Body ends after **5** bytes.
3. `SMUGGLED` sits in the back end's buffer and is parsed as the beginning of the next request.

The 8 leftover bytes demonstrate a framing disagreement; SMUGGLED alone is not a complete valid HTTP request. This is the boundary mechanism behind CL.TE smuggling. Fix: reject requests with both headers and close the connection on framing errors.

lessons.title: HTTP/1.1 reuse, pipelining and upload approval
lessons.summary: Persistent connections save handshakes, while pipelined responses must remain in request order.
lessons.body:
## Persistent connections and pipelining

Persistent connections are the default in HTTP/1.1; `Connection: close` opts out. Reusing a connection avoids a new TCP (and TLS) handshake per request.

**Pipelining** lets a client send several requests without waiting, but responses must come back **in order**. A slow earlier response can delay later responses. Clients can instead use parallel connections, subject to their own limits.

One more mechanism: a client uploading a large body can send `Expect: 100-continue` and wait for an interim `100 Continue` before sending the body. If the server would reject the upload (too big, unauthorised), it can send a final error such as `413` or `401` before the body. Clients may send after a bounded wait, so Expect does not guarantee that no body bytes are transmitted.

### Trace a reusable connection

Suppose a client pipelines three GETs on one TCP connection. The first response needs two seconds of application work, while the next two are ready almost immediately. Those later responses still wait for the first response to finish: HTTP/1.1 cannot interleave their bodies. Even correct Content-Length values only identify boundaries; they do not relax response ordering. Parallel TCP connections can avoid sharing this particular response queue, but each connection has its own setup and congestion state.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A takeaway counter with unnumbered orders
> A takeaway kitchen cooks three orders at once, but the receipts carry no order numbers, so the counter must hand out food in the order it was ordered. The first order is a slow-cooked dish; the next two are ready in a minute and sit on the pass until it is done.
>
> **How it maps:** The counter is one persistent HTTP/1.1 connection and the receipts are pipelined requests. The server may prepare responses in parallel, but with no request identifiers it must send them in request order, so a slow first response delays ready ones. A second counter is a parallel connection, with its own setup cost.
>
> **Where it stops:** A real counter could shout names and hand food out in any order. HTTP/1.1 has no equivalent; HTTP/2 adds stream numbers so responses can interleave, although lost packets can still delay them at the TCP layer.

When debugging an apparently idle client, distinguish an application waiting for the earlier response from a parser waiting for EOF. A length-framed response can finish while the connection remains open for reuse. Reading until close discards that distinction. Reusing a connection is safe only when the current message has been fully consumed under the framing rules. A framing error should end reuse rather than leave uncertain bytes for the next request.

## Key takeaways
- Persistent connections save handshakes, while pipelined responses must remain in request order.
- Expect: 100-continue permits early rejection but cannot guarantee that no body bytes are sent.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9112](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112)
- [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)

questions.prompt: An HTTP/1.1 client pipelines GETs /slow, /a, /b on one persistent connection. Assume their complete responses are ready at 2 s, 10 ms, 10 ms; neglect serialization and propagation, with no failures or other delays. When can the client receive /b?

options.text: After about 10 ms, because the server handles requests in parallel
options.explanation: Even if the server computes all three in parallel, HTTP/1.1 has no request IDs, so responses must be sent in request order.

options.text: After about 4 s, because each request waits for the previous one to be sent
options.explanation: Pipelining sends all requests immediately. The responses wait only on `/slow`, so total is about 2 s plus a few ms.

options.text: After about 2 s, behind `/slow`, because pipelined responses must come back in order
options.explanation: Correct. This is application-level head-of-line blocking: `/a` and `/b` are ready early but must wait for `/slow` to finish.

options.text: Never; the server drops pipelined requests
options.explanation: Pipelining is allowed. Under the stated successful persistent exchange, responses are sent in request order; implementations may close connections, so universal acceptance of arbitrary pipelines is not promised.

questions.workedExample: The client associates responses with requests by order. Even with /a and /b ready at 10 ms, their responses follow /slow. Under the stated negligible-transmission-time model, /b therefore arrives at about 2 s. Parallel connections or HTTP/2 stream multiplexing address this application-level ordering constraint.

lessons.title: Cookie scope, lifetime and script access
lessons.summary: Omitting Domain creates a host-only cookie; deleting a cookie must match its stored scope.
lessons.body:
## Cookies: state on a stateless protocol

HTTP is a stateless protocol at the level of its semantics; applications and connections can still maintain state. **HTTP cookies** ([RFC 6265](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6265); its revision, "6265bis", was approved but still waiting in the RFC Editor queue in October 2026) add state: the server sets a name/value pair, and the browser sends it back on later requests.

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: sid=a3f9; Path=/; Secure;
  HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=3600
```

(Shown wrapped; on the wire it is one line.) Later requests carry only the name/value pairs, never the attributes:

```
Cookie: sid=a3f9; theme=dark
```

One quirk: combining repeated field lines is allowed only when the field definition permits it. `Set-Cookie` **must not be folded into one comma-separated field**, because cookie dates (`Expires=Wed, 21 Oct...`) contain commas. Each cookie needs its own `Set-Cookie` line.

### The attributes

| Attribute | Effect |
|---|---|
| `Expires` / `Max-Age` | Lifetime; none means session cookie |
| `Domain` | Widen scope to subdomains |
| `Path` | Only send under this path |
| `Secure` | Send only over connections the browser considers secure |
| `HttpOnly` | Exclude from non-HTTP cookie APIs such as document.cookie |
| `SameSite` | Control cross-site sending |
| `Partitioned` | Add a top-level-site partition key in supporting browsers; requires Secure |

**Lifetime.** `Max-Age` (seconds) takes precedence over `Expires` (a date) if both appear. With neither, the cookie is a *session cookie*, deleted when the browser session ends (though "restore tabs" features often keep them). To delete a cookie, set it again with `Max-Age=0` and matching name, domain/host-only scope and path, in the same partition if applicable.

**Domain.** If you *omit* `Domain`, the cookie is **host-only**: set by `app.example.com`, it goes only to `app.example.com`. Setting `Domain=example.com` allows host matching for `example.com` *and its subdomains*, subject to path, security, SameSite and browser policy. The setting host must domain-match that Domain value. Counter-intuitively, omitting `Domain` is the stricter choice. Public-suffix rejection prevents a tenant from setting a parent-suffix cookie for other tenants. The algorithm has a host-only exception when the setting host itself equals the suffix; lists and browser policy matter.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A wristband for one venue or the whole festival
> At a festival, a wristband stamped for one tent gets you into that tent only. A wristband stamped for the whole site gets you into every tent, including ones run by contractors you have never met.
>
> **How it maps:** A host-only cookie (no `Domain`) is the one-tent band: the browser sends it only to the exact host that set it. `Domain=example.com` is the whole-site band: every subdomain receives it, including a forgotten staging host.
>
> **Where it stops:** Browsers also apply path, `Secure`, `SameSite` and privacy rules before sending a cookie, and a sibling host can try to *set* a parent-domain cookie with the same name, which a wristband has no equivalent for. The `__Host-` prefix in the next unit addresses that.

**Path** limits which URLs receive the cookie, but it is **not a security boundary**: same-origin script may access a matching-path document, subject to framing policy. Path does not isolate mutually distrustful applications on one origin; HttpOnly separately restricts script cookie access.

**Secure** normally requires HTTPS; browsers may treat localhost as a trusted exception. **HttpOnly** stops script from reading the cookie through document.cookie and similar non-HTTP APIs. It does not guarantee that XSS cannot expose a token through another vulnerable application feature, and injected script can still make authenticated requests.

## Key takeaways
- Omitting Domain creates a host-only cookie; deleting a cookie must match its stored scope.
- Path controls sending, while HttpOnly restricts non-HTTP cookie APIs; neither supplies complete XSS protection.

## Further reading
- [RFC 6265](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6265)
- [Cookie revision draft](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html)

questions.prompt: A page on `https://app.example.com` sets `Set-Cookie: sid=abc; Secure; HttpOnly` with **no** `Domain` attribute. Which host can match this cookie’s host scope, assuming the cookie was accepted and other sending conditions permit it?

options.text: `example.com` and all its subdomains
options.explanation: That is what `Domain=example.com` does. Omitting `Domain` is stricter, not broader.

options.text: `app.example.com` and its subdomains, such as `x.app.example.com`
options.explanation: Subdomains are included only when `Domain` is set explicitly. Without it the cookie is host-only.

options.text: Only `app.example.com`
options.explanation: Correct. With no `Domain` attribute the cookie is host-only: it is returned to exactly the host that set it.

options.text: Any site, because no SameSite attribute was given
options.explanation: SameSite controls whether the cookie is attached to *cross-site requests to app.example.com*, not which hosts receive it. Scope is set by Domain and Path.

questions.workedExample:
1. Look for a `Domain` attribute. There is none.
2. RFC 6265: no Domain means the **host-only** flag is set; the cookie matches only the exact host.
3. So `api.example.com`, `example.com` and `x.app.example.com` never see it.
4. If you instead wrote `Domain=example.com`, example.com and its subdomains would match its host scope, subject to the other cookie-sending rules.

Many developers add `Domain=` thinking it restricts the cookie; it does the opposite.

questions.prompt: From https://app.example.com/app/page, a server wants to delete an accepted, unpartitioned cookie set as Set-Cookie: pref=1; Domain=example.com; Path=/app. The browser permits cookie updates. Which header matches its scope and expires it?

options.text: `Set-Cookie: pref=; Domain=example.com; Path=/app; Max-Age=0`
options.explanation: Correct. It matches the name, domain-cookie scope and path in the same unpartitioned context, then gives it zero remaining lifetime.

options.text: `Set-Cookie: pref=; Max-Age=0`
options.explanation: Here it would target app.example.com as host-only, not the existing example.com domain cookie. The default path alone cannot repair that mismatch.

options.text: `Clear-Cookie: pref`
options.explanation: Clear-Cookie is not the deletion mechanism. Clear-Site-Data: "cookies" is a broader operation whose cookie scope can extend across the registrable domain; it is not a named-cookie deletion header.

options.text: `Cookie: pref=deleted`
options.explanation: Cookie carries request cookies. This response field does not perform the Set-Cookie update needed here.

questions.workedExample: Match pref, the example.com domain-cookie scope, and /app, then set Max-Age=0. For a host-only cookie reproduce host-only scope; partitioned cookies also require the corresponding partition context. RFC 6265bis includes the host-only flag in cookie identity. A mismatched scope may expire a different cookie instead.

lessons.title: SameSite, cookie prefixes and repeated bytes
lessons.summary: SameSite uses site relationships and request context; __Host- prefixes constrain supporting browsers.
lessons.body:
A cookie is a stored name/value pair with scope and security attributes. Earlier units covered host-only cookies, Domain, Path, Secure and HttpOnly. This unit adds cross-site sending rules and cookie-name prefixes, then looks at the cost of repeating cookies on every request.

### SameSite and the meaning of "site"

For these ordinary domain URLs, a **schemeful site** is the scheme plus the *registrable domain* (eTLD+1): `https://shop.example.co.uk` and `https://api.example.co.uk` are the **same site**, though different origins.

- `Strict`: sent only on same-site requests. On a cross-site navigation, that cookie is withheld from the initial request; what the user sees depends on application behaviour.
- `Lax`: also sent on **top-level navigations** with safe methods (clicking a link, a GET form). Not sent on cross-site `POST`s, iframes, images or `fetch`.
- `None`: removes the SameSite restriction and requires Secure in supporting browsers. Domain/path rules, partitioning and third-party-cookie policies still apply.

The 6265bis draft specifies Lax-style default enforcement and allows a user-agent-chosen recent-cookie exception for cookies with no explicit SameSite value. Explicit Lax excludes that exception. SameSite helps against cross-site CSRF, but does not cover same-site sibling attacks or every application workflow. Use appropriate CSRF protection for state-changing requests; GET should not perform state changes.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: An assistant who carries your membership card
> Your assistant automatically shows your club membership card on every errand to the club. A stranger hands the assistant a sealed note for the club saying "transfer £500". Without a rule, the assistant shows your card and the club acts on the note as if you sent it.
>
> **How it maps:** The assistant is the browser, the card is a cookie, and the stranger's note is a cross-site request. `Strict` means "show the card only on errands I started from the club's own pages". `Lax` adds "or when a stranger's link just sends you to the club's front page", which is a top-level navigation with a safe method such as GET. It still withholds the card from a cross-site POST and from requests embedded in the stranger's page, such as images or `fetch`.
>
> **Where it stops:** "Same site" means the same scheme and registrable domain, so every subdomain of the club counts as the club, including a compromised one. Browser policies also differ, so SameSite supplements CSRF protection rather than replacing it.

### Prefixes

Supporting browsers enforce cookie-name prefixes:

- `__Secure-name`: must be set with `Secure` from an HTTPS page.
- `__Host-name`: must be `Secure`, have `Path=/` and **no** `Domain`. This prevents a sibling from setting a parent-domain cookie under that prefixed name. It does not isolate ports on the same host or authenticate a Cookie header supplied by an arbitrary client.

> [!tip] A good session cookie
> `Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=<random>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax`

### Limits

RFC 6265 asks browsers to support **at least** 4096 bytes per cookie, 50 cookies per domain and 3000 in total, as recommended minimum capabilities in that RFC, not universal current limits. Cookie inclusion also depends on path, security, SameSite, credentials mode and browser policy.

Because HTTP/1.1 repeats the `Cookie` header on every request, large cookies multiply. A page that makes 80 requests, each carrying 3,000 bytes of cookies, uploads about 240,000 bytes of cookie values before any other header overhead. On a slow mobile uplink that can be noticeable. Two practical fixes are keeping cookies small (a short random session ID rather than stored state) and serving static files from a host the cookies are not scoped to.

This assumes every request is eligible to carry the cookies and that nothing compresses them. Cache hits can avoid requests; HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 compression savings depend on encoder/table decisions.

## Pitfalls

- **Hand-rolled parsers.** Reading until close, ignoring `HEAD`/`304` rules or trusting chunk boundaries to match `recv` calls are classic bugs.
- **Mixed framing headers.** Any hop that accepts both `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding` is a smuggling risk.
- **`Domain=` by habit.** It widens scope to every subdomain, including the forgotten staging box.
- **Treating cookie attributes as complete XSS protection.** HttpOnly is a real restriction on cookie APIs, but does not prevent injected script from making authenticated requests. Path is not an isolation boundary.

## Key takeaways
- SameSite uses site relationships and request context; __Host- prefixes constrain supporting browsers.
- Cookie-size estimates count actual eligible requests and state compression assumptions.

## Further reading
- [RFC 6265](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6265)
- [Cookie revision draft](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html)
- [CHIPS design](https://privacysandbox.google.com/cookies/chips)

questions.prompt: A bank authenticates this transfer solely with a session cookie explicitly set SameSite=Lax. In a browser enforcing that attribute, evil.example submits a top-level POST to https://bank.example/transfer, without redirects. Does this cross-site request include that cookie?

options.text: Yes, because form submissions are top-level navigations
options.explanation: Lax allows top-level navigations only with safe methods such as GET. A cross-site POST is excluded, which is exactly the CSRF case Lax was designed to stop.

options.text: Yes, unless the cookie is also HttpOnly
options.explanation: HttpOnly only hides the cookie from JavaScript. It has no effect on which requests carry the cookie.

options.text: No, because the request is a cross-site POST, which Lax excludes
options.explanation: Correct. Lax sends cookies on cross-site top-level GET navigations (following a link) but not on cross-site POSTs, iframes, images or fetches.

options.text: No, because cookies are never sent to a different origin than the current page
options.explanation: Cookie host matching uses the destination. SameSite=None;Secure could permit this request to carry a cookie, but other cookie and privacy policies can still block it.

questions.workedExample:
1. Is the request cross-site? Page site: `https://evil.example`; target site: `https://bank.example`. Different registrable domains, so yes.
2. SameSite=Lax rule: attach on cross-site requests only if it is a top-level navigation **and** the method is safe (GET, HEAD).
3. The method is POST, so the cookie is withheld.
4. The bank receives an unauthenticated request and the CSRF fails.

Caveat: if the bank changed state on a GET, a simple cross-site link could still trigger it under Lax.

questions.prompt: A shop's product page on `https://www.shop.example` makes 61 HTTP/1.1 requests to that same host: the HTML and 60 images. Each request carries a 2,500-byte `Cookie` header (a large `prefs` cookie plus the session cookie, both host-only). Users on weak mobile uplinks report slow loads. Which changes directly reduce the repeated cookie bytes sent? Select all that apply.

options.text: Serve the images from a separate host, such as `img.shop-static.example`, that these cookies are not scoped to
options.explanation: Correct. Host-only cookies for www.shop.example are not sent to another host, so the 60 image requests stop carrying 2,500 bytes each.

options.text: Add `HttpOnly` to both cookies
options.explanation: HttpOnly hides a cookie from script APIs such as document.cookie. The browser still attaches it to every eligible HTTP request, so the upload is unchanged.

options.text: Add `SameSite=Strict` to both cookies
options.explanation: The image requests are same-site requests from the shop's own page, so SameSite does not withhold the cookies. It controls cross-site sending, not request size.

options.text: Replace the large `prefs` cookie with server-side storage keyed by a short session ID
options.explanation: Correct. Every eligible request still sends a Cookie header, but it now carries a few dozen bytes instead of 2,500.

options.text: Raise `Max-Age` so the browser stops re-sending cookies it has already sent
options.explanation: Max-Age sets how long the browser keeps a cookie. HTTP/1.1 has no 'already sent' state: a stored, eligible cookie is attached to every request.

questions.workedExample:
1. In HTTP/1.1 the browser attaches every eligible cookie to **every** request, so 61 requests × 2,500 bytes is roughly 150 kB of repeated upload.
2. Ask which changes affect *whether* a cookie is attached or *how big* it is.
3. Scope: a host-only cookie for www.shop.example is not sent to a different host, so moving the images removes 60 copies.
4. Size: a short session ID shrinks every copy.
5. HttpOnly (script access), SameSite (cross-site sending; these are same-site requests) and Max-Age (lifetime) do not change what this page uploads.

HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 header compression can also shrink repeats, but savings depend on the encoder's table decisions, and sensitive cookies may be sent without indexing.

questions.prompt: Your app runs at `https://www.example.com`. An old marketing microsite at `promo.example.com` is hosted by a third party and could be compromised. Which session-cookie choices stop the microsite from **overwriting or reading** your session cookie? Assume a browser that enforces cookie prefixes, HTTPS on both hosts, and no compromise of www itself. Select all that apply.

options.text: Name it `__Host-sid` and set `Path=/; Secure` with no `Domain`
options.explanation: Correct. The browser only accepts a `__Host-` cookie that is host-only, Secure and Path=/, so `promo.example.com` cannot set one that would be sent to `www`, nor will it receive yours.

options.text: Set `Domain=example.com` so the scope is explicit
options.explanation: This is the worst option: it sends your session cookie to `promo.example.com` too.

options.text: Set `HttpOnly`
options.explanation: HttpOnly blocks non-HTTP script cookie access, but does not change Domain scope or stop a sibling server setting an ordinary parent-domain cookie with the same unprefixed name.

options.text: Set `SameSite=Strict`
options.explanation: `promo.example.com` and `www.example.com` are the **same site** (same eTLD+1), so SameSite gives no protection between them.

questions.workedExample: A parent-domain cookie may be sent to the sibling; a host-only cookie avoids that host match. A sibling can also set an ordinary parent-domain cookie with the same name, producing ambiguous same-name cookies at www. Server parsing varies. In the stated supporting browser, __Host-sid must be Secure, host-only and Path=/, so the sibling cannot set a parent-domain version. This is browser storage enforcement, not proof that an arbitrary client’s Cookie header is authentic. SameSite does not isolate these HTTPS sibling hosts; same-host ports are not isolated by cookie prefixes either.

lessons.title: HTTP/2 frame headers and pseudo-headers
lessons.summary: HTTP/2 interleaves streams over one TCP connection using fixed nine-byte frame headers.
lessons.body:
HTTP/2 keeps HTTP methods, statuses and headers but changes their wire representation. Reading a frame requires separating its fixed header from its length-delimited payload.

## HTTP/2: binary frames on one connection

HTTP/2 ([RFC 9113](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113)) keeps HTTP's semantics (methods, status codes, headers) but replaces the text format with binary **HTTP/2 frames**. Each HTTP/2 frame addresses an **HTTP/2 stream** or the connection (stream ID 0). HTTP request/response exchanges use streams; connection-control HTTP/2 frames are not individual requests. Many streams interleave on one TCP connection.

### The connection preface

Over TLS, the client and server agree on HTTP/2 through ALPN (the token `h2`). The client then sends a fixed 24-byte magic string, followed by a SETTINGS frame:

```
PRI * HTTP/2.0\r\n\r\nSM\r\n\r\n
```

The string is chosen so that an HTTP/1.1 server that receives it by mistake fails loudly rather than misinterpreting HTTP/2 frames.

### The frame header

Every frame starts with exactly **9 bytes**:

```
+-----------------------------+
| Length (24 bits)            |
+--------------+--------------+
| Type (8)     | Flags (8)    |
+-+------------+--------------+
|R| Stream Identifier (31)    |
+-+---------------------------+
| Payload (Length bytes) ...  |
+-----------------------------+
```

- **Length** is the payload size, excluding the 9-byte header. The default maximum is **16,384 bytes** (16 KiB); a peer can raise it with `SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE` up to the largest number a 24-bit field can hold, 16,777,215 bytes (just under 16 MiB).
- **Stream ID 0** is the connection itself, used for connection-control HTTP/2 frames. **Client-initiated streams are odd** (1, 3, 5...), server-initiated ones even. IDs only increase and are never reused. The 31-bit field tops out at about 2.1 billion, so one connection can open about 1.07 billion client streams; a long-lived connection that runs out must be replaced.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Labelled parcels sharing one van
> A courier packs parcels for many customers into one van. Every parcel carries the same small label: how big it is, what kind of item it is, and which customer it belongs to. Notes for the depot itself are addressed to customer 0.
>
> **How it maps:** The van is the single TCP connection, each parcel is a frame, and the label is the fixed 9-byte header: length, type, flags and stream ID. A customer's parcels are one stream, and customer 0 is the connection-control traffic on stream 0. Because every label has the same layout, the receiver can always find where one frame ends and the next begins.
>
> **Where it stops:** A real courier who loses one parcel can still hand over the others. TCP cannot: it delivers bytes strictly in order, so one lost segment holds back every later HTTP/2 frame, whatever its stream, until it is resent. The QUIC units return to this limit.

The frame types:

| Type | Name | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 0x0 | DATA | Body bytes |
| 0x1 | HEADERS | Header block |
| 0x3 | RST_STREAM | Cancel one stream |
| 0x4 | SETTINGS | Connection parameters |
| 0x5 | PUSH_PROMISE | Server push |
| 0x6 | PING | Liveness, RTT |
| 0x7 | GOAWAY | Graceful shutdown |
| 0x8 | WINDOW_UPDATE | Flow control |
| 0x9 | CONTINUATION | More header block |

(0x2, PRIORITY, is deprecated.) Important flags are `END_STREAM` (0x1, this side is done), `END_HEADERS` (0x4) and `ACK` (0x1 on SETTINGS and PING).

A bodyless GET whose field block fits in one frame can use HEADERS with END_HEADERS and END_STREAM (0x05). Larger field blocks use CONTINUATION frames. A response may end on HEADERS, DATA or trailing HEADERS; informational responses and trailers add further possibilities.

```
00 00 0d   length 13
01         type HEADERS
05         END_STREAM|END_HEADERS
00 00 00 01 stream 1
<13 bytes of HPACK>
```

### Pseudo-headers

The request line becomes **pseudo-header fields**, which start with a colon and must come first: `:method`, `:scheme`, `:authority` (replacing `Host`) and `:path`. Responses have `:status`. All header names must be **lowercase**, and connection-specific headers (`Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Transfer-Encoding`) are forbidden.

## Key takeaways
- HTTP/2 interleaves streams over one TCP connection using fixed nine-byte frame headers.
- Stream IDs and pseudo-headers identify exchanges; lowercase names and field rules still apply.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9113](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113)

questions.prompt:
An HTTP/2 frame begins with these 9 bytes:

```
00 00 10 00 01 00 00 00 03
```

What is it?

options.text: A 10-byte HEADERS frame on stream 1
options.explanation: This reads the hex length `10` as decimal and confuses the flags byte with the type. The fourth byte (`00`) is the type, DATA.

options.text: A 16-byte SETTINGS frame on the connection (stream 0)
options.explanation: SETTINGS is type 0x4, and it must use stream 0. The last four bytes here say stream 3.

options.text: A DATA frame on stream 3 whose payload is 4,096 bytes
options.explanation: The 24-bit length is `00 00 10`, i.e. 0x000010 = 16, not 0x1000.

options.text: A DATA frame with 16 payload bytes on stream 3 and END_STREAM set
options.explanation: Correct. Length `00 00 10` = 16, type `00` = DATA, flags `01` = END_STREAM, stream ID `00 00 00 03` = 3.

questions.workedExample:
Split the 9 bytes by field:

```
00 00 10    length  = 0x10 = 16
00          type    = DATA
01          flags   = END_STREAM
00 00 00 03 R + stream ID = 3
```

The length field is hexadecimal, so `00 00 10` is sixteen, not ten: 16 payload bytes follow the 9-byte header.

Stream 3 is odd, so the client opened it. A DATA frame with END_STREAM from the client means this is the last chunk of a request body (for example a POST).

lessons.title: HTTP/2 credit, shutdown and reset abuse
lessons.summary: Stream and connection windows both limit DATA; credit feedback can constrain throughput.
lessons.body:
### Flow control

**HTTP/2 flow control** applies **per stream and per connection**, on top of TCP's receive credit. Before settings, each has a **65,535-byte** window. SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE adjusts stream windows; the connection window is enlarged with WINDOW_UPDATE. Sending DATA uses up window; the receiver returns credit with WINDOW_UPDATE. Only DATA payloads count, including their pad-length and padding bytes, but excluding the 9-byte frame header.

This lets a proxy stop one slow download from filling its buffers without stalling the other streams. It also caps speed. The sender can have at most one window of unacknowledged DATA outstanding, and fresh credit takes a round trip to come back, so in an ideal model with prompt credit return and no other bottleneck:

```formula essential
T_max ≈ W / RTT
where
T_max: the highest sustained rate the window allows, in bytes per second (B/s)
W: the flow-control window, in bytes (B); 65,535 B unless SETTINGS or WINDOW_UPDATE changes it
RTT: the round-trip time for DATA to reach the receiver and its WINDOW_UPDATE credit to come back, in seconds (s)
≈: approximately equal to; this is an upper bound under ideal assumptions
B: bytes
s: seconds
In words: at most one window of data can be delivered per round trip, so the ceiling grows with a bigger window and shrinks with a longer round trip, regardless of link speed.
```

With the default 64 KiB window and a 100 ms round trip, one stream tops out near 5 Mbit/s even on a gigabit link. Doubling the window or halving the RTT doubles the ceiling; delayed credit and other bottlenecks lower it. Because both windows apply, a receiver that wants faster transfers must raise the stream window (SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE or WINDOW_UPDATE on the stream) **and** give enough connection credit (WINDOW_UPDATE on stream 0). Opening more streams does not help when the shared connection window is the limit.

### GOAWAY, RST_STREAM and Rapid Reset

GOAWAY reports the highest peer-initiated stream ID on which the sender might have acted or might still act. Higher-numbered requests were not processed and may be retried; lower-numbered unfinished requests may have ambiguous outcomes. That makes graceful restarts possible.

`RST_STREAM` cancels one stream cheaply. In 2023 attackers abused this in the **Rapid Reset** attack (CVE-2023-44487): open a stream with HEADERS, immediately reset it, repeat. The stream never counts against `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` for long, but the server still starts work on each request. Google reported a peak of about 398 million requests per second. Mitigations can limit abusive creation/reset work or terminate offending connections; deployed protection depends on implementation and configuration.

### Priorities and push

RFC 9113 deprecated the original tree-based priority scheme. Its replacement ([RFC 9218](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9218)) is a simple `priority` header, such as `u=1, i` (urgency 0 to 7, default 3; `i` means incremental). Chrome’s published removal rationale included limited performance benefit and cache-related waste; it disabled HTTP/2 server push by default starting with Chrome 106 in 2022. Other clients and non-browser use differ.

## Key takeaways
- Stream and connection windows both limit DATA; credit feedback can constrain throughput.
- GOAWAY distinguishes unprocessed higher stream IDs from potentially acted-on lower IDs.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9113](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113)
- [RFC 9218](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9218)
- [Google: Rapid Reset research](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/how-it-works-the-novel-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack)
- [Chrome server-push removal](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/removing-push/)

questions.prompt: A client downloads one large file over HTTP/2 from a server 150 ms away and gets a steady 3.5 Mbit/s on an otherwise idle 1 Gbit/s path. CPU, TCP's windows and congestion control are not limiting. The client never changed HTTP/2 flow-control settings, so its stream and connection windows are both 65,535 bytes and it returns credit only as it consumes data. Which change most directly raises this ceiling?

options.text: Split the download into several byte-range requests on more streams of the same connection
options.explanation: Each new stream gets its own 65,535-byte stream window, but all DATA also draws on the single 65,535-byte connection window. That shared window still caps the total at about one window per round trip.

options.text: Ask the server to send larger DATA frames by raising SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE
options.explanation: Frame size changes how DATA is chopped up, not how much credit the sender has. The window, not the frame size, limits bytes in flight.

options.text: Send HTTP/2 PING frames more often to keep the connection warm
options.explanation: PING measures liveness and round-trip time. It grants no flow-control credit, so the ceiling is unchanged.

options.text: Have the client advertise a much larger stream window and send WINDOW_UPDATE on stream 0 to enlarge the connection window
options.explanation: Correct. At most one window can be delivered per round trip: 65,535 bytes every 0.15 s is about 3.5 Mbit/s. A bigger stream window (SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE or WINDOW_UPDATE) plus enough connection credit raises that ceiling.

questions.workedExample:
1. Spot the symptom: a steady rate far below link capacity, with nothing else limiting, points to a credit ceiling.
2. The lesson relationship: at most one window of DATA per round trip. A 65,535-byte window every 150 ms is about 437 kilobytes per second, roughly 3.5 Mbit/s, which matches the observation.
3. Two windows apply to every DATA frame: the stream's and the connection's. Both start at 65,535 bytes.
4. More streams add stream credit but not connection credit, so the total stays capped. Frame size and PING do not grant credit.
5. Fix: the client (the receiver here) raises its stream window and sends WINDOW_UPDATE on stream 0 so the connection window is large too. A client that never changes the defaults stays at this ceiling however fast the link is.

questions.prompt: Which of these are true of the HTTP/2 Rapid Reset attack (CVE-2023-44487)? Select all that apply.

options.text: The attacker sends HEADERS and immediately RST_STREAM, repeating at high rate
options.explanation: Correct. Each stream is opened and cancelled at once.

options.text: It evades SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS because reset streams stop counting as open
options.explanation: Correct. The concurrency limit counts open streams; a stream reset straight away is closed, so the client can open another immediately.

options.text: It requires breaking TLS
options.explanation: The attacker need not break TLS; it establishes its own legitimate encrypted connections and abuses HTTP/2 stream processing.

options.text: Servers mitigate it by limiting or counting client resets and closing abusive connections
options.explanation: Such controls can help; exact patches and policies differ. Some implementations also budget stream creation and outstanding backend work.

options.text: It works because HPACK lets the attacker forge other users' stream IDs
options.explanation: Stream IDs are per connection and HPACK only compresses headers. The attack stays within the attacker's own connections.

questions.workedExample: A concurrent-stream cap alone does not bound the rate of stream creation and cancellation. Resets can close protocol streams while dispatched work remains expensive. This can exhaust finite server capacity across attacker connections; it does not imply infinite work or that a single connection produced the reported aggregate attack rate. Mitigations should account for creation/reset work and implementation-specific resource use.
