lessons.title: HPACK tables and indexed fields
lessons.summary: HPACK shares static and dynamic table state independently in each connection direction.
lessons.body:
## HPACK: header compression

HTTP/1.1 headers repeat on every request: the same `user-agent`, `accept` and cookies, hundreds of bytes each time. HPACK ([RFC 7541](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7541)) compresses them using three tools.

**1. An HPACK static table** of 61 common fields, numbered from 1:

| Index | Name | Value |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | :authority | |
| 2 | :method | GET |
| 3 | :method | POST |
| 4 | :path | / |
| 6 | :scheme | http |
| 7 | :scheme | https |
| 8 | :status | 200 |

**2. An HPACK dynamic table** per connection direction. Fields the encoder chooses to index are added at index **62**, pushing older entries to higher numbers. Both sides charge each entry the same size, so their tables stay identical without any messages about evictions:

```formula reference
E = n + v + 32 B
where
E: the size an entry counts against the dynamic table limit, in bytes (B)
n: the length of the header name, in bytes
v: the length of the header value, in bytes
B: bytes
In words: each stored field costs its name length plus its value length plus a flat 32 bytes of bookkeeping, so short fields cost more table space than their text suggests.
```

When adding an entry would push the total over the limit (default 4,096 bytes), the oldest entries are evicted first. An entry larger than the whole table empties it and is not stored.

**3. Static Huffman coding** for literal strings, with a code tuned to header text. Common characters take 5 or 6 bits.

### Representations

The first bits of each field say what follows:

| Prefix | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `1xxxxxxx` | Indexed: whole field from table |
| `01xxxxxx` | Literal, add to dynamic table |
| `0000xxxx` | Literal, don't index |
| `0001xxxx` | Literal, never index |

So a field already in a table costs one byte while its index is below 127: the top bit is set and the other seven bits hold the index. `:method: GET` (index 2) is `0x82`, and `:scheme: https` (index 7) is `0x87`. A repeated 300-byte cookie that the encoder chose to index can likewise shrink to a byte or two on later requests, as long as it is still in the table.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A shared numbered phrasebook
> Two colleagues on a long radio link each keep an identical notebook. The first time one says a long phrase, both write it down as the newest entry, numbered 62; afterwards the speaker can just say "entry 62". A printed list of common phrases, numbered 1 to 61, came in both notebooks from the start.
>
> **How it maps:** The printed list is the static table, the handwritten entries are the dynamic table, and "entry 62" is an indexed field. Writing a phrase down is a literal with incremental indexing; saying it without writing it down is a literal without indexing.
>
> **Where it stops:** HPACK renumbers as it goes: the newest entry is always 62, so older entries' numbers grow and the oldest drop off the end. Real notebooks could be compared if they disagreed; HPACK decoders cannot. Both sides must process every field block in the same order and evict the same entries, or every later index points at the wrong field. Each direction of a connection also keeps its own separate table.

## Key takeaways
- HPACK shares static and dynamic table state independently in each connection direction.
- Dynamic entries cost their name and value bytes plus 32 bytes, with oldest-entry eviction.

## Further reading
- [RFC 7541](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7541)

questions.prompt: On one HTTP/2 connection, a browser's first request sends a 300-byte `cookie` field as a literal **with incremental indexing**, so both sides add it to their dynamic tables. The second request carries the identical cookie. Assume the entry has not been evicted and the encoder chooses to reference it. How is the field most likely sent the second time?

options.text: As the full 300-byte literal again, because only static-table fields can be indexed
options.explanation: Dynamic-table entries can be referenced exactly like static ones. Indexing the first copy is what makes the second copy cheap.

options.text: Not at all; the decoder assumes any field missing from a request is unchanged from the previous request
options.explanation: HPACK has no 'same as last time' rule. Each field block lists its fields; the saving comes from referring to a table entry, not from omitting the field.

options.text: As an indexed field: a short reference to the dynamic-table entry, a single byte here
options.explanation: Correct. The entry sits at index 62 or above, so an indexed representation (top bit set, index in the remaining bits) replaces 300 bytes with about one byte while the index stays below 127.

options.text: As a Huffman-coded literal, since Huffman coding is HPACK's only compression
options.explanation: Huffman coding shrinks literal strings, but the big saving for repeated fields comes from the static and dynamic tables.

questions.workedExample:
1. The first request used *literal with incremental indexing*, so encoder and decoder both stored the cookie in their dynamic tables, newest at index 62.
2. On the second request the encoder can send an **indexed field**: one byte with the top bit set and the index in the other seven bits, while the index is below 127.
3. The decoder looks the index up in its own identical table and reconstructs the full field.
4. This only works while both tables agree. If the entry had been evicted, or the encoder chose a never-indexed form for a sensitive cookie, the field would go as a literal again.

This is why HPACK makes repeated headers, such as cookies and user-agent strings, cheap on long-lived connections.

questions.prompt: HPACK counts each dynamic-table entry as its name length plus its value length plus 32 bytes. An encoder adds `user-agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11)` (name 10 bytes, value 17 bytes) to a dynamic table that already holds 4,050 bytes. The table limit is 4,096. What happens?

options.text: The entry is rejected because it does not fit
options.explanation: An entry is only rejected (with the whole table emptied) if it is larger than the entire table limit. Otherwise old entries are evicted to make room.

options.text: The new entry is added with a size of 27 bytes, so it fits without eviction
options.explanation: This forgets the 32-byte per-entry overhead HPACK adds. 4,050 + 27 would fit, but the real size is 59.

options.text: The oldest entries are evicted until the new 59-byte entry fits within 4,096 bytes
options.explanation: Correct. Entry size is 10 + 17 + 32 = 59 bytes. The table needs at least 13 bytes freed, so it evicts oldest entries (one or more) until the new entry fits.

options.text: The table grows beyond 4,096 until the peer sends a SETTINGS update
options.explanation: The limit is a hard bound the encoder and decoder both enforce. Exceeding it would desynchronise the tables.

questions.workedExample:
1. Size the new entry with the stated rule: 10 + 17 + 32 = 59 bytes, not 27.
2. 4,050 + 59 = 4,109 bytes would exceed the 4,096-byte limit by 13 bytes.
3. HPACK evicts from the oldest end (the highest index) until the new entry fits. Every entry costs at least 32 bytes, so evicting the single oldest entry already frees enough.
4. The new entry goes in at index 62; everything else shifts up.

Both sides run the same algorithm on the same field blocks, so the decoder's table stays identical without any explicit eviction messages. Only an entry larger than the whole table is not stored, and that case empties the table.

lessons.title: HPACK integer prefixes and a header-block trace
lessons.summary: HPACK fills a bit prefix, then sends any remainder in little-endian seven-bit groups.
lessons.body:
HPACK compresses HTTP/2 fields using shared tables. The static table has 61 entries; newly indexed dynamic fields start at 62. An indexed representation sets its top bit, while a literal representation carries a name or name index and a value. This unit follows the integer encoding and one complete field block.

Integers use an **N-bit prefix**: the first byte has a few bits left over for the number (5 bits in the example below; the RFC calls this count N). If the value is smaller than the all-ones pattern of those bits, it is stored directly in them. Otherwise the prefix is set to all ones and the remainder follows in 7-bit groups, least significant first, with the top bit of each byte meaning "more follows".

For 1337 with a 5-bit prefix: five bits hold at most 31, so the prefix is set to 31 (the "more follows" marker) and 1306 remains. Its low seven bits are 26, sent as 154 (26 with the continue bit, worth 128, set); the rest is 10, sent as a final byte without the continue bit. The decoder reverses this: 31, plus 26, plus 10 lots of 128, gives 1337.

The same integer-prefix algorithm in Python:

```python
def enc_int(value, n):
    if (type(value) is not int or value < 0
            or type(n) is not int
            or not 1 <= n <= 8):
        raise ValueError("bad integer")
    # All ones marks continuation.
    limit = (1 << n) - 1
    if value < limit:
        return [value]
    out = [limit]
    # Only encode the remaining value.
    value -= limit
    # Emit low groups with a continue bit.
    while value >= 128:
        out.append(value % 128 + 128)
        value //= 128
    # The final group has no continue bit.
    out.append(value)
    return out

print(enc_int(10, 5))    # [10]
print(enc_int(1337, 5))  # [31, 154, 10]
```

The design keeps small numbers to a single byte, which matters because most indexes and string lengths in a header block are small.

### Decoding a real header block

The first request in RFC 7541's examples is:

```
82 86 84 41 0f 77 77 77 2e 65 78
61 6d 70 6c 65 2e 63 6f 6d
```

1. `82`: indexed 2, `:method: GET`.
2. `86`: indexed 6, `:scheme: http`.
3. `84`: indexed 4, `:path: /`.
4. `41` = `01 000001`: literal with indexing, name from index 1 (`:authority`).
5. `0f`: a 15-byte string, not Huffman-coded (top bit 0): `www.example.com`.

The decoder adds `:authority: www.example.com` to the dynamic table at index 62. That entry costs 57 bytes of table space (10 name bytes, 15 value bytes and HPACK's 32-byte overhead). The literal took 17 bytes on the wire (the `41` byte, the `0f` length byte and 15 bytes of text); once stored, a later request can send the single byte `be` (index 62 with the top bit set) instead. That saving applies only while the entry is still at index 62 and the encoder chooses to reference it.

### Why "never index" exists

The 2012 **CRIME** attack showed that compressing secrets alongside attacker-controlled data leaks the secret through compressed sizes. HPACK resists this because table entries match only whole fields, but an attacker who can inject guesses can still test whether a guessed field value is already in the table. The **never-indexed** form tells every hop, including proxies re-encoding the headers, not to put a value such as a short cookie or `authorization` token in a table.

## Key takeaways
- HPACK fills a bit prefix, then sends any remainder in little-endian seven-bit groups.
- A never-indexed representation tells re-encoding intermediaries to keep the field out of dynamic tables.

## Further reading
- [RFC 7541](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7541)

questions.prompt: The lesson encoder uses a five-bit prefix. How does it represent the integer 31, before adding any representation-type bits?

options.explanation: All-ones prefix is a continuation marker, so a zero remainder still needs a following byte.
The prefix is filled with 31; the zero remainder is encoded as a final continuation byte.
The first byte carries the prefix marker, rather than a zero followed by the original value.
A continuation byte with its high bit set promises another byte and cannot terminate this integer.

questions.workedExample:
1. Five prefix bits have an all-ones value of 31.
2. Values strictly below 31 fit directly. Equality takes the continuation path.
3. Subtracting the prefix value leaves zero. The encoder appends that final zero byte, giving [31, 0].

lessons.title: QUIC packets, protection and amplification limits
lessons.summary: QUIC adds reliable streams above UDP and protects payloads plus selected header bits.
lessons.body:
## QUIC and HTTP/3

HTTP/2's streams are independent in the protocol but not on the wire. TCP delivers one ordered byte stream, so when a segment carrying part of one response is lost, every later byte waits for the retransmission, including bytes of other responses that arrived safely. On a lossy mobile link one loss can briefly stall every request on the connection. This is transport-level **head-of-line blocking**; already delivered data remains usable. QUIC ([RFC 9000](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)) moves streams, reliability and congestion control into a UDP-based protocol with TLS 1.3 built in. HTTP/3 ([RFC 9114](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114)) maps HTTP onto it.

### Packets and QUIC frames

A UDP datagram carries one or more QUIC **packets**. Protected data packets carry **QUIC frames** (Retry and Version Negotiation have different payload formats): STREAM (data), ACK, CRYPTO (TLS handshake bytes), MAX_DATA and MAX_STREAM_DATA (flow control), NEW_CONNECTION_ID, PATH_CHALLENGE / PATH_RESPONSE, CONNECTION_CLOSE and so on.

There are two header formats:

- **Long header** (first bit 1), used during the handshake. Types: Initial, 0-RTT, Handshake and Retry. It carries the version and both connection IDs, with their lengths.
- **Short header** (first bit 0), used for 1-RTT data once the appropriate keys are available, potentially before handshake confirmation. It carries only the **Destination Connection ID** (whose length the receiver already knows) and the packet number.

```
Short header (1-RTT)
+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+
|0|1|S|R|R|K|P P|  first byte
+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+
| Dest Conn ID (0-160 bits)  |
| Packet Number (8-32 bits)  |
| Protected payload ...      |
```

In this wire diagram, S is the optional spin bit, R marks reserved bits, K is the key-phase bit and the two P bits encode a packet-number length of one, two, three or four bytes. The first zero selects the short-header form and the following fixed bit is one in QUIC version 1. The receiver already knows the connection-ID length from connection state.

The payload is encrypted. Header protection masks the packet number and selected low bits of the first byte (five for short headers, four for protected long headers). Connection IDs and other routing fields remain visible; the short-header spin bit is also outside that mask. This reduces what middleboxes can depend on, without making traffic untrackable or all headers confidential.

Initial packets are encrypted too, but with keys derived from the Destination Connection ID and a published salt, so anyone on the path can decrypt them. Initial protection does not authenticate the peer against a party able to derive those public keys; TLS authenticates the handshake.

UDP has no handshake, so a server cannot tell whether a new client's source address is genuine. An attacker could spoof a victim's address and make the server send its large handshake reply to the victim. QUIC limits this in two ways:

- A client must expand the **UDP payload** of each datagram carrying Initial packets to at least 1,200 bytes, by padding or coalescing packets.
- Until the server has validated the client's address, it may send at most **three times** the bytes it has received from that address. One 1,200-byte Initial therefore allows at most 3,600 bytes in reply.

A large certificate chain can hit that limit. The server then waits for more bytes from the client (its acknowledgements and probes also count) or for address validation, which can cost an extra round trip; RFC 9000 requires clients to keep sending on a probe timeout so the two sides cannot deadlock. The limit bounds pre-validation amplification; it does not eliminate denial-of-service attacks or all reflection.

## Key takeaways
- QUIC adds reliable streams above UDP and protects payloads plus selected header bits.
- Publicly derived Initial keys do not authenticate a peer; address validation bounds server amplification.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9000](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)
- [RFC 9001](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001)
- [RFC 9114](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114)

questions.prompt: A QUIC server receives one 1,200-byte Initial datagram from a new, unvalidated client address. Its TLS certificate chain makes its first flight about 5,000 bytes. What does RFC 9000 allow it to do?

options.text: Send all 5,000 bytes at once, because Initial packets are encrypted
options.explanation: Initial keys are derived from public values, so anyone can decrypt Initial packets, and encryption does nothing to show that the source address is genuine. The amplification limit still applies.

options.text: Send nothing until the client completes a Retry exchange
options.explanation: Retry is an optional tool a server may use to validate addresses first. Without it, the server can still reply within the three-times budget.

options.text: Send up to 3,600 bytes, then wait until more client bytes arrive or the address is validated before sending the rest
options.explanation: Correct. Before validation the server may send at most three times what it has received. The client's later datagrams (acknowledgements, probes, Handshake packets) raise the budget or validate the address, which can cost a round trip.

options.text: Send 5,000 bytes, because the limit applies only to Version Negotiation packets
options.explanation: The anti-amplification rule covers everything the server sends to an unvalidated address, not one packet type.

questions.workedExample:
1. The address is new and unvalidated, so the server cannot know whether it is the real sender or a spoofed victim.
2. RFC 9000 caps what it may send to three times the bytes received: 3 × 1,200 bytes allows 3,600 bytes.
3. The 5,000-byte flight does not fit, so the server sends what it can and stops.
4. The client's next datagrams (for example padded Initial acknowledgements, or a probe after a timeout) add to the received count, and a Handshake packet from the client validates the address. Then the server can finish.
5. Practical effect: a very large certificate chain can add a round trip to a QUIC handshake. Smaller chains, or certificate compression (RFC 8879), can avoid it.

The point of the rule: a spoofed 1,200-byte packet can trigger at most about 3,600 bytes towards a victim.

lessons.title: Decoding QUIC variable-length integers
lessons.summary: QUIC varints use two length bits followed by a big-endian integer in one, two, four or eight bytes.
lessons.body:
QUIC frames carry fields such as stream IDs and byte counts. Many fields use the variable-length integer format defined in RFC 9000; its length marker differs from HPACK continuation bits.

### Variable-length integers

QUIC encodes most numbers as **varints**. The top two bits of the first byte give the total length:

| Bits | Bytes | Max value |
|---|---|---|
| 00 | 1 | 63 |
| 01 | 2 | 16,383 |
| 10 | 4 | ~1.07 billion |
| 11 | 8 | ~4.6 quintillion |

Each maximum is simply the largest number that fits in the bits left after the two length bits: 6, 14, 30 or 62 bits. Values up to 63, common for small counts and lengths, cost one byte, while the format can still carry very large byte offsets.

Except where a field imposes its own shortest-encoding rule, QUIC varints need not use the shortest representation. For example, 37 can be the one byte `25` or the two bytes `40 25`. QUIC frame-type fields require the shortest form.

To decode, read the top two bits of the first byte to learn the length, clear those two bits (AND with `0x3F`), then append each following byte as the next 8 bits, most significant first. For `7b bd`, the top bits `01` say 2 bytes; clearing them turns `7b` into `3b` (59), and `3b bd` read as one big-endian number is 15,293.

```python
def varint(data):
    if not data:
        raise ValueError("empty varint")
    # Top bits select 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes.
    length = 1 << (data[0] >> 6)
    if len(data) < length:
        raise ValueError("truncated varint")
    # Remove the two length bits.
    v = data[0] & 0x3F
    for b in data[1:length]:
        # Append the next big-endian byte.
        v = (v << 8) | b
    return v, length

print(varint(bytes.fromhex("25")))
# (37, 1)
print(varint(bytes.fromhex("7bbd")))
# (15293, 2)
```

## Key takeaways
- QUIC varints use two length bits followed by a big-endian integer in one, two, four or eight bytes.
- A decoder must check the available length before consuming the selected representation.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9000](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)

questions.prompt: Decode the QUIC variable-length integer `0x40 0x25`.

options.explanation: That is 0x4025 read as a plain 16-bit integer, forgetting to strip the two length bits.

options.text: 37, using 2 bytes
options.explanation: Correct. Top bits `01` mean 2 bytes. Masking them leaves `0x0025` = 37. It is a valid but non-minimal encoding of 37.

options.text: 64, followed by a separate value 37
options.explanation: The first byte's top bits `01` say the integer is 2 bytes long, so both bytes are one value.

options.text: Invalid, because 37 must be encoded in one byte
options.explanation: RFC 9000 allows non-minimal encodings in most places (its own examples show 37 as `0x4025`); senders usually use the shortest form.

questions.workedExample:
1. First byte `0x40` = `01000000`. Top two bits `01` → length 2 bytes.
2. Remaining 6 bits of byte one: `000000`.
3. Combine with byte two: `000000 00100101` = 0x0025 = **37**.

Once the two length bits are cleared, the first byte contributes nothing, and the second byte, hex `25`, is 37.

The same value in one byte is `0x25` (top bits `00`, value 37 ≤ 63).

lessons.title: QUIC stream IDs, QPACK and loss recovery
lessons.summary: QUIC stream IDs encode initiator and direction in their two low bits.
lessons.body:
QUIC carries several independently ordered byte streams over a connection. HTTP/3 maps requests to client-initiated bidirectional streams and uses dedicated streams for control and QPACK compression state.

### Streams

Stream IDs are varints whose two low bits encode the type: `0x0` client-initiated bidirectional, `0x1` server-initiated bidirectional, `0x2` client unidirectional, `0x3` server unidirectional. The remaining bits count streams of that type, so each type uses every fourth number. Either side can therefore open a new stream (within the peer's advertised stream limit) without a separate setup exchange, and the ID alone tells the receiver who opened it and whether it can reply on it.

Each stream is ordered on its own. When a packet is lost, only the streams that had data in that packet wait for the retransmission; other streams keep delivering. This is how HTTP/3 avoids the transport-level head-of-line blocking that HTTP/2 suffers over TCP. The benefit is partial: a packet carrying QUIC frames from several streams blocks all of them, so senders avoid mixing more streams into a packet than they need. All streams also still share one connection's congestion control and flow-control limits.

So client request streams are 0, 4, 8... HTTP/3 uses unidirectional streams for its control stream and for **QPACK** ([RFC 9204](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9204)), HPACK's successor. HPACK assumes headers arrive in order; QPACK sends table updates on dedicated streams and declares dependencies. Header blocks that reference unavailable dynamic entries can still block; encoders can avoid such references or bound the number of blocked streams.

### Packet numbers and loss recovery

TCP's sequence numbers count bytes, and a retransmission reuses them, so when an ACK arrives the sender cannot tell whether it acknowledges the original or the retransmission. TCP avoids ambiguous samples using rules such as Karn’s algorithm; timestamps can also disambiguate samples.

QUIC packet numbers increase and are never reused **within each number space**. Required lost information is carried in new packets; it need not preserve old frame boundaries, and not every frame type is retransmitted. ACK ranges identify transmissions, avoiding TCP’s retransmission ambiguity. ACK-delay correction follows RFC 9002 rules; reported delay and scheduling can still affect estimates. There are three separate **packet number spaces**: Initial, Handshake and application data. There are four encryption levels: 0-RTT and 1-RTT share the application-data number space.

## Key takeaways
- QUIC stream IDs encode initiator and direction in their two low bits.
- Packet numbers identify transmissions within three number spaces; lost data can move to new packets.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9000](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)
- [RFC 9002](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9002)
- [RFC 9204](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9204)

questions.prompt: A QUIC sender's packet 7 carrying STREAM data for bytes 1000–1999 is declared lost. Assume those bytes remain needed, unacknowledged elsewhere, and the stream has not been reset. Which retransmission is valid?

options.text: A new packet (e.g. number 12) with a STREAM frame for bytes 1000–1999, possibly combined with other QUIC frames
options.explanation: Correct. Required stream bytes are carried in a new packet number within that number space. Their framing may be split or combined; retransmission need not reproduce the old STREAM frame.

options.text: Packet 7 again, byte for byte, so the receiver can match it
options.explanation: QUIC never reuses packet numbers. Resending packet 7 would bring back TCP's retransmission ambiguity.

options.text: Nothing; QUIC streams are unreliable like UDP
options.explanation: Ordinary QUIC streams provide reliable ordered byte delivery unless reset or the connection fails. RFC 9221 DATAGRAM is an extension for unreliable application datagrams.

options.text: The whole stream from byte 0, because QUIC uses go-back-N
options.explanation: QUIC acknowledges packet ranges and resends information still needed for reliable delivery. It does not restart the stream from byte 0 after every gap. Spurious loss or lost ACKs can cause duplicate transmission.

questions.workedExample:
1. Packet numbers increase monotonically in each number space and are never reused.
2. The lost information is a STREAM frame (stream ID, offset 1000, length 1000).
3. The sender puts an equivalent STREAM frame into the next packet it builds, say packet 12, perhaps beside a new ACK frame.
4. The stream **offset** tells the receiver where the bytes go, so the packet number does not need to match.
5. When packet 12 is ACKed, the ACK identifies this transmission rather than a reused packet number. ACK delay, scheduling and estimator rules still matter.

questions.prompt: An HTTP/3 page fetches three images on the client's first three request streams, IDs 0, 4 and 8. One packet is lost, and it carried only stream 4's data. Assume no other loss. What happens next, compared with the same page over HTTP/2 on one TCP connection?

options.text: Streams 0 and 8 keep delivering while stream 4 waits for its retransmission; over HTTP/2 on TCP all three would wait behind the gap
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC orders each stream separately, so only streams with data in the lost packet are blocked. TCP has one ordered byte stream, so a gap holds back every HTTP/2 stream's later bytes.

options.text: All three streams wait, because QUIC delivers the whole connection in order just as TCP does
options.explanation: That describes TCP. QUIC's streams are independently ordered; per-stream ordering is exactly what removes transport-level head-of-line blocking across streams.

options.text: Stream 4's image is abandoned, because QUIC streams are unreliable like UDP
options.explanation: QUIC runs over UDP but its streams are reliable: the lost data is sent again in a new packet. Unreliable delivery needs the separate DATAGRAM extension.

options.text: Streams 0 and 8 stall too, because IDs 0, 4 and 8 share the same type bits and so form one ordered group
options.explanation: The two low bits only record who opened a stream and its direction. Streams of the same type are still ordered independently of each other.

questions.workedExample:
1. IDs 0, 4 and 8 are client-initiated bidirectional streams (low bits `00`), the type HTTP/3 uses for requests. The type bits create no ordering link between them.
2. QUIC keeps a separate byte order for each stream, using each STREAM frame's offset.
3. The lost packet held only stream 4's data, so only stream 4 has a gap. Streams 0 and 8 can hand their data to the application as it arrives.
4. The sender puts the missing stream 4 bytes in a new packet; stream 4 resumes when they arrive.
5. Over HTTP/2, all three streams share one TCP byte stream. The gap left by the lost segment holds back every later byte, whichever stream it belongs to, until the retransmission arrives.

Caveat: if the lost packet had carried QUIC frames from several streams, all of those streams would wait.

questions.prompt: Why does HTTP/3 use QPACK instead of reusing HPACK unchanged?

options.text: HPACK's Huffman code is too slow for QUIC's speeds
options.explanation: QPACK uses the same Huffman code. Speed is not the issue.

options.text: QUIC encrypts headers, so compression is no longer allowed
options.explanation: Encryption does not forbid compression; HTTP/2 over TLS compresses too.

options.text: HPACK is limited to 61 headers
options.explanation: 61 is the size of HPACK's static table, not a limit on headers. QPACK's static table is actually larger (99 entries).

options.text: HPACK assumes header blocks arrive in a single total order; over independent QUIC streams that would reintroduce head-of-line blocking or desynchronise tables
options.explanation: Correct. HPACK's dynamic table updates are implicit in the order of header blocks. QPACK puts table updates on dedicated unidirectional streams and lets each request state which table entries it depends on.

questions.workedExample:
1. HPACK: request A's header block inserts entry 62; request B's block references 62.
2. Within one direction of HTTP/2's ordered TCP field-block sequence, A is decoded before B, so this dependency works.
3. On QUIC, A and B are on different streams. If A's packet is lost, B may arrive first and reference an entry the decoder lacks.
4. Options: block B until A arrives (head-of-line blocking again) or break.
5. QPACK's fix: encoder instructions travel on a separate stream, and each header block declares the table state it needs. Encoders can choose to avoid references that could block.

lessons.title: QUIC address changes and HTTP/3 discovery
lessons.summary: Suitable connection IDs and routing let QUIC retain connection state across some address changes.
lessons.body:
## Connection migration

Ordinary TCP identifies an established connection by its endpoint addresses and ports. A changed externally visible tuple cannot simply continue that connection without additional mechanisms. A brief outage can recover if the tuple and state survive; VPNs, stable addressing or Multipath TCP can change handover behaviour. NAT rebinding can disrupt ordinary TCP, but neither every handover nor every idle period necessarily changes that tuple.

A QUIC connection is identified by **connection IDs**, not addresses. So the server can keep a connection alive when packets arrive from a new address:

```
Client (Wi-Fi 192.0.2.7)    Server
  | 1-RTT DCID=A ----------->|
  .. switches to 5G ........
Client (5G 198.51.100.4)
  | 1-RTT DCID=B ----------->| new path!
  |<---- PATH_CHALLENGE(x) --|
  | PATH_RESPONSE(x) ------->|
  |       path validated     |
```

1. **Spare connection IDs.** When nonzero connection IDs are used, endpoints can issue spare IDs with NEW_CONNECTION_ID. On a deliberate new local-address path, a fresh peer-issued ID avoids linking paths by reusing that ID. It does not prevent correlation by timing, packet sizes or an observer that sees both paths.
2. **Path validation.** The server sends PATH_CHALLENGE with 8 random bytes to the new address and needs them echoed in PATH_RESPONSE. A matching protected response validates reachability on that path. It does not establish a user’s physical location or defeat an attacker that can relay traffic. Until validation, the anti-amplification limit applies.
3. **Congestion state is reset.** The new path may have completely different bandwidth and RTT, so validation normally triggers resetting congestion and RTT state. RFC 9000 permits retaining state for a port-only address change, with caution about potentially different path characteristics.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Moving house without closing your bank account
> When you move, your bank keeps your account because it is identified by an account number, not your address. Before posting statements to the new address, a careful bank sends a random code there and waits for you to read it back.
>
> **How it maps:** The account number is the connection ID, which keeps the QUIC connection alive when the client's address changes. The random code is PATH_CHALLENGE, and reading it back is PATH_RESPONSE. Until the code comes back, the bank sends little to the new address, as the anti-amplification limit requires. Using a fresh connection ID on the new path is like quoting a new reference so observers cannot easily link the two addresses.
>
> **Where it stops:** In QUIC, the connection's encryption keys show that packets come from the same peer; path validation itself only proves that someone at the new address can receive and return packets, which a relay could also do. A bank also does not reset anything when you move, whereas QUIC normally restarts congestion control because the new network may be much slower or faster.

Only the **client** may migrate actively. A server can advertise preferred_address during the handshake. disable_active_migration restricts deliberate migration to the specified server address; it does not prohibit NAT rebinding or a permitted move to the server’s preferred address.

> [!warning] Migration and load balancers
> If a layer-4 load balancer hashes the 4-tuple, a changed tuple may select a different server without connection state; hash collisions or state shared between servers can produce other outcomes. A coordinated CID-aware design can maintain routing across issued IDs, using a mapping or an encoded routing hint. It must also handle Initial routing and ID lifecycle.

## HTTP/3 discovery

A client can learn HTTP/3 support from configuration, cached knowledge, DNS or an `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"` response header, and may then open a QUIC connection. The `HTTPS` DNS record ([RFC 9460](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9460)) can advertise `alpn=h3` before the first connection. Clients can race or fall back to TCP when QUIC is unavailable; policy varies and UDP blocking is one possible cause.

## Key takeaways
- Suitable connection IDs and routing let QUIC retain connection state across some address changes.
- Path validation checks reachability; migration does not guarantee availability or anonymity.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9000](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)
- [RFC 9460](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9460)
- [RFC 7838](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7838)

questions.prompt: A phone on Wi-Fi has an active QUIC connection. It moves to 5G, and its next packet arrives from a new IP address with a new destination connection ID. What must the server do **before** sending large amounts of data to the new address?

options.text: Send PATH_CHALLENGE and wait for a matching PATH_RESPONSE, sending at most limited data meanwhile, then reset congestion state for the new path
options.explanation: Correct. Path validation proves reachability at the new address; until then anti-amplification limits apply. The congestion controller starts afresh because the new path's capacity is unknown.

options.text: Nothing; the connection ID proves the packet is genuine, so it can send at full rate immediately
options.explanation: A connection ID is visible routing information, not authentication. Successful packet authentication uses cryptographic keys, and still does not establish reachability at an unvalidated source address.

options.text: Perform a new TLS handshake to derive fresh keys
options.explanation: Migration keeps the existing keys; no new handshake is needed. That is the whole point.

options.text: Reject the packet, because only the server may migrate
options.explanation: It is the other way round: only the client can actively migrate under RFC 9000.

questions.workedExample:
1. The packet decrypts with the connection's keys and uses a connection ID the server issued, so it belongs to the connection.
2. But the source address could be spoofed: an on-path attacker could rewrite it to aim traffic at a victim.
3. So the server sends PATH_CHALLENGE (8 random bytes) to the new address. An authenticated echo validates path reachability; a relay can also forward traffic, so this is not proof of physical location.
4. Meanwhile it limits what it sends there: until the path is validated, no more than three times the bytes it has received from the new address.
5. After validation it resets cwnd and RTT estimates, since 5G may differ wildly from Wi-Fi.

questions.prompt: You run QUIC behind a layer-4 load balancer that hashes the UDP 4-tuple to pick a backend. Users report HTTP/3 connections dropping when they walk between Wi-Fi and cellular, or after NAT rebinding. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: After migration the 4-tuple changes, so the balancer likely sends packets to a backend with no state for the connection
options.explanation: A changed hash input can select a different backend lacking state. It need not do so on every migration, so confirm the selected backend in logs.

options.text: A coordinated CID-aware routing design can retain the backend across migrations
options.explanation: A mapping or routing information encoded in issued CIDs can keep established-connection packets at the correct backend. Initial packets and ID changes also need coordinated handling.

options.text: Setting `disable_active_migration` stops NAT rebinding from changing the client's address
options.explanation: The parameter restricts deliberate migration under its specified conditions; it cannot stop a NAT rebinding. The resulting changed tuple may map to another backend.

options.text: Because the connection ID is in the clear in short headers, the balancer can read it without decryption keys
options.explanation: Correct. The destination connection ID is not encrypted (it must be readable for routing), though the packet number and payload are protected.

questions.workedExample: A changed tuple may map to another backend without state; confirm this rather than treating it as inevitable. Connection IDs remain visible, so coordinated routing can use them without decrypting QUIC payloads. Nonzero issued IDs, Initial routing and lifecycle changes need handling. disable_active_migration does not stop NAT rebinding.

lessons.title: DNS headers and length-prefixed names
lessons.summary: DNS has a twelve-byte header and four sections; names use length-prefixed labels.
lessons.body:
DNS is a compact binary protocol. Its transaction identifiers and matching rules matter because a resolver must not accept an arbitrary arriving datagram as the answer to its query.

## The message format

Queries and responses share one format: a 12-byte **DNS header** followed by four sections.

```
+---------------------------+
| Header (12 bytes)         |
+---------------------------+
| Question   (QDCOUNT)      |
| Answer     (ANCOUNT RRs)  |
| Authority  (NSCOUNT RRs)  |
| Additional (ARCOUNT RRs)  |
+---------------------------+
```

The header:

```
Flags word (16 bits):
+--+------+--+--+--+--+---+-----+
|QR|Opcode|AA|TC|RD|RA| Z |RCODE|
| 1|  4   | 1| 1| 1| 1| 3 |  4  |
+--+------+--+--+--+--+---+-----+

Header: six 16-bit fields, in order
ID, flags, QDCOUNT, ANCOUNT,
NSCOUNT, ARCOUNT
```

- **ID**: chosen by the client and copied into the response. It is how a client matches answers to questions over connectionless UDP.
- **QR**: 0 query, 1 response. The **DNS opcode** is almost always 0 (standard query).
- **AA**: authoritative answer. **TC**: truncated. **RD**: recursion desired (set by stub clients). The **RA bit**: recursion available.
- The Z bits now include **AD** (authenticated data) and **CD** (checking disabled) for DNSSEC.
- **RCODE**: 0 NOERROR, 1 FORMERR, 2 SERVFAIL, 3 NXDOMAIN, 5 REFUSED.

### What a resolver does with "no such name"

Two different negative answers are easy to confuse:

- **NXDOMAIN** (RCODE 3): the name does not exist at all, for any record type.
- **NODATA**: RCODE 0 (NOERROR) with an empty answer section. The name exists, but has no records of the type asked for, for example an AAAA query for a name that has only an A record.

Resolvers cache negative answers too (**negative caching**, RFC 2308), so a typo'd or missing name does not send a fresh query to the authoritative servers every time. The authoritative server puts the zone's **SOA record** in the authority section, and the negative answer may be cached for the smaller of the SOA record's own TTL and its MINIMUM field. An NXDOMAIN is cached for the name (any type); a NODATA answer only for that name and type. A negative answer without an SOA should not be cached.

The practical consequence: if someone looks up `new.example.com` just before you create it, their resolver can keep answering NXDOMAIN until that negative TTL runs out, even though the record now exists.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A receptionist's "no such person" note
> You ask a receptionist to put you through to a new colleague. The staff list says nobody of that name works there, so the receptionist jots "no such person, recheck after lunch" and gives every later caller the same answer until lunchtime, even if the new colleague starts at 11.
>
> **How it maps:** The receptionist is the recursive resolver, the staff list is the authoritative zone, and "recheck after lunch" is the negative-caching time taken from the zone's SOA record. NXDOMAIN is "nobody of that name"; NODATA is "that person exists but has no desk phone".
>
> **Where it stops:** The resolver does not choose the time freely: it follows the SOA values in the answer (and may cap them further), and the note covers exactly the name, or name and type, that was asked.

### Names as labels

Names are not dotted strings on the wire. Each label is a length byte followed by that many bytes, ending with a zero-length root label:

```
www.example.com  becomes
03 77 77 77 07 65 78 61 6d 70 6c 65
03 63 6f 6d 00
```

A label is at most 63 bytes, and a whole name at most 255 bytes. The 63 comes from the length byte: its top two bits must be `00` (the pattern `11` marks a compression pointer, covered in the next unit), leaving six bits, which count up to 63.

## Key takeaways
- DNS has a twelve-byte header and four sections; names use length-prefixed labels.
- Flag fields describe query or response handling, while a label and whole name have separate length bounds.
- NXDOMAIN (no such name) and NODATA (no records of that type) are both cached for a time set by the zone's SOA record.

## Further reading
- [RFC 1035](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035)
- [RFC 2308](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2308)
- [RFC 4035](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4035)

questions.prompt: How is the name `mail.example.org` encoded in a DNS question?

options.text: `mail.example.org\0` as ASCII with dots
options.explanation: DNS does not send dotted strings; dots are replaced by length bytes before each label.

options.text: `10 mail.example.org`, a single length then the text
options.explanation: There is one length per label, not one for the whole name. A single label is limited to 63 bytes.

options.text: `04 mail 07 example 03 org 00`
options.explanation: Correct. Each label is preceded by its length, and the name ends with a zero-length root label.

options.text: `mail 04 example 07 org 03 00`, lengths after each label
options.explanation: The length must come first so the parser knows how many bytes to read.

questions.workedExample:
1. Split on dots: `mail`, `example`, `org`.
2. Prefix each with its length: 4, 7, 3.
3. End with `00` (the root).

```
04 6d 61 69 6c
07 65 78 61 6d 70 6c 65
03 6f 72 67
00
```

Total 5 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 18 bytes.

questions.prompt: At 10:00 a user's resolver looks up `new.example.com` and receives NXDOMAIN (RCODE 3). The zone's SOA record has a TTL of 3,600 seconds and a MINIMUM field of 600 seconds, and the response carries it in the authority section. At 10:02 you add the name, and your authoritative servers answer for it immediately. At 10:05 the same user, using the same resolver, still gets NXDOMAIN. Assuming the resolver applies no shorter limit of its own, what explains this?

options.text: The resolver cached the NXDOMAIN for the SOA record's TTL, so it will keep answering NXDOMAIN until about 11:00
options.explanation: RFC 2308 uses the smaller of the SOA record's TTL and its MINIMUM field. Here that is 600 seconds, not 3,600.

options.text: Resolvers never cache negative answers, so the authoritative servers must still be returning NXDOMAIN
options.explanation: Negative caching exists precisely so that missing names do not trigger a fresh authoritative query each time. The prompt says the authoritative servers already have the name.

options.text: The resolver cached the NXDOMAIN for the smaller of the SOA TTL and MINIMUM, 600 seconds, so it should start resolving at about 10:10
options.explanation: Correct. The negative answer is reused for its negative-caching time, even though the record now exists. Once it expires, the next lookup goes to the authoritative servers and finds the new name.

options.text: Only AAAA lookups are affected; an A lookup for the name would already succeed
options.explanation: That describes NODATA, which is cached per name and type. NXDOMAIN says the name does not exist at all, so it is reused for every type of that name.

questions.workedExample:
1. RCODE 3 is NXDOMAIN: the whole name does not exist, for any type.
2. The resolver caches negative answers (RFC 2308), using the SOA record the authoritative server put in the authority section.
3. The negative-caching time is the smaller of the SOA record's own TTL (3,600 s) and its MINIMUM field (600 s): 600 seconds, or 10 minutes. RFC 2308 has the authoritative server put that smaller value on the SOA copy in the response.
4. The answer was cached at 10:00, so this resolver keeps answering NXDOMAIN for any type of `new.example.com` until about 10:10, even though the name was added at 10:02.
5. Practical lesson: when you plan to create a name, avoid querying it beforehand, or keep the zone's negative-caching time short. A resolver may also impose its own lower cap.

lessons.title: Build a DNS query and decode compressed names
lessons.summary: A DNS question combines a fixed header, encoded name and four bytes of type/class.
lessons.body:
A DNS name is encoded as a length byte before each label, followed by the zero-length root label. The twelve-byte message header precedes the question. Resource-record names may instead reuse earlier name data through compression pointers.

### Building a query by hand

This builds an ordinary ASCII-label question, not a full resolver. It accepts an optional trailing `.`, checks wire-length bounds, and uses a random DNS transaction ID unless a test ID is supplied. Internationalised presentation names require a suitable IDNA conversion before this restricted encoder.

```python
import secrets, struct

def build_query(name, qtype=1, qid=None):
    if qid is None:
        # Unpredictable sixteen-bit ID.
        qid = secrets.randbelow(65536)
    if (type(qid) is not int
            or not 0 <= qid <= 65535
            or type(qtype) is not int
            or not 0 <= qtype <= 65535):
        raise ValueError("bad field")
    if name == ".":
        labels = []
    else:
        if name.endswith("."):
            name = name[:-1]
        labels = [p.encode("ascii")
                  for p in name.split(".")]
        if any(not 1 <= len(p) <= 63
               for p in labels):
            raise ValueError("bad label")
    # Prefix each label, then add root.
    qname = b"".join(
        bytes([len(p)]) + p
        for p in labels) + b"\0"
    if len(qname) > 255:
        raise ValueError("name too long")
    # ! selects network byte order.
    # RD set; one question, no answers.
    header = struct.pack("!HHHHHH",
        qid, 0x0100, 1, 0, 0, 0)
    # Type plus Internet class end it.
    return header + qname + struct.pack(
        "!HH", qtype, 1)

q = build_query("example.com", qid=0xABCD)
print(len(q))  # 29
print(q[:4].hex(" "))  # ab cd 01 00
```

The 29 bytes are the 12-byte header, 13 bytes of encoded name and 4 bytes of type and class. The encoded name is two bytes longer than the dotted text `example.com` (11 characters): one length byte per label replaces each `.` separator, plus the leading length and the root byte. A hypothetical reply with flags `0x8180` would decode as `QR=1, RD=1, RA=1` and RCODE 0.

### Resource records and compression

Each answer is a **resource record** (RR): name, TYPE (16 bits), CLASS (16), TTL (32-bit seconds), RDLENGTH (16) and RDATA. An A record's RDATA is 4 bytes; AAAA's is 16.

Names repeat constantly in a response, so DNS uses **compression pointers**. A length byte whose top two bits are `11` is not a length: it and the next byte form a 14-bit offset into the message where the rest of the name can be found. An illustrative A answer could begin with this compressed owner name:

```
c0 0c  name: pointer to offset 12
00 01  TYPE A
00 01  CLASS IN
00 00 01 0e  TTL 270 s
00 04  RDLENGTH 4
xx xx xx xx  IPv4 address
```

Clear the two `11` marker bits and the remaining 14 bits are a byte offset from the start of the message: `c0 0c` points to offset 12. The other fields are ordinary big-endian numbers; `00 00 01 0e` is a TTL of 270 seconds.

Offset 12 is where the question's name starts, straight after the header, so `c0 0c` means "example.com". Parsers must guard against pointer loops; a self-referential pointer can otherwise cause an infinite loop or resource exhaustion. Parsers also need bounds and expanded-name-length checks.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: "See note 3" in a footnote
> A book that cites the same long source many times writes it out once, then says "see note 3" each time after that.
>
> **How it maps:** The first full copy of `example.com` in the question is the original note, and `c0 0c` is "see the name at byte 12". A pointer can also stand for the end of a name, so `www` followed by a pointer to `example.com` spells `www.example.com`.
>
> **Where it stops:** A reader would notice a note that only says "see this note". A parser will not, unless it limits how many pointers it follows, insists that pointers lead to earlier bytes, or keeps the expanded name within 255 bytes. A hostile message can otherwise trap it in a loop.

## Key takeaways
- A DNS question combines a fixed header, encoded name and four bytes of type/class.
- Compression pointers are message-relative offsets; parsers also need loop and bounds checks.

## Further reading
- [RFC 1035](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035)

questions.prompt: An answer record's NAME field is the two bytes `c0 0c`. What does it mean?

options.text: A label of length 192
options.explanation: Labels are at most 63 bytes, so a first byte with top bits `11` can't be a length. It marks a compression pointer.

options.text: The root name `.`
options.explanation: The root is a single `00` byte.

options.text: A reference to the 12th record in the answer section
options.explanation: Pointers are byte offsets into the message, not record numbers.

options.text: The name found at byte offset 12 of the message, normally the question's name
options.explanation: Correct. Top bits `11` mark a pointer; the remaining 14 bits (0x000C = 12) are an offset from the start of the message. The question name starts right after the 12-byte header.

questions.workedExample:
1. `c0` = `11000000`. Top two bits `11` → this is a pointer, not a label length.
2. Clear those two marker bits. The remaining 14 bits of `c0 0c` are `0x000c`, which is 12. (In code: `0xc00c & 0x3fff`.)
3. Bytes 0 to 11 are the header, so offset 12 is the first byte of the question name.
4. The record's name is therefore the same as the question, e.g. `example.com`, in 2 bytes instead of 13.

questions.prompt: The lesson's `build_query` rejects any empty label: `www..example.com` raises `ValueError("bad label")`. Suppose a colleague removes that check. What would the encoder then send for `www..example.com`, and why is that a problem?

options.text: It would quietly drop the empty label and send `www.example.com`
options.explanation: Nothing in the encoder skips empty labels; it writes a length byte for every piece produced by `split(".")`, including the empty one.

options.text: A zero length byte after `www`, which a server reads as the root label ending the name, so the question becomes `www.` and the remaining bytes are misread as type, class or garbage
options.explanation: Correct. The empty label encodes as `00`, the same byte as the root label that terminates every name. The server stops reading the name early and misparses everything after it.

options.text: A two-byte compression pointer, because a zero-length label is how DNS marks repeated names
options.explanation: Pointers are marked by a first byte whose top two bits are `11`, such as `c0`. A `00` byte is the root label, not a pointer.

options.text: Nothing different: DNS servers ignore doubled dots, so the check is purely cosmetic
options.explanation: On the wire there are no dots, only length bytes. A doubled dot becomes a zero-length label, which changes where the name ends.

questions.workedExample:
1. `"www..example.com".split(".")` gives `www`, an empty piece, `example` and `com`.
2. Each piece is written as a length byte followed by its bytes, so the empty piece becomes the single byte `00`.
3. Encoded: `03 www 00 07 example 03 com 00`.
4. A server reading the name sees `03 www`, then `00`. A zero length is the root label, so the name is complete: `www.`.
5. It then reads `07 65` as QTYPE and `78 61` as QCLASS, and the rest of the bytes are left over or misread.

The empty-label check (and the 63-byte label and 255-byte name limits) keeps the encoder from producing bytes whose meaning differs from the name the caller asked for.

lessons.title: DNS truncation, EDNS and TCP fallback
lessons.summary: Without EDNS the ordinary UDP DNS message limit is 512 bytes; required data can force TCP fallback.
lessons.body:
## Size limits, EDNS and TCP

Classic DNS over UDP limits messages to **512 bytes**. If required response data does not fit, the server sets the **TC bit** and a resolver can retry over **TCP** (port 53, with each message prefixed by a 2-byte length).

**EDNS(0)** ([RFC 6891](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6891)) extends DNS without changing the header. The client adds an **OPT** pseudo-record to the additional section that advertises a larger UDP buffer size and carries flags such as **DO** ("DNSSEC OK", please include signatures) and options such as cookies and client subnet.

UDP datagrams exceeding path capacity can be fragmented, dropped or trigger an error, depending on IP version, flags and path. Fragment handling can create reliability and spoofing risks. The 2020 **DNS Flag Day** recommended an EDNS buffer of **1,232 bytes**. The figure comes from IPv6: every IPv6 link must carry 1,280-byte packets, and removing the 40-byte IPv6 header and 8-byte UDP header leaves 1,232 bytes for the DNS message, so the whole packet fits without fragmentation.

This reduces fragmentation risk with those assumptions; extension headers, tunnels and IPv4 paths can require different budgets. Larger required answers can fall back to TCP.

## Key takeaways
- Without EDNS the ordinary UDP DNS message limit is 512 bytes; required data can force TCP fallback.
- The 1,232-byte EDNS budget assumes a basic IPv6 header and UDP without additional overhead.

## Further reading
- [RFC 6891](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6891)
- [RFC 7766](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7766)
- [DNS Flag Day 2020](https://www.dnsflagday.net/2020/)

questions.prompt: A resolver asks for the `TXT` records of a domain with many email SPF and verification strings. It sends no EDNS OPT record. The full answer would be 1,900 bytes. Assume the required answer RRset itself cannot fit 512 bytes, a conforming server, TCP connectivity and a resolver configured to retry truncation over TCP. What happens?

options.text: The server sends 1,900 bytes over UDP, fragmented by IP
options.explanation: Without EDNS the client has not advertised a buffer bigger than 512 bytes, so the server must not exceed it.

options.text: The server sends what fits in 512 bytes with TC set, and the resolver retries over TCP
options.explanation: Correct. TC signals truncation; the client repeats the query over TCP, where messages can be up to 65,535 bytes (2-byte length prefix).

options.text: The server returns SERVFAIL
options.explanation: Size is not a server failure; truncation plus TCP fallback is the designed mechanism.

options.text: The server silently drops records until it fits, with no indication
options.explanation: That would make answers silently incomplete. The TC bit exists precisely to tell the client.

questions.workedExample:
1. No OPT record → classic DNS → 512-byte UDP limit.
2. 1,900 > 512, so the server sets TC=1 and sends a partial (often empty) answer.
3. The resolver opens TCP to port 53 and resends with a 2-byte length prefix.
4. The full 1,900-byte answer arrives over TCP.

With EDNS advertising 1,232, it would still not fit, so TCP fallback happens either way. This is why blocking TCP 53 on firewalls breaks DNS.

questions.prompt: Why did DNS Flag Day 2020 recommend an EDNS UDP buffer size of 1,232 bytes rather than, say, 4,096?

options.text: 1,232 is the largest message DNSSEC signatures allow
options.explanation: DNSSEC answers can be much larger; the limit concerns transport, not signatures.

options.text: To reduce fragmentation risk: 1,232 + 40 bytes of basic IPv6 header + 8 bytes of UDP equals the 1,280-byte IPv6 minimum
options.explanation: Correct. Fragments are often dropped by firewalls and can be spoofed for cache poisoning. Keeping UDP answers unfragmented and falling back to TCP for larger ones is more reliable.

options.text: Because the DNS header's length field is limited to 1,232
options.explanation: The DNS header has no length field. Over TCP the 2-byte prefix allows up to 65,535 bytes.

options.text: To reduce amplification from 4,096 to 1,232, making DDoS impossible
options.explanation: It does reduce amplification somewhat, but that is a side benefit; the stated aim was avoiding fragmentation, and amplification is not made impossible.

questions.workedExample:
1. Every IPv6 link must carry packets of at least 1,280 bytes, the IPv6 minimum MTU.
2. A UDP DNS packet also carries a 40-byte basic IPv6 header and an 8-byte UDP header.
3. That leaves 1,232 bytes for the DNS message if the packet is to fit any IPv6 link without fragmentation.
4. Advertising 4,096 instead invites responses that must be fragmented, and fragments are often dropped by firewalls or can be spoofed.

Extension headers, encapsulation and IPv4 path constraints can require a different budget, so this is not a never-fragment guarantee. Larger required answers can use truncation and TCP fallback. Forged noninitial fragments can evade checks placed in the initial fragment, but successful injection also depends on reassembly identifiers, checksums, timing and cache rules.

lessons.title: DNS spoofing races and guessing-space models
lessons.summary: Forged UDP responses must match the outstanding query and race the legitimate answer.
lessons.body:
## Cache poisoning

A recursive resolver caches answers for their TTL. If an attacker gets a forged answer accepted, later matching lookups may receive poisoned cached data until expiry or replacement. Other caches, record types, validation and application authentication affect the result. That is **cache poisoning**.

For ordinary outstanding UDP queries, necessary response-matching checks include:

- the question (name, type, class),
- the transaction **ID**,
- the source IP and port it sent to, arriving at the **source port** it sent from.

An off-path attacker cannot see the query, so they must guess. With a fixed, known source port, the only unknown is the 16-bit ID: 65,536 possible values. One blind forged reply therefore matches once in 65,536 tries, and an attacker who races 100 forged replies in before the real answer covers about 1 in 650 of the possibilities. It must also beat the legitimate answer, which ends the race the moment it arrives.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Forging a reply to someone else's letter
> You write to your bank quoting a five-digit reference number and accept the first reply that quotes it back. A fraudster who cannot read your post wants to slip in a fake reply first. They must guess the reference, and each fake letter has only a tiny chance of carrying the right one.
>
> **How it maps:** The reference number is the DNS transaction ID (and, later, the source port). The genuine bank reply is the legitimate DNS answer: once it arrives, the race is over. A fake that matches is accepted and remembered, like a poisoned cache entry.
>
> **Where it stops:** A fraudster might wait weeks for your next letter. Kaminsky's method, below, lets an attacker trigger a fresh "letter" whenever they like, so they can make hundreds of attempts in quick succession.

### The Kaminsky attack (2008)

A simple vulnerable-resolver model offers a race only when a target name's cached answer expires. Dan Kaminsky's 2008 technique avoids that wait by causing fresh lookups and attempting to replace delegation data:

1. Make the resolver look up a fresh random name unlikely to have a cached answer: `x71.bank.example`.
2. Race the real answer with a flood of forged responses with guessed IDs.
3. Each forged response says "I don't know `x71`, but the name server for **bank.example** is `ns.bank.example` at **192.0.2.66**" (attacker-controlled), in the authority and additional sections.
4. If a forged response wins and its delegation records are admitted, the vulnerable resolver caches the attacker's server for the target zone.
5. If none wins, try `x72.bank.example` immediately. There is no TTL to wait for.

The odds per attempt have not changed; what changed is the number of attempts. If each attempt independently has about a 1-in-650 chance, roughly 450 attempts give an even chance that at least one succeeds, and a resolver that answers quickly lets an attacker make those attempts in a short time. This is a simplified probability model, not a measured attack duration: real caching rules, response checks and DNSSEC change whether forged data is admitted. The defences in the next unit enlarge what the attacker must guess and restrict which records a reply can install.

## Key takeaways
- Forged replies must match outstanding-query fields and beat the legitimate answer.
- The independent ID-guess model estimates attempts, not real attack duration.

## Further reading
- [RFC 5452](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5452)

questions.prompt: Before 2008, many operators thought a resolver with random 16-bit DNS transaction IDs was safe enough: an attacker could race forged replies only when a target name's cached answer expired, perhaps once a day. Dan Kaminsky's attack did not change how likely any single forged reply was to match. Why was it nonetheless so much more dangerous?

options.text: It made each forged reply much more likely to carry the right DNS transaction ID
options.explanation: The per-guess odds were unchanged: a random 16-bit ID still has 65,536 possibilities. The danger came from the number of attempts, not from better guesses.

options.text: It required the attacker to sit on the network path and read the resolver's queries
options.explanation: An on-path attacker could simply copy the ID. Kaminsky's attack works off-path, by guessing.

options.text: It needed the target's real authoritative servers to be offline
options.explanation: The attack races the real answer rather than waiting for an outage; each fresh query gives a new race.

options.text: It asked for fresh random names under the target zone, so no cached answer blocked a new race; forged replies tried to install the attacker's server for the whole zone, and attempts could be repeated at once until one won
options.explanation: Correct. Each attempt still had small odds, but unlimited immediate retries turn small odds into near-certain success, and a won race poisons the delegation for the whole zone rather than one name.

questions.workedExample:
1. A forged reply must match an outstanding query, including its 16-bit DNS transaction ID, and arrive before the real answer.
2. In the old model the attacker could only race when a specific cached name expired, so attempts were rare.
3. Kaminsky's attacker makes the resolver look up `x71.bank.example`, `x72.bank.example` and so on. None is cached, so every lookup is a new race.
4. Each forged reply also claims that `bank.example`'s name server is the attacker's machine. Winning one race can redirect the whole zone.
5. With, say, a 1-in-650 chance per attempt, a few hundred attempts give an even chance of success, and they can be made quickly.

The fix was not a better ID alone: resolvers added source port randomisation, stricter acceptance rules and, where deployed, DNSSEC validation.
