lessons.title: DNS poisoning defences and their assumptions
lessons.summary: Randomness and response validation raise distinct barriers to off-path poisoning.
lessons.body:
A forged UDP DNS answer must match an outstanding query and arrive in time to be accepted. A uniformly random sixteen-bit DNS transaction ID offers 65,536 possibilities. This unit examines additional barriers and the assumptions behind their combined guessing space.

## Defences

- **Source port randomisation.** The emergency fix after Kaminsky: pick a random UDP source port per query. The attacker must now guess the port *and* the ID, so the possibilities multiply. A pool of about 28,000 ports turns 65,536 possibilities into roughly 1.8 billion. Actual resolver pools, NAT behaviour and predictability determine the real gain; RFC 5452 warns that a NAT which assigns outgoing ports sequentially, or from a small range, can dramatically reduce it.
- **Bailiwick checking.** Restrict which supplied records can update cache entries under the responding server’s authority and the resolver’s delegation context. A response about `x71.bank.example` must not set records for `google.com`.
- **0x20 encoding.** Randomise the letter case of the query (`wWw.ExAmPlE.cOm`) and require the reply's question to echo it exactly. Each letter whose case is chosen at random doubles the possibilities, so `www.example.com`, with 13 letters, multiplies them by 8,192. It only works with servers that preserve the question's case, and resolvers need a fallback policy for those that do not.
- **DNS cookies** (RFC 7873) and TCP make some off-path spoofing harder, but do not provide DNSSEC’s signed-data chain or protect against every on-path attacker.
- **DNSSEC** cryptographically authenticates covered RRsets through a configured trust chain. Other authenticated transports protect their own endpoints and hops; these guarantees are different.

The random ID, the random port and random letter case combine because independent random choices multiply:

```formula reference
S = 2^16 × P × 2^ℓ
where
S: the number of equally likely combinations an off-path attacker must cover with forged replies
2^16: the 65,536 possible DNS transaction IDs
P: the number of source ports the resolver chooses from, independently and uniformly
ℓ: the number of letters in the query name whose case is randomised and checked
^: "to the power of"; 2^ℓ doubles once for every letter
In words: every independent random choice the attacker must match multiplies the guessing space, so ID, port and letter case together make a blind match far less likely than the ID alone.
```

Port randomisation is not the end of the story. The 2020 **SAD DNS** attack used a side channel (the global rate limit on ICMP "port unreachable" replies in Linux) to discover which port a resolver was using, bringing back the guessing game on the 16-bit ID alone.

## Key takeaways
- Independent port and case randomness can enlarge an off-path guessing space.
- Cache-admission rules, DNS cookies, signed data and authenticated transports have distinct guarantees.

## Further reading
- [RFC 5452](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5452)
- [RFC 7873](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7873)
- [SAD DNS original paper](https://www.cs.ucr.edu/~zhiyunq/pub/ccs20_dns_poisoning.pdf)

questions.prompt: Consider cache poisoning of an unsigned answer in a recursive resolver through forged replies to its UDP authoritative-server queries. Which checks can make the stated off-path attack harder? Assume case-preserving servers for the case-randomisation option. Select all that apply.

options.text: Randomising the UDP source port of each query
options.explanation: Correct. If ports are chosen independently and uniformly from a pool, the guessing space is multiplied by the number of ports in the pool; every doubling of the pool adds one bit. Predictability, NAT and the actual pool can reduce that benefit.

options.text: Randomising the letter case of query names (0x20 encoding)
options.explanation: Correct under the stated compatibility assumption, when the resolver checks the echoed case. Not every authoritative server preserves question case.

options.text: Ignoring out-of-bailiwick records in responses
options.explanation: Correct. A response to a query in `bank.example` cannot plant records for unrelated zones.

options.text: Using DoH between laptop and resolver
options.explanation: DoH protects the stub-to-resolver hop. Cache poisoning targets the resolver's queries to authoritative servers, which DoH does not cover.

options.text: Lowering every record's TTL to 5 seconds
options.explanation: Short TTLs mean more queries, giving the attacker *more* chances, and Kaminsky's method doesn't depend on TTL anyway.

questions.workedExample: A forged response must pass query matching and the resolver’s cache-admission rules. Independent random ports and checked case patterns increase the guessing space; bailiwick rules restrict admissible data. DoH only between the stub and recursive resolver does not protect this authoritative-query hop. Lower TTLs are not an authentication measure. DNSSEC provides a signed-data chain; authenticated transports provide different endpoint/hop integrity guarantees.

lessons.title: DNSSEC trust chains and authenticated denial
lessons.summary: DNSSEC authenticates covered RRsets through configured trust anchors without encrypting queries.
lessons.body:
## DNSSEC: signed answers

DNSSEC adds **authenticity and integrity**, not confidentiality. A signed zone publishes signatures over covered RRsets, and a validating resolver checks the signatures up a chain to a key it already trusts.

New record types:

| Type | Holds |
|---|---|
| DNSKEY | The zone's public keys |
| RRSIG | A signature over an RRset |
| DS | Key tag, algorithm and digest fields binding a child owner name and DNSKEY, in the parent |
| NSEC / NSEC3 | RRsets used with signatures for authenticated denial of a name/type or delegation properties |

Signatures cover an **RRset** (records with the same owner name, class and type) and have an inception and expiry time, so signatures must be renewed before they expire; affected data becomes bogus for validating resolvers enforcing the chain if no valid signatures remain.

A split-key design uses a **KSK** to authenticate the DNSKEY RRset and a **ZSK** for other signed RRsets. These are operational roles, not mandatory two-key enforcement; a combined signing key is possible. A parent DS authenticates a selected child DNSKEY, which then authenticates the child DNSKEY set.

```
configured root trust anchor
  verifies root DNSKEY RRset
  root key verifies DS RRset for com.
  DS authenticates com. DNSKEY
  child key verifies its DNSKEY RRset
  com. key verifies example.com DS
  DS authenticates child DNSKEY set
  child key verifies A RRset RRSIG
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A chain of signed references
> You trust one head office whose signature you already know. Head office signs a note vouching for a regional office's stamp; the regional office signs a note vouching for a branch's stamp; the branch stamps the document you care about. You can check the document without ever having met the branch.
>
> **How it maps:** The head office signature you already know is the root trust anchor. Each vouching note is a DS record in the parent zone, the stamps are each zone's DNSKEYs, and the stamped document is an RRset with its RRSIG.
>
> **Where it stops:** A stamped document can still be read by anyone: DNSSEC gives no secrecy. And a broken link is not a weaker answer but a failed one: if the parent's note names a stamp the branch no longer uses, a validating resolver rejects the data (normally SERVFAIL) rather than accepting it with less confidence.

A validating resolver walks this chain. AD can signal that the relevant answer/authority data was validated, subject to request flags and response rules. With checking enabled, bogus data normally produces SERVFAIL; an authenticated unsigned delegation is an **insecure delegation**, not automatically bogus. CD can request data without that rejection. A non-validating stub must trust the resolver and protected path for its AD assertion; a validating stub can check signatures itself.

### Proving non-existence

An attacker could also forge "this name does not exist". To sign a negative answer without signing every possible name, **NSEC** records chain the zone's existing names in sorted order: "the next name after `alpha` is `delta`" proves the exact covered name does not exist; a complete NXDOMAIN proof also needs appropriate wildcard/closest-encloser handling. The side effect is **zone walking**: following a conventional static NSEC chain can enumerate names represented in that chain. Delegations, empty nonterminals and online-signed denial techniques require care. **NSEC3** chains hashes of names instead, which slows walking but does not prevent offline dictionary attacks against the hashes.

### Costs and pitfalls

- **Bigger answers.** Signatures and keys make responses much larger, which means more truncation, TCP fallback and fragmentation, and makes signed zones more attractive for **amplification attacks** (a form of DDoS). Algorithm choice matters: an ECDSA P-256 (algorithm 13) signature is 64 bytes, against 256 bytes for RSA-2048.
- **Operational fragility.** Expired signatures or a key rollover with a stale DS record can make affected signed data fail validation once usable cached data and overlapping valid chains are exhausted.
- **Validator DoS.** The 2024 KeyTrap vulnerability showed that crafted key-tag collisions and many candidate signatures can force excessive validation work in vulnerable implementations. It exploited how validators match keys to signatures, not a break of the signature cryptography.
- **Last mile.** DNSSEC authenticates signed data to whichever endpoint performs validation, through intervening caches or transports. It does nothing about who can *see* your queries.

## Key takeaways
- DNSSEC authenticates covered RRsets through configured trust anchors without encrypting queries.
- Signed denial has precise name/type and wildcard conditions; rollover mistakes and validation work have operational costs.

## Further reading
- [RFC 4034](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4034)
- [RFC 4035](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4035)
- [RFC 5155](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5155)
- [RFC 6781](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6781)
- [RFC 6840](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6840)

questions.prompt: Your company moves `example.com` to a new DNS provider that re-signs the zone with a new KSK. You forget to update the DS record at the `.com` registry. Assume only the new key remains, the stale DS is the sole supported authenticated DS, checking is enabled (CD=0), no local exception applies, and old validated cached data is exhausted. What happens to fresh signed answers from that zone?

options.text: Nothing changes; the new signatures are valid
options.explanation: The signatures are valid under the new key, but the chain of trust links `.com` to the *old* key via DS. The new key cannot be authenticated.

options.text: NXDOMAIN for every name
options.explanation: NXDOMAIN means the name doesn't exist. A validation failure produces SERVFAIL.

options.text: Answers arrive but without the AD bit
options.explanation: That would happen if the zone became unsigned *and* the DS were removed (an insecure delegation). A DS that points to a missing key makes the zone bogus, not insecure.

options.text: SERVFAIL when those answers cannot be authenticated through the stale DS
options.explanation: Correct. The validator cannot match the new DNSKEY to the parent's DS, treats the zone as bogus and refuses to return answers.

questions.workedExample: The authenticated parent DS identifies the old child DNSKEY; under the assumptions, no remaining key matches it. The validator therefore classifies the fresh signed data as bogus and normally returns SERVFAIL with checking enabled. Non-validating clients or CD requests can behave differently. A real rollover must coordinate DNSKEYs, signatures and parent DS with overlap and cache-expiry timing; replacing the DS before its new key is available can also cause an outage. Follow a documented rollover method rather than treating one ordering rule as sufficient.

link.title: RFC 4033: DNS Security Introduction and Requirements — IETF

questions.prompt: A conventional static NSEC chain in example.com has adjacent names alpha.example.com and delta.example.com. Which signed interval covers the exact absent name charlie.example.com, and what information does following such a chain expose? A complete NXDOMAIN proof may additionally need wildcard denial.

options.text: alpha.example.com NSEC delta.example.com; it exposes adjacent names in the conventional chain
options.explanation: Correct. Charlie sorts strictly between alpha and delta. A validated NSEC RRset covers that gap; additional proof can be required to exclude a wildcard answer.

options.text: `charlie NSEC delta`; it reveals nothing else
options.explanation: In the stated static chain, charlie is absent and is not an existing chain owner. The relevant signed interval is bounded by alpha and delta.

options.text: `delta NSEC kilo`; it proves everything before kilo is absent
options.explanation: That record covers the gap between delta and kilo. `charlie` sorts before delta.

options.text: No record; DNSSEC cannot prove non-existence
options.explanation: Authenticated denial of existence is exactly what NSEC and NSEC3 are for.

questions.workedExample: In the specified canonical interval, alpha<charlie<delta. The authenticated NSEC link covers the exact-name gap, while complete denial checks also account for wildcard applicability and delegation context. Following a conventional static NSEC chain exposes its represented names. NSEC3 replaces cleartext ordering with hashed names, which still permits offline dictionary guesses; it does not promise secrecy.

lessons.title: Encrypted DNS and the limits of resolver privacy
lessons.summary: DoT, DoH and DoQ protect a client-to-resolver transport rather than independently proving authoritative data.
lessons.body:
## Encrypted DNS: DoT and DoH

Classic DNS is plaintext. An observer on an unprotected DNS transport can inspect its messages and attempt modification; caches avoid some lookups, and validation can detect tampering. Encrypted transports protect the hop between stub and recursive resolver.

| | DoT | DoH | DoQ |
|---|---|---|---|
| RFC | 7858 | 8484 | 9250 |
| Transport | TLS/TCP | HTTPS | QUIC |
| Port | 853 | 443 | 853 (UDP) |

**DNS over TLS** wraps the normal TCP DNS format (2-byte length, then message) in TLS. Because it has its own port, networks can easily identify and block it. Android supports DoT, and Google announced in July 2022 that updated devices from Android 11 onwards use DoH over HTTP/3 instead for some well-known resolvers that support it. The selected transport depends on version, updates and configuration.

**DNS over HTTPS** sends the same binary message as an HTTP request with media type `application/dns-message`, either POSTed or base64url-encoded in a GET (`/dns-query?dns=...`). Sharing HTTPS transport can make classification less direct than a dedicated port, but resolver addresses, endpoint policy and traffic patterns can still enable blocking. DoH is not guaranteed indistinguishable from other HTTPS. Browsers such as Firefox and Chrome can use it directly.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Sealed questions to a reference librarian
> Instead of shouting your questions across a crowded room, you post them to a reference librarian in sealed envelopes. Nobody handling the post can read them, but the librarian opens every one, and if the librarian is careless or dishonest, the answers can be wrong.
>
> **How it maps:** The sealed envelope is DoT, DoH or DoQ protecting the stub-to-resolver hop. The librarian is the recursive resolver, which still sees every name you ask about. Checking the librarian's answers against the original publisher's signature is DNSSEC validation.
>
> **Where it stops:** The post office still sees which library you write to and when, just as the network sees the resolver's address and traffic timing. And what you do with the answer, such as connecting to the site's IP address, is visible again.

What encrypted DNS does **not** do:

- It does not hide your queries from the **resolver** itself; you have moved trust from your ISP to, say, Cloudflare or Google. Oblivious DoH (RFC 9230) adds a proxy to separate client addressing from query contents under its non-collusion and deployment assumptions. Correlation, colluding parties and identifying query contents remain limits.
- It authenticates and integrity-protects the transport to the selected resolver, but does not independently authenticate authoritative *data*; a malicious or compromised resolver can still lie. That is DNSSEC's job.
- It does not hide the destination entirely: the server's IP address, and often the TLS SNI, still reveal where you went. Encrypted Client Hello ([RFC 9849](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9849), published in March 2026) can hide the SNI, but only when both the browser and the site support it.

An independently selected DoH resolver can bypass policies implemented only in the network’s default resolver, which is why administrators can disable it by policy and why Firefox checks a "canary" domain (`use-application-dns.net`) before enabling it automatically.

## Key takeaways
- DoT, DoH and DoQ protect a client-to-resolver transport rather than independently proving authoritative data.
- Resolvers still see queries; oblivious designs add assumptions and destination metadata can remain visible.

## Further reading
- [RFC 7858](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7858)
- [RFC 8484](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8484)
- [RFC 9250](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9250)
- [RFC 9230](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9230)

questions.prompt: A user switches their browser to DNS over HTTPS with a public resolver. Assume ordinary DoH over correctly authenticated HTTPS, no TLS-intercepting trusted proxy, and queries actually sent to that resolver with no plaintext fallback. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The local Wi-Fi cannot directly read or undetectably modify the protected DNS message contents in transit
options.explanation: Authenticated HTTPS protects message confidentiality and integrity on that transport. The network can still block traffic or analyse exposed addresses, sizes and timing.

options.text: The public resolver can see the DNS names submitted to it
options.explanation: Correct. DoH encrypts the transport; the resolver decrypts and processes the queries. Trust has moved, not disappeared.

options.text: Answers are now guaranteed authentic even if the resolver is malicious
options.explanation: DoH authenticates the resolver, not the data. A lying resolver can still return forged records; DNSSEC validation addresses data authenticity.

options.text: The ISP can no longer tell which sites they visit at all
options.explanation: Destination IPs remain visible, and so does TLS SNI unless Encrypted Client Hello is used.

options.text: Corporate DNS-based filtering on that network may be bypassed
options.explanation: Correct. The browser no longer asks the network's resolver, so DNS policies there don't apply. This is why enterprises can disable DoH by policy.

questions.workedExample: DoH provides confidentiality and integrity for the authenticated client-resolver transport. The selected resolver sees submitted queries and can still return false data unless independently checked; local DNSSEC validation can authenticate covered signed RRsets. On-path addresses and traffic patterns remain observable, and SNI can remain visible without ECH. Using another resolver may bypass policies enforced only by the network’s default DNS service.

lessons.title: Email delivery, MX selection and SMTP replies
lessons.summary: Clients submit mail to a provider; MTAs relay to MX destinations and retrieval uses separate protocols.
lessons.body:
SMTP began as a mail-transfer protocol without built-in encryption or sender-domain authentication. Submission authentication, transport security and DNS-based authentication mechanisms address different parts of the problem.

## The path of a message

```
 Alice's client (MUA)
   | SMTP submission, port 587/465
   v
 Alice's provider (MSA/MTA)
   | DNS: MX for bob.example?
   | SMTP relay, port 25
   v
 Bob's provider (MTA -> MDA)
   | stores in mailbox
   v
 Bob's client  <-- IMAP 993 / POP3 995
```

- A **mail user agent** (MUA) is the client: Outlook, Apple Mail, Thunderbird.
- **Mail submission** (port **587** with STARTTLS, or **465** with implicit TLS) is where your client hands mail to your provider, after authenticating. [RFC 8314](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8314) now recommends implicit TLS on 465.
- **Relay** between providers uses port **25**. Some access networks restrict outbound port 25 to reduce abuse; availability depends on the provider.
- The receiving server stores the message, and Bob's client fetches it with **IMAP** or **POP3**. SMTP is push-only; retrieval is a separate protocol.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Posting a parcel through two depots
> You hand a parcel to your local depot after showing ID. Your depot looks up which depot serves the recipient's town and drives it there. The recipient later collects it from their own locker.
>
> **How it maps:** Handing it over with ID is authenticated submission on port 587 or 465. The depot-to-depot drive is relay over port 25, and looking up the destination depot is the MX lookup. Collecting from the locker is IMAP or POP3, a separate protocol from the one that delivered it.
>
> **Where it stops:** A real depot can usually confirm who sent a parcel. Plain SMTP relay cannot; that is the job of the email SPF, DKIM and DMARC checks covered later. Mail can also wait in queues and be retried for days, which parcel services rarely do.

### Finding the destination: MX records

To deliver to `bob@bob.example`, the sending MTA looks up `MX` records for `bob.example`:

```
bob.example.  MX 10 mx1.bob.example.
bob.example.  MX 20 mx2.bob.example.
```

The **lower** preference number wins. A sender randomises equal-preference destinations unless it has a reason to favour one. Connection failures can lead it to try another destination; a permanent rejection of a recipient is not an instruction to bypass that rejection at a backup server. If there is no MX at all, the sender falls back to the domain's A/AAAA record (the "implicit MX"). A domain that never receives mail should publish a **null MX** (`MX 0 .`, RFC 7505) so senders fail fast.

## An SMTP session

SMTP ([RFC 5321](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321)) is a line-based text protocol. The client sends commands; the server answers with 3-digit codes. `C:` is the client, `S:` the server:

```
S: 220 mx1.bob.example ESMTP
C: EHLO mail.alice.example
S: 250-mx1.bob.example
S: 250-SIZE 52428800
S: 250-STARTTLS
S: 250 8BITMIME
C: STARTTLS
S: 220 Ready to start TLS
   ...TLS handshake, then EHLO again...
C: MAIL FROM:<alice@alice.example>
S: 250 OK
C: RCPT TO:<bob@bob.example>
S: 250 OK
C: DATA
S: 354 End data with <CRLF>.<CRLF>
C: From: Alice <alice@alice.example>
C: To: Bob <bob@bob.example>
C: Subject: Lunch?
C: Date: Mon, 5 Oct 2026 12:00:00 +0100
C:
C: Thursday at 1?
C: .
S: 250 OK queued as 7F3A2
C: QUIT
S: 221 Bye
```

The multi-line `250-` replies list **extensions** the server supports. A line `250 ` with a space marks the last one.

The first digit of each reply code is what matters:

| Code | Meaning | Sender should |
|---|---|---|
| 2xx | Success | Carry on |
| 3xx | Positive intermediate reply | Continue as requested (354 asks for the message text after the DATA command) |
| 4xx | Temporary failure | Retry the affected delivery later |
| 5xx | Permanent failure | Do not repeat the unchanged failed request |

A transient recipient failure such as `451` leaves that delivery eligible for retry. RFC 5321 recommends a give-up time generally at least 4–5 days, with retry spacing; local policy and failure conditions matter. A permanent delivery failure, or expiration after temporary failures, can produce a delivery-status notification for previously accepted mail. No such notification is sent to a null reverse path. **Greylisting** temporarily rejects unfamiliar deliveries to distinguish senders that retry; it does not reliably separate all legitimate messages from spam.

## Key takeaways
- Clients submit mail to a provider; MTAs relay to MX destinations and retrieval uses separate protocols.
- SMTP 4xx permits later retry, while an unchanged failed 5xx request should not be repeated.

## Further reading
- [RFC 5321](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321)
- [RFC 8314](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8314)
- [RFC 7505](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7505)

questions.prompt: `bob.example` publishes `MX 20 mxa.bob.example`, `MX 10 mxb.bob.example` and `MX 10 mxc.bob.example`. With no special routing policy and ordinary connection-failure fallback, which destination preference is correct?

options.text: `mxa`, because 20 is the highest priority
options.explanation: MX preference works the other way: lower numbers are preferred. `mxa` is the backup.

options.text: All three in parallel, using whichever answers first
options.explanation: This ignores the published preference ordering. Parallel connection attempts and duplicate message delivery are different issues.

options.text: `mxb` or `mxc`, chosen between them (often randomly), falling back to `mxa` only if both fail
options.explanation: Lower preference is tried first. Equal-preference destinations are randomised unless the sender has a reason to favour one; this spreads attempts without guaranteeing even load.

options.text: The A record of `bob.example`
options.explanation: The A/AAAA fallback (implicit MX) is used only when there are no MX records at all.

questions.workedExample:
1. Order destinations by preference: 10 (mxb, mxc), then 20 (mxa).
2. Randomise the equal-preference group absent a reason to favour one.
3. Connection failure can lead to trying another destination.
4. Temporary delivery failure leaves the message in the sender's queue for a later retry.
5. A permanent recipient rejection should not be bypassed simply by trying a backup.

link.title: RFC 5321: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol — IETF

questions.prompt: During delivery a receiving server replies `451 4.7.1 Try again later` to `RCPT TO`. What should a well-behaved sending MTA do?

options.text: Keep the message queued and retry later, giving up only after a long period (typically days)
options.explanation: Correct. 4xx means transient failure; the message stays in the queue and is retried later, at increasing intervals.

options.text: Immediately bounce the message to the sender
options.explanation: An immediate bounce is inappropriate for this temporary recipient failure. A later queue expiration can still cause a failure notification; bounces are not limited to 5xx replies.

options.text: Retry the same command in a tight loop until it succeeds
options.explanation: Hammering the server is antisocial and likely to get the sender blocked. Retries should back off over minutes and hours.

options.text: Switch to port 587 and try again
options.explanation: 587 is for client submission with authentication, not server-to-server relay.

questions.workedExample:
1. The first digit 4 indicates a transient failure.
2. Preserve the failed recipient delivery for retry rather than retrying in a tight loop.
3. RFC 5321 recommends a give-up time generally at least 4–5 days; retry schedules depend on policy.
4. Queue expiration can generate a failure notification for previously accepted mail, unless the reverse path is null.

Greylisting relies on retries, but retrying is not proof that a sender is legitimate.

lessons.title: SMTP envelopes versus message headers
lessons.summary: SMTP envelope recipients and bounce addresses are separate from visible message headers.
lessons.body:
Python's `smtplib` drives the same dialogue. This function submits through a configured provider, explicitly verifies the TLS certificate and hostname, and fails if STARTTLS is unavailable. Supply credentials separately; debug logging can expose authentication data and message contents. The example is not executed against a real provider here.

```python
import smtplib
import ssl
from email.message import EmailMessage
from email.utils import formatdate

msg = EmailMessage()
msg["From"] = "alice@alice.example"
msg["To"] = "bob@bob.example"
msg["Subject"] = "Lunch?"
msg["Date"] = formatdate(localtime=True)
msg.set_content("Thursday at 1?")

def submit(host, user, password):
    # Trust configured CAs and check names.
    tls = ssl.create_default_context()
    with smtplib.SMTP(
            host, 587, timeout=10) as s:
        # Encrypt before credentials.
        s.starttls(context=tls)
        s.login(user, password)
        # Set the separate SMTP envelope.
        return s.send_message(
            msg,
            from_addr=(
                "bounces@alice.example"),
            to_addrs=["bob@bob.example"])
```

Notice that `from_addr` and `to_addrs` are passed separately from the message headers. That is the next idea.

### Envelope versus header

There are **two** sets of addresses:

- The **SMTP envelope**: `MAIL FROM` (the *return path*, where bounces go) and `RCPT TO` (who actually receives it). These are SMTP commands.
- The **message header**: the `From:`, `To:` and `Cc:` lines inside the message ([RFC 5322](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5322)). These are what your mail client displays.

They need not match. In a common Bcc implementation, the recipient appears in `RCPT TO` while the Bcc header is removed before delivery. RFC 5322 also permits other Bcc-header handling for separate copies. Mailing lists set the envelope sender to the list's bounce address. And a spammer can put *anything* in `From:`, which is the core spoofing problem email SPF, DKIM and DMARC address.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: The envelope and the letterhead
> The post office delivers a letter using only what is written on the envelope. The letter inside can carry any letterhead, any "To" line and any signature, and the post office never reads them.
>
> **How it maps:** The envelope is `MAIL FROM` and `RCPT TO`: they decide where the message goes and where failures return. The letter's own headers, `From:`, `To:` and `Cc:`, are what the recipient sees. A Bcc copy is like an extra envelope addressed to Carol containing the same letter, which does not mention her.
>
> **Where it stops:** Envelopes are thrown away on arrival but SMTP keeps a trace: the receiver records the envelope sender in a `Return-Path:` header. And because anyone can print any letterhead, receivers need email SPF, DKIM and DMARC to judge whether a visible `From:` is genuine.

Bounces are sent with an empty envelope sender, `MAIL FROM:<>`, so conforming servers do not generate another delivery failure notification in response.

## Key takeaways
- SMTP envelope recipients and reverse paths are independent of visible message headers.
- Submit credentials only after establishing authenticated TLS; message headers do not determine envelope delivery.

## Further reading
- [RFC 5321](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321)
- [RFC 5322](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5322)
- [Python smtplib](https://docs.python.org/3/library/smtplib.html)

questions.prompt: Alice sends a message with `To: bob@x.example` and Bcc to `carol@y.example`. How does Carol receive it without her address appearing in the headers?

options.text: The sending server encrypts her address in the header
options.explanation: Headers aren't encrypted per recipient. Bcc relies on the separation of envelope and header.

options.text: Bob's server forwards a copy to Carol
options.explanation: In this example Alice's provider delivers separately to Carol's domain; Bob's server is not responsible for forwarding that copy.

options.text: Her address appears in the SMTP envelope (`RCPT TO`) but not in the message headers
options.explanation: Correct. Delivery is decided by `RCPT TO`; the headers are just part of the message content.

options.text: Carol's client fetches it from Alice's sent folder over IMAP
options.explanation: Carol has no access to Alice's mailbox. Mail is delivered by SMTP to Carol's provider.

questions.workedExample:
1. Alice's client submits with `RCPT TO:<bob@x.example>` and `RCPT TO:<carol@y.example>`.
2. The message headers contain `To: bob@x.example` and no Bcc line (the client strips it).
3. Alice's server delivers to x.example with `RCPT TO` Bob, and to y.example with `RCPT TO` Carol, both with the same headers.
4. Carol sees a message apparently addressed only to Bob.

lessons.title: Mailbox synchronisation with IMAP identities
lessons.summary: IMAP sequence numbers can move; a durable cached identity needs mailbox context, UIDVALIDITY and UID.
lessons.body:
## Retrieval: IMAP and POP3

**POP3** (port 110, or 995 with implicit TLS) retrieves messages and supports deletion; clients can also leave messages on the server. It lacks IMAP's richer server-side mailbox and flag model.

**IMAP** (port 143, or **993** with TLS; current version IMAP4rev2, [RFC 9051](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9051)) keeps mail **on the server** and lets many clients view and modify it. Folders, read and flagged states, and moves all sync between devices.

Each IMAP command starts with a client-chosen label, an **IMAP tag**, used to match responses. Some commands can be outstanding concurrently, subject to protocol ordering rules. This abbreviated exchange assumes TLS is already established; the FETCH response body and other required SELECT responses are omitted:

```
C: a1 LOGIN bob secret
S: a1 OK LOGIN completed
C: a2 SELECT INBOX
S: * 172 EXISTS
S: * OK [UIDVALIDITY 3857529045]
S: a2 OK [READ-WRITE] SELECT done
C: a3 UID FETCH 4827 (FLAGS BODY[])
S: * 172 FETCH (UID 4827 FLAGS ...
S: a3 OK FETCH completed
```

Lines starting with `*` are **untagged responses**: data or notifications. Key ideas:

- **Message sequence numbers** (1 to 172 here) are positions in the mailbox and shift when earlier messages are **expunged**, not merely marked `\Deleted`.
- **UIDs** increase with message assignment and remain stable within a mailbox's UIDVALIDITY generation. A cache identity includes the server/account, mailbox, UIDVALIDITY and UID; mutable flags still need synchronisation.
- **UIDVALIDITY** says whether cached UIDs are still meaningful. If it changes (the mailbox was rebuilt), the client must invalidate the old UID mappings and resynchronise, rather than assume a reused number identifies the same message.
- **Flags** such as `\Seen`, `\Flagged`, `\Deleted` record state. Deleting is two steps: set `\Deleted`, then `EXPUNGE`.
- **IDLE** lets the server send mailbox updates while the client waits. Connections can time out; the client terminates and reissues IDLE periodically and reconnects when needed.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Queue positions and cloakroom tickets
> In a queue, "third in line" changes whenever someone ahead leaves. A cloakroom ticket number does not: ticket 4827 stays with your coat however many other coats are collected. If the cloakroom closes and reopens with a fresh roll of tickets, old ticket numbers mean nothing.
>
> **How it maps:** Queue positions are message sequence numbers, which shift when earlier messages are expunged. Ticket numbers are UIDs, which stay with one message. The fresh roll of tickets is a UIDVALIDITY change: the client must discard its cached UIDs and resynchronise.
>
> **Where it stops:** Cloakroom tickets usually run consecutively; IMAP only promises that each new message in the mailbox gets a higher UID than earlier ones, so gaps are normal. A ticket also says nothing about the coat's state, whereas IMAP flags such as `\Seen` change and must be synchronised separately.

Applications can also use provider APIs or JMAP (RFC 8620), a JSON-based synchronisation framework over HTTP; JMAP Mail is specified separately in RFC 8621.

## Key takeaways
- IMAP sequence numbers can move; a durable cached identity needs mailbox context, UIDVALIDITY and UID.
- Deletion flags, expunging and live updates are distinct operations.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9051](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9051)
- [RFC 1939](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1939)
- [RFC 8620](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8620)

questions.prompt: An IMAP client caches messages by UID for `INBOX`. On reconnecting, `SELECT INBOX` returns a different `UIDVALIDITY` from the one it stored. What should the client do?

options.text: Nothing; UIDs are permanent
options.explanation: UIDs are only meaningful together with UIDVALIDITY. A new UIDVALIDITY means old UIDs may now refer to different messages.

options.text: Switch to using sequence numbers, which are stable
options.explanation: Sequence numbers are less stable: they shift every time a message is expunged.

options.text: Discard its cached UIDs for INBOX and resynchronise the mailbox
options.explanation: Correct. The server is signalling that the UID numbering was reset (for example the mailbox was rebuilt), so the cache can't be trusted.

options.text: Report a corrupted server and stop
options.explanation: A UIDVALIDITY change is a normal, specified event, not corruption.

questions.workedExample: Within the server/account, the cache identity includes mailbox, UIDVALIDITY and UID. A changed UIDVALIDITY means UID 4827 cannot be assumed to identify the old message. Invalidate old UID mappings and resynchronise the current mailbox. This does not require destroying unrelated locally saved copies. Mutable flags require updates even when the UID identity remains valid.

lessons.title: Email SPF envelope checks and DKIM content signatures
lessons.summary: Email SPF checks a connecting sender against an envelope-domain policy; it does not authenticate the visible From.
lessons.body:
## Authentication: email SPF, DKIM and DMARC

Nothing in SMTP stops a server from claiming `MAIL FROM:<ceo@yourbank.example>` and `From: CEO <ceo@yourbank.example>`. Three DNS-published mechanisms let receivers check.

### email SPF: which IPs may send for this domain?

Email SPF ([RFC 7208](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208)) is a TXT record listing the servers allowed to send mail for a domain:

```
alice.example. TXT "v=spf1
  ip4:192.0.2.0/24
  include:_spf.google.com
  -all"
```

(Shown wrapped for readability; publish one TXT record whose concatenated strings contain the policy with spaces between terms.) The receiver checks the **connecting IP** against the email SPF record of the **envelope sender's** domain (`MAIL FROM`, or the HELO name for bounces). The final `all` sets the default: `-all` fail, `~all` softfail, `?all` neutral.

Email SPF's limits:

- It checks the **SMTP envelope**, not the visible `From:` header. A spammer can pass email SPF for their own domain while showing your domain in `From:`.
- It **can fail on forwarding**: when `bob@uni.example` forwards to Gmail, Gmail sees the university's IP, which may not be authorised by alice.example's record.
- Evaluation permits at most **10 evaluated DNS-query-causing terms** across the recursive check: `include`, `a`, `mx`, `ptr`, `exists` and `redirect`. Exceeding that limit gives *permerror*. This is not a cap of ten individual DNS packets: some terms cause several queries, and additional per-mechanism and void-lookup limits apply. Evaluation stops when a mechanism matches.

### DKIM: a signature over the message

DKIM ([RFC 6376](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6376)) has the sending server sign selected headers and the body, and add the result as a header:

```
DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256;
  c=relaxed/relaxed; d=alice.example;
  s=mail2026; h=from:to:subject:date;
  bh=2jUSOH9NhtVGCQWNr9BrIAPreKQjO6Sn...;
  b=AuUoFEfDxTDkHlLXSZEpZj79LICEps6e...
```

- `d=` is the signing domain and `s=` the **DKIM selector**. The receiver fetches the public key from `mail2026._domainkey.alice.example` (TXT).
- `bh=` hashes the canonicalised body (or the prefix selected by optional `l=`); `b=` signs the selected canonicalised headers and the DKIM-Signature field with its `b=` value empty.
- `c=relaxed/relaxed` canonicalisation normalises specified whitespace and header **field-name** case. It does not make arbitrary changes to header values or body text harmless.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: An approved-courier list and a wax seal
> A company publishes a list of couriers allowed to deliver on its behalf, and it also seals each letter with its own wax seal. A receptionist can check the courier at the door against the list, or check the seal on the letter.
>
> **How it maps:** The courier list is email SPF: it checks the connecting server's IP against the envelope domain's published policy. The wax seal is DKIM: a signature over the message that anyone can verify with the public key published under `d=` and the selector.
>
> **Where it stops:** Neither check says the company named on the letterhead, the visible `From:`, is the one whose list or seal was checked; DMARC adds that link. A DKIM signature also fails if covered content changes beyond what its canonicalisation tolerates, not only when something is opened. A forwarded message arrives with a different courier, so email SPF often fails while the seal survives.

DKIM selectors let a domain have several keys at once: one per provider, and new ones for rotation. DKIM can survive forwarding when the signed content remains valid and the key/signature remains usable. A change to a signed subject or covered body content invalidates it; an unsigned header or content outside an `l=` prefix is a different case.

## Key takeaways
- Email SPF checks a connecting sender against an envelope-domain policy; it does not authenticate the visible From.
- DKIM binds selected canonicalised headers and body content to a signing domain.

## Further reading
- [RFC 7208](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208)
- [RFC 6376](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6376)
- [RFC 8301](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8301)

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical email SPF evaluation, no early mechanism matches. Five top-level `include` terms and four nested DNS-query-causing terms are evaluated, followed by `mx` and `a`. All other DNS responses and syntax are valid. Why does the evaluation return `permerror`?

options.text: The record has more than one `include`
options.explanation: Multiple includes are permitted. The budget counts evaluated DNS-query-causing terms across recursive evaluation.

options.text: It attempts an eleventh DNS-query-causing term, exceeding the ten-term limit
options.explanation: RFC 7208 section 4.6.4 limits these evaluated terms to ten. This is not a limit of ten individual DNS queries or packets.

options.text: `-all` is too strict and causes permerror
options.explanation: `-all` sets a hard fail for unlisted IPs; it is not an error.

options.text: TXT records cannot be longer than 255 characters
options.explanation: Each string in a TXT record is limited to 255 bytes, but one record can contain several strings that are concatenated. Length gives a different error, if any.

questions.workedExample:
Count only the DNS-query-causing terms that evaluation actually reaches, across the whole recursive check:

1. Five top-level `include` terms: 5.
2. Four nested query-causing terms inside those includes: 9.
3. `mx`: 10, which is still within the limit.
4. `a`: the eleventh, which exceeds RFC 7208's limit of ten, so evaluation stops with permerror.

An earlier matching mechanism would have stopped evaluation sooner.

Remove unnecessary authorised senders or separate sending domains appropriately. Flattening dynamic provider policies into static IP lists requires reliable updates. An email SPF permerror does not supply a DMARC pass; a valid aligned DKIM signature could still do so.

lessons.title: DMARC alignment, forwarding and rollout
lessons.summary: One aligned email SPF or DKIM pass can satisfy DMARC; unaligned authentication does not.
lessons.body:
Email SPF authenticates the connecting source for an envelope domain. DKIM authenticates selected signed content under its d= signing domain. DMARC connects those results to the domain in the message header that users see.

### DMARC: tie it to the visible From

Neither email SPF nor DKIM on its own protects the `From:` header the user sees. **DMARC** ([RFC 9989](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9989), published in May 2026 and replacing RFC 7489) adds **alignment**: a message passes DMARC if

- Email SPF passes **and** the envelope domain aligns with the `From:` domain, **or**
- DKIM passes **and** the `d=` domain aligns with the `From:` domain.

One aligned pass is enough, and an unaligned pass counts for nothing: a phisher's server can pass email SPF for `phish.example`, but that cannot produce a DMARC pass for a message showing `From: it@alice.example`.

"Aligned" by default (relaxed mode) means the same organisational domain, so `mail.alice.example` aligns with `alice.example` when both have organisational domain `alice.example`. RFC 9989 discovers that boundary through DNS tree walks; do not assume every two-label suffix is an organisation. Strict alignment (`aspf=s`, `adkim=s`) requires an exact match.

The policy is a TXT record at `_dmarc`:

```
_dmarc.alice.example. TXT
  "v=DMARC1; p=reject;
   rua=mailto:dmarc@alice.example"
```

- `p=none` requests no DMARC-specific enforcement; `quarantine` requests suspicious treatment and `reject` requests rejection. Receivers retain local discretion: RFC 9989 tells fully participating receivers not to reject a message solely because the policy says `reject`, but to weigh other evidence, for example about mailing lists.
- RFC 9989 drops the old `pct=` percentage tag. A domain trying out a stricter policy can add `t=y` (test mode), which asks receivers to apply one level less than the stated policy, so `reject` is treated as `quarantine`. Guides written for RFC 7489 can be out of date.
- `rua=` requests aggregate reports about observed sources and authentication results. Reporting is not guaranteed; current report formats are in RFC 9990.

A staged rollout inventories legitimate senders, monitors reports with `p=none`, fixes authentication and alignment, then considers enforcement. A fixed number of weeks cannot guarantee that every infrequent sender has appeared.

The receiver’s pass rule and the domain owner’s conformance requirements are different. For full participation, RFC 9989 section 8 requires domain owners to send with **both aligned email SPF and aligned DKIM**, publish the required policies, and collect and analyse aggregate reports. It explicitly forbids relying solely on email SPF when the Author Domain policy is `p=reject`. One aligned pass still suffices for a receiver’s message result; that does not make a sender’s email SPF-only deployment fully conformant.

> [!example] A spoof that DMARC catches
> A phisher sends from their own server with `MAIL FROM:<x@phish.example>` and `From: <it@alice.example>`. Email SPF passes for phish.example, but it does not align with alice.example. There is no valid alice.example DKIM signature. DMARC fails. A receiver applying the requested `p=reject` policy without a local override refuses it.

Since February 2024, Google's published sender rules (unchanged when checked in October 2026) require senders of 5,000 or more messages a day to personal Gmail accounts to use email SPF, DKIM and DMARC. One-click unsubscribe applies to marketing and subscribed messages. Yahoo also has bulk-sender requirements, but the Gmail numeric threshold should not be assumed to define Yahoo's classification. Consult each provider's current policy.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Checking the seal matches the letterhead
> A letter arrives on Alice Ltd letterhead. It came by an approved courier and carries an intact wax seal, but both belong to Phish Ltd. Each check passed, yet neither shows that Alice Ltd sent it.
>
> **How it maps:** The letterhead is the visible `From:` domain. The courier and seal are the email SPF and DKIM results, each tied to its own domain. DMARC asks whether at least one passing check belongs to the same organisation as the letterhead (relaxed alignment) or to exactly the same domain (strict), and the letterhead's owner publishes what to do when none does.
>
> **Where it stops:** A receptionist can phone Alice Ltd to ask; a receiver cannot, so it relies on the published policy and its own judgement. Forwarders and mailing lists also change couriers or contents in transit, which can break both checks even for genuine mail.

**ARC** (RFC 8617) helps forwarders and mailing lists: each intermediary records the authentication results it saw and signs them, so the final receiver can choose to trust a known forwarder's verdict even though email SPF and DKIM now fail.

## Pitfalls

- **Forgotten senders.** Moving to `p=reject` before every SaaS tool signs with your domain can cause legitimate invoices and password resets to be rejected when they lack any aligned authentication pass.
- **Email SPF lookup limit.** Evaluated nested terms can exceed the ten-term budget and produce permerror.
- **Short DKIM keys.** RFC 8301 requires RSA signing keys of at least 1024 bits and recommends at least 2048; key rotation and supported algorithms need an operational policy.
- **Plaintext relay.** Opportunistic relay without an effective authenticated-TLS requirement is vulnerable to downgrade; local mandatory-TLS policies are another possible protection.

## Key takeaways
- One aligned email SPF or DKIM pass can satisfy DMARC; unaligned authentication does not.
- Enforcement rollout must include every legitimate sender and account for forwarding or content changes.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9989](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9989)
- [RFC 9990](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9990)
- [RFC 8617](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8617)
- [Google sender policy](https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126)

questions.prompt: A message arrives from IP 203.0.113.9 with `MAIL FROM:<news@promo.shop.example>` and `From: Shop <hello@shop.example>`. email SPF for `promo.shop.example` passes; there is no DKIM signature. `_dmarc.shop.example` says `v=DMARC1; p=reject` with default (relaxed) alignment. Does it pass DMARC? Assume both domains have organisational domain `shop.example`.

options.text: Yes, because email SPF passed and `promo.shop.example` aligns with `shop.example` under relaxed alignment
options.explanation: Correct. Both share the organisational domain `shop.example`, and one aligned pass (email SPF here) is enough.

options.text: No, because the envelope domain is not exactly the From domain
options.explanation: That would be true only under strict alignment (`aspf=s`). Relaxed alignment compares organisational domains.

options.text: No, because DMARC requires both email SPF and DKIM to pass
options.explanation: DMARC needs email SPF **or** DKIM to pass with alignment, not both.

options.text: Yes, because email SPF passing is always enough for DMARC
options.explanation: email SPF passing is only enough if it is also aligned with the From domain. Without alignment, a spammer's own email SPF pass would count.

questions.workedExample:
1. Visible From domain: `shop.example`.
2. email SPF: checked against `promo.shop.example` → pass.
3. Alignment (relaxed): organisational domain of `promo.shop.example` is `shop.example` → matches → **aligned**.
4. DKIM: absent, but not needed.
5. One aligned pass → DMARC **pass**.

With `aspf=s` it would fail, because `promo.shop.example` is not exactly `shop.example`.

questions.prompt: Bob forwards mail to Gmail without altering the envelope sender or signed content. Alice's email SPF record ends in `-all` and does not authorise the university's IP. Alice's aligned DKIM signature remains valid at Gmail, and her DMARC policy is `p=reject`. What authentication result follows?

options.text: It is rejected, because email SPF fails at Gmail
options.explanation: email SPF does fail (the university's IP is not Alice's), but DMARC only needs one aligned pass.

options.text: It passes email SPF, because the university is a trusted forwarder
options.explanation: email SPF only knows about IPs in Alice's record. It has no notion of trusted forwarders (ARC addresses that separately).

options.text: It is quarantined, because forwarding always breaks email authentication
options.explanation: email SPF fails under the stated authorisation conditions, but the still-valid aligned DKIM signature suffices for DMARC.

options.text: It passes DMARC via DKIM, because the signature survives an unmodified forward
options.explanation: Correct. DKIM signs the content, not the path. The signature still verifies and `d=` aligns with Alice's From domain.

questions.workedExample:
At Gmail, email SPF fails because the university IP is not authorised for the preserved envelope sender. DKIM passes and aligns, so DMARC passes. This does not guarantee inbox delivery.

Modifying a signed subject or covered body content could instead break DKIM. A footer outside an optional `l=` signed prefix is not necessarily covered, and an unsigned subject is a different case.

questions.prompt: You're moving `corp.example` from `p=none` to `p=reject`. Aggregate reports show three sources claiming your domain: your Microsoft 365 tenant (email SPF and DKIM pass, aligned), an invoicing SaaS sending from its own IPs with `MAIL FROM:<bounce@invoicer.example>` and DKIM `d=invoicer.example`, and unknown IPs in another country (all fail). What must you do before switching? You want full Domain Owner participation under RFC 9989.

options.text: Nothing; the invoicer passes email SPF and DKIM so it will pass DMARC
options.explanation: It passes email SPF and DKIM for **invoicer.example**, not for corp.example. Neither aligns with `From: billing@corp.example`, so DMARC fails.

options.text: Add the unknown foreign IPs to email SPF so their mail is delivered
options.explanation: Do not authorise unidentified sources merely to clear failures. Geography and authentication failure alone do not prove spoofing: investigate ownership and legitimate sending paths.

options.text: Switch strict alignment on so the invoicer's subdomain matches
options.explanation: Strict alignment makes matching harder, not easier, and invoicer.example is a different organisational domain anyway.

options.text: Configure both an aligned custom return path with email SPF authorising the invoicer and a valid aligned DKIM signature; investigate unidentified sources
options.explanation: RFC 9989 section 8 requires fully participating Domain Owners to send with both aligned email SPF and aligned DKIM, and forbids relying solely on email SPF with p=reject. A receiver can still pass an individual message on either aligned result.

questions.workedExample: Microsoft 365 already supplies aligned email SPF and DKIM. The invoicer authenticates only invoicer.example, which is unaligned with corp.example, so its messages can fail DMARC. For the full participation requested here, configure and verify an aligned return-path domain whose email SPF authorises the invoicer, plus DKIM with an aligned signing domain. A receiver’s individual-message pass rule remains either aligned email SPF or aligned DKIM; RFC 9989 section 8 imposes stronger sending requirements, including no reliance solely on email SPF with p=reject. Investigate unknown sources before classifying them: their country does not establish spoofing. Collect and analyse reports and monitor delivery failures during rollout.

questions.prompt: A mailing list receives a valid aligned DKIM-signed message from `alice@alice.example` (DMARC `p=reject`). The signature covers Subject and the full body. The list changes both, keeps Alice's From header, and uses its own unaligned envelope domain, with no other aligned signature. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Alice's DKIM signature fails, because signed headers and the body changed
options.explanation: Correct. Both `bh=` (body hash) and the header signature cover what the list modified.

options.text: email SPF is evaluated for the list's envelope domain; even a pass for that unaligned domain does not provide a DMARC pass
options.explanation: The preserved visible From domain is alice.example, which does not align with the list's stated envelope domain.

options.text: The message may be rejected, because no aligned pass remains
options.explanation: Correct. That's why many lists rewrite `From:` to the list's own address ("Alice via team") for p=reject senders.

options.text: ARC can let a receiver trust the list's record that DKIM passed on arrival
options.explanation: Correct. ARC seals let a receiver that trusts the intermediary use its authentication results.

options.text: DMARC automatically exempts mailing lists
options.explanation: There is no automatic exemption; that is exactly the long-standing interoperability problem.

questions.workedExample: The subject and covered body modifications invalidate Alice's signature. email SPF for the list's unaligned envelope domain cannot supply alignment. DMARC therefore fails; a receiver may apply p=reject or use local policy, including trusted ARC evidence, to override disposition. Alternatives include preserving the signed content or changing From to an appropriately authenticated list identity. An ARC chain is not an automatic exemption.

lessons.title: SMTP parser agreement and enforced relay TLS
lessons.summary: Relay security depends on both consistent framing and an effective authenticated-TLS policy.
lessons.body:
An SMTP sender transmits an envelope followed by message headers and body. Email SPF authenticates a connecting IP for an envelope domain; DKIM binds covered content to a signing domain, and DMARC checks alignment with the visible From. Those authentication results do not replace safe SMTP framing or confidential, authenticated transport.

## Dot-stuffing and SMTP smuggling

The message ends with a line containing just `.`. A body line that starts with `.` is sent with an extra `.` (as `..`), which the receiver strips. That is **dot-stuffing**.

In 2023, researchers showed **SMTP smuggling**: some servers accepted a bare `\n.\n` as end of data while others required `\r\n.\r\n`. An attacker could hide a second, forged message inside the first, which the receiving server then treated as a separate message from the sending provider. Same lesson as HTTP request smuggling: when two parsers disagree on framing, attackers live in the gap.

### TLS between servers

With **opportunistic STARTTLS** on port 25 and no policy requiring authenticated TLS, stripping the offer can induce plaintext delivery. Enforcing senders instead defer or fail delivery. Two policy mechanisms are:

- **MTA-STS** (RFC 8461): an HTTPS policy in `enforce` mode requires authenticated TLS to approved MX hosts. Cached policies protect against stripping; initial DNS policy discovery can still be suppressed before a sender has a policy.
- **DANE** (RFC 7672): DNSSEC-authenticated TLSA records associate acceptable certificates or keys, including supported trust-anchor forms, to the SMTP service.

## Key takeaways
- Dot-stuffing preserves message boundaries only when both hops apply compatible end-of-data parsing.
- Opportunistic STARTTLS and enforced authenticated TLS have different downgrade guarantees.
- MTA-STS and SMTP DANE constrain relay security under different discovery and trust assumptions.

## Further reading
- [RFC 5321](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321)
- [RFC 8461: MTA-STS](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8461)
- [RFC 7672: SMTP DANE](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7672)
- [SMTP smuggling original research](https://sec-consult.com/blog/detail/smtp-smuggling-spoofing-e-mails-worldwide/)

questions.prompt: Which statements about SMTP security are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Without a mandatory authenticated-TLS policy, stripping an opportunistic STARTTLS offer can induce plaintext SMTP relay
options.explanation: Correct. The STARTTLS offer is in a plaintext EHLO response, so a man-in-the-middle can remove it.

options.text: MTA-STS lets a receiving domain tell senders to require valid TLS for its MX hosts

options.text: DKIM encrypts the message body between servers
options.explanation: DKIM signs; it provides integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality.

options.explanation: Correct. RFC 8314 recommends implicit TLS for submission.

options.text: email SPF prevents attackers from reading mail in transit
options.explanation: email SPF is a sender authorisation check; it does nothing for confidentiality.

STARTTLS can be downgraded when the sender permits plaintext. Effective MTA-STS enforce policies and DNSSEC-validated DANE records constrain delivery, with different discovery assumptions. Port 465 starts TLS before SMTP. email SPF checks sender authorisation, DKIM checks a signed domain/content binding, and DMARC checks alignment; none encrypts the message.

options.explanation: Correct. After the fake end-of-data, the attacker's text is parsed as new SMTP commands (`MAIL FROM`, `RCPT TO`, `DATA`) arriving from the legitimate provider's IP.
