lessons.title: NTP drift and the four-timestamp exchange
lessons.summary: Four NTP timestamps estimate clock offset and network round-trip delay under an explicit timing model.
lessons.body:
## NTP: agreeing on the time

Clocks drift. A clock's error rate is quoted in parts per million (ppm): how many microseconds it gains or loses per second. A clock that is 20 ppm fast gains about 1.7 seconds a day if nothing corrects it. This is an illustrative rate; actual oscillators and environmental conditions differ. Clock synchronisation matters for logs, certificates, Kerberos tickets, TOTP codes and lease timeouts. Acceptable error depends on each protocol and application policy.

**NTP** (version 4, [RFC 5905](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5905)) runs over **UDP port 123**. Servers are arranged in **strata**: reference clocks (such as GPS or atomic sources) are informally called stratum 0, stratum 1 is a server attached to one, stratum 2 syncs from stratum 1, and so on. Stratum 16 means "unsynchronised". In an NTP packet, a stratum field of zero instead means unspecified/invalid and can identify a Kiss-o'-Death response; it is not an ordinary reference-clock server reply.

### Four timestamps

One request/response gives the client four times:

```
client           server
 t1 ---request--->
                  t2  (server rx)
                  t3  (server tx)
 t4 <--response---
```

The first and fourth timestamps come from the client's clock; the middle two come from the server's clock. From them the client estimates how far its clock is from the server's, and how long the network took:

```formula essential
θ = ((t_2 − t_1) + (t_3 − t_4)) / 2
δ = (t_4 − t_1) − (t_3 − t_2)
where
θ: theta, the clock offset: the estimate of server time minus client time, in seconds (s). Positive means the client is behind
δ: delta, the round-trip delay: the whole exchange time minus the time the server held the request, in seconds
t_1: client send time in seconds (s), by the client's clock
t_2: server receive time in seconds (s), by the server's clock
t_3: server send time in seconds (s), by the server's clock
t_4: client receive time in seconds (s), by the client's clock
s: seconds
In words: the offset averages the apparent clock difference seen in each direction, which cancels the travel time if both directions take equally long; the delay is the time on the wire.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Checking your watch against a friend's by letter
> You post a letter noting the time on your watch when you sent it. Your friend notes their watch time when it arrives and again when they post a reply. When the reply reaches you, you note your watch again. From those four times you can work out both how long the post took and how far apart your watches are.
>
> **How it maps:** Your two notes are the client's send and receive times, and your friend's two notes are the server's receive and send times. Subtracting the time your friend held the letter gives the time spent in the post (the round-trip delay). Averaging the two apparent watch differences, one from each direction, cancels the postal time and leaves the offset.
>
> **Where it stops:** That cancelling only works if the post takes equally long each way; the next unit shows what happens when it does not. NTP also repeats this exchange many times and filters the results rather than trusting one letter.

**Round-trip delay** is the round trip minus the server processing time. **Clock offset** estimates server time minus client time under the model that each clock runs at a steady rate and the path delay is symmetric; it is not an instruction to step the clock immediately.

Why does averaging work? Subtracting the client-send timestamp from the server-receive timestamp gives the offset *plus* outbound travel time. Subtracting the client-receive timestamp from the server-send timestamp gives the offset *minus* return travel time. Adding them cancels the travel times only when the two are equal. The same arithmetic in Python:

```python
def ntp(t1, t2, t3, t4):
    # Average apparent differences.
    offset = ((t2 - t1) + (t3 - t4)) / 2
    # Exclude the server handling interval.
    delay = (t4 - t1) - (t3 - t2)
    return offset, delay

# client clock 130 ms behind,
# 20 ms each way, 2 ms processing
o, d = ntp(10.000, 10.150,
           10.152, 10.042)
print(round(o, 3), round(d, 3))
# 0.13 0.04
```

Check it: the client sends at its 10.000, which is server time 10.130; 20 ms later the server receives at 10.150. It replies at 10.152; 20 ms later it is server time 10.172, which on the client's clock is 10.042. The two apparent differences are 150 ms outbound and 110 ms on the return; their average is the true 130 ms offset, because the 20 ms travel times cancel. The 2 ms the server held the request is subtracted from the 42 ms exchange, leaving a 40 ms round trip. The ideal arithmetic recovers 130 ms exactly; the printed values are rounded because floating-point computation has small errors.

## Key takeaways
- Four NTP timestamps estimate clock offset and network round-trip delay under an explicit timing model.
- The delay calculation subtracts the time spent handling the request at the server.

## Further reading
- [RFC 5905](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5905)

questions.prompt: An NTP server becomes overloaded and now holds each request for 200 ms before replying, instead of 1 ms. Network paths are unchanged and symmetric, and the timestamps are accurate. What happens to the client's computed offset and round-trip delay?

options.text: The delay rises by about 200 ms, but the offset is unchanged
options.explanation: The delay calculation subtracts the server's own receive-to-send interval, so time spent inside the server is not counted as network delay.

options.text: The offset is wrong by about 100 ms, because the holding time is split between the two directions
options.explanation: The extra hold raises the server's send time and the client's receive time by the same amount, so the return-direction difference is unchanged and nothing is split into the offset.

options.text: Neither changes much: the server timestamps both when it received and when it sent, so its holding time is removed from the delay and cancels out of the offset
options.explanation: Correct. Both server timestamps move apart by the extra hold, and the client's receive time moves by the same amount. The delay subtracts that interval, and the offset's return-direction difference is unaffected.

options.text: The exchange fails, because NTP rejects any sample with server processing over 100 ms
options.explanation: NTP has no such fixed rule. It filters samples and prefers low-delay ones, but slow server processing is measured and removed rather than treated as an error.

questions.workedExample:
1. The server records two timestamps: when the request arrived and when its reply left. The gap between them is its holding time.
2. Delay is the whole exchange measured by the client minus that holding time. Adding 199 ms of holding lengthens the whole exchange by 199 ms and the subtracted interval by the same 199 ms, so the delay is unchanged.
3. The offset averages two apparent clock differences. The outbound one (server receive minus client send) does not involve the hold at all. The return one (server send minus client receive) moves both times later by the same 199 ms, so it is unchanged too.
4. So a busy server does not, by itself, distort the estimates. What does distort them is a difference between the two network directions, covered in the next unit.

This is why NTP needs four timestamps rather than two.

lessons.title: NTP path asymmetry, slewing and monotonic time
lessons.summary: Unequal one-way delays bias an NTP offset estimate; low delay does not prove symmetry.
lessons.body:
NTP estimates server time minus client time by averaging the apparent difference in each direction. It estimates network round-trip delay by subtracting server handling time from the complete exchange. Those estimates cannot by themselves identify one-way path asymmetry.

### The symmetry assumption

The offset calculation assumes the outbound and return trips take **equal** time. If they don't, the estimate is biased by half the difference between them. Suppose the request takes 5 ms but the reply takes 35 ms, for example because of congestion on the return path. The round trip is 40 ms, and the offset comes out 15 ms too low: the client appears 15 ms further ahead of the server than it really is.

```formula essential
ε = (d_out − d_back) / 2
|ε| ≤ δ / 2
where
ε: epsilon, the error in the offset estimate caused by unequal paths, in milliseconds (ms)
d_out: the one-way time from client to server, in ms
d_back: the one-way time from server back to client, in ms
δ: delta, the measured round-trip network delay, in ms
|ε|: the size of the error, ignoring its sign
≤: is at most
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: unequal paths shift the offset by half their difference, and that shift can never be bigger than half the round trip.
```

The four timestamps alone cannot tell this bias apart from a real clock offset. The bound assumes nonnegative delays and otherwise ideal timestamps. Low-delay samples reduce the bound but do not prove symmetry; multiple sources and filtering can help reject bad measurements.

### Disciplining the clock

Clock-discipline behaviour depends on implementation and configuration. Wall-clock steps can disrupt duration calculations and timestamp ordering:

- **Slewing**: run the clock slightly fast or slow until the offset is gone. The time needed is the offset divided by the slew rate: at an illustrative 500 ppm (half a millisecond per second), correcting a 1-second offset takes about 33 minutes. This is not a universal Linux limit: chrony supports higher slew rates on Linux.
- **Stepping the clock**: set the time directly when policy permits. Classic ntpd uses a 128 ms step threshold with state-machine safeguards; stepping is not inherently restricted to boot. Large offsets are usually stepped because slewing them would take too long.

Programs should measure durations with a **monotonic clock** (`time.monotonic()` in Python), which is never stepped, and use wall-clock time only for timestamps.

**Leap seconds** add a further wrinkle. Google documents a 24-hour **leap smear** centred on a leap second; it changes the clock's rate instead of presenting an abrupt insertion. Its offset from unsmeared UTC reaches half a second. Different smear policies need not agree, so do not mix incompatible sources. CGPM Resolution 4 (2022) calls for increasing the permitted UT1−UTC difference by or before 2035, allowing much longer intervals without leap adjustments; it does not specify an unconditional permanent abolition date.

## Key takeaways
- Unequal one-way delays bias an NTP offset estimate; low delay does not prove symmetry.
- Slew and step policies differ, while duration measurements should use a monotonic clock.

## Further reading
- [RFC 5905](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5905)
- [chrony configuration](https://chrony-project.org/doc/4.7/chrony.conf.html)
- [Google leap smear](https://developers.google.com/time/smear)
- [CGPM resolution 4](https://www.bipm.org/en/cgpm-2022/resolution-4)

questions.prompt: A client and an NTP server are both known to be correct (each is checked against its own GPS receiver). Yet a single NTP sample, with a 28 ms round-trip delay, computes an offset of about −10 ms: the client appears 10 ms ahead of the server. What best explains this?

options.text: The return path from server to client is about 20 ms slower than the request path
options.explanation: Correct. Unequal paths bias the offset by half their difference. A slow return makes the reply look late, so the client seems ahead: (4 − 24) / 2 = −10 ms for 4 ms out and 24 ms back.

options.text: The request path from client to server is about 20 ms slower than the return path
options.explanation: That asymmetry has the opposite sign: a slow outbound trip makes the server's receive time look late, so the client would appear behind, giving a positive offset.

options.text: The server took 10 ms to process the request, and NTP does not subtract processing time
options.explanation: NTP records when the server received and sent, so processing time is removed from the delay and cancels out of the offset.

options.text: Nothing is wrong: a single sample can be off by any amount, so −10 ms tells you nothing
options.explanation: The error from path asymmetry is bounded by half the round trip, here 14 ms. A −10 ms bias fits within that bound and has a specific cause worth diagnosing.

questions.workedExample:
1. Both clocks are known to be right, so the true offset is 0. The computed −10 ms must come from the measurement.
2. Server processing cancels out of the offset, so the likely cause is unequal one-way delays.
3. The bias is half of (outbound time − return time). A −10 ms bias means the return trip was about 20 ms longer than the outbound trip.
4. With a 28 ms round trip, that fits 4 ms out and 24 ms back, for example a congested downlink.
5. The bias can be at most half the round trip, 14 ms, so this sample is within the possible range.

The four timestamps alone cannot tell this apart from a real clock error. That is why NTP prefers the lowest-delay samples, compares several servers and filters before adjusting the clock.

link.title: RFC 5905: Network Time Protocol Version 4 — IETF

questions.prompt: A service measures request latency as `time.time()` at the end minus `time.time()` at the start. Occasionally it logs negative latencies. What is the likely cause and fix?

options.text: Integer overflow in the subtraction; use a 64-bit type
options.explanation: Python floats don't overflow at these magnitudes. The wall clock itself went backwards.

options.text: The wall clock was stepped backwards by NTP (or an admin); measure durations with `time.monotonic()`
options.explanation: Correct. Wall-clock time can jump; the monotonic clock never goes backwards, so it is the right tool for intervals.

options.text: Leap seconds always produce negative intervals; ignore them
options.explanation: A leap second can cause this, but so can any step. Ignoring it hides real bugs; using a monotonic clock fixes it.

options.text: The CPU executed the lines out of order
options.explanation: Out-of-order execution is invisible at this level; program order is preserved for the results.

questions.workedExample: Wall-clock time can jump. A 300 ms backward step during a 50 ms request gives an apparent −250 ms duration. Use time.monotonic() for elapsed time: it does not go backwards because the wall clock was reset. Python uses platform-specific clocks (CLOCK_MONOTONIC is one implementation, not a universal mapping); frequency adjustment and suspend behaviour depend on the platform.

lessons.title: NTP timestamp fields, eras and authentication
lessons.summary: NTP timestamps split seconds and fractions into 32-bit fields, so era context matters when the seconds count rolls over in 2036.
lessons.body:
### Wire format and security

The basic NTP header is 48 bytes (extensions/authentication can add bytes): leap indicator, version, mode, stratum, poll, precision, root delay and dispersion, reference ID, then four 64-bit timestamps. Each timestamp is 32 bits of seconds since **1 January 1900** and 32 bits of fraction. The fraction splits each second into about 4.3 billion steps of roughly 233 picoseconds, far finer than any real clock or network measurement. The seconds count holds about 136 years, so it rolls back to zero in **February 2036**. Era-aware implementations use other date information, which RFC 5905 says can come from external means such as the file system or dedicated hardware, to decide which 136-year era a timestamp belongs to; the 32-bit field alone cannot.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Two-digit years
> A form that records only the last two digits of the year cannot say whether "36" means 1936 or 2036. People resolve it from context: a birth date on a new passport application is unlikely to be 2036.
>
> **How it maps:** NTP's 32-bit seconds field is the two-digit year: it repeats every 136 years. The "context" is the era an implementation infers from other time information it already has.
>
> **Where it stops:** People fix two-digit years by writing four digits; NTPv4 keeps the 32-bit on-wire field and relies on era handling, so a device with no idea of the current date, such as one whose clock reset to zero, can still pick the wrong era.

Plain NTP is unauthenticated, so an on-path attacker can shift your clock and, for example, make expired certificates look valid. **NTS** (Network Time Security, [RFC 8915](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8915)) uses TLS key establishment (TCP port 4460), then protects NTP exchanges with negotiated AEAD keys and authenticators. Opaque cookies carry server state; they are not themselves the per-packet integrity check. Authentication does not prevent an on-path attacker from delaying valid packets.

Legacy ntpd's unauthenticated `monlist` response could amplify spoofed requests, documented as CVE-2013-5211. Exposure depends on implementation, version and access controls.

**PTP** (IEEE 1588) can achieve sub-microsecond synchronisation in appropriately engineered networks. Hardware timestamping and PTP-aware transparent clocks reduce timestamp and switch-residence errors; the protocol name alone does not guarantee a particular accuracy.

## Key takeaways
- NTP timestamps split seconds and fractions into 32-bit fields, so era context matters when the seconds count rolls over in 2036.
- NTS authenticates exchanges but cannot stop an on-path attacker delaying valid packets.

## Further reading
- [RFC 5905](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5905)
- [RFC 8915](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8915)
- [NTP amplification advisory](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2014/01/13/ntp-amplification-attacks-using-cve-2013-5211)

questions.prompt: A client uses correctly authenticated NTS exchanges. An on-path attacker cannot forge their authenticators but can delay valid response packets. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Authentication proves that both one-way delays are equal
options.explanation: Authenticity does not prove network-path symmetry.

options.text: The 32-bit fraction measures the physical clock to 233 picoseconds
options.explanation: A field's representable resolution does not establish the accuracy of the clock or measurement.

options.text: NTS prevents all clock-offset errors
options.explanation: Authentication does not remove delay bias, oscillator error or implementation limits.

options.text: Packet forgery is resisted, but delayed authentic packets can still bias timing
options.explanation: NTS authenticates origin/integrity under its cryptographic assumptions; path-delay manipulation remains outside that guarantee.

questions.workedExample:
1. NTS keys and authenticators let the client reject forged or altered exchanges.
2. An unchanged authentic packet can still be held on the path.
3. NTP timing depends on packet travel time, so authentication alone cannot establish the true one-way delay or remove its effect.

lessons.title: SSH transport, host trust and authentication
lessons.summary: SSH establishes a protected transport, authenticates users and then multiplexes useful channels.
lessons.body:
## SSH: three protocols in a stack

SSH (RFCs 4251 to 4254) runs over **TCP port 22** and is really three protocols layered on top of each other:

```
+-----------------------------+
| Connection: channels       |
|  (shell, exec, sftp, -L)   |
+-----------------------------+
| User authentication        |
|  (publickey, password)     |
+-----------------------------+
| Transport: key exchange,   |
|  encryption, integrity     |
+-----------------------------+
| TCP                        |
+-----------------------------+
```

### Transport layer

1. Both sides send a **version string** in plaintext, such as `SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6`.
2. Both send **KEXINIT** listing supported algorithms in preference order: key exchange, host key types, ciphers, message authentication codes, compression. Negotiation generally follows client preference among mutually supported choices, subject to compatibility rules between key-exchange and host-key algorithms.
3. **Key exchange**: an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange, these days `curve25519-sha256` or a post-quantum hybrid. OpenSSH 9.0 (April 2022) made `sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com` the default, and OpenSSH 10.0 (April 2025) switched to `mlkem768x25519-sha256`.
4. The server **signs** the exchange hash with its **host key**. The client checks that key against `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. Without a preconfigured trusted host key or host-certificate authority, a first connection can prompt for **trust on first use** (TOFU). Independently checking the fingerprint avoids blindly trusting that first peer.
5. Session keys are derived from the shared secret and the exchange hash. The first exchange hash becomes the permanent **SSH session ID**.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Remembering a regular courier's face
> The first time a courier arrives claiming to be from your usual firm, you have little to go on, so you take their word and remember their face. On later visits you compare. A stranger claiming to be the same courier is noticed at once.
>
> **How it maps:** The face is the server's host key and your memory is `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. Accepting the first visit is trust on first use, and the "host key has changed" warning is spotting a stranger. Checking the fingerprint through another channel, or trusting a host-certificate authority, is like phoning the firm to confirm who they sent.
>
> **Where it stops:** If an impostor turns up on that very first visit, you memorise the impostor. And a host key proves the server holds a private key, not that the server is well run: a compromised genuine server still has the right "face".

After the version strings, SSH already uses the **binary packet protocol**; initial key-exchange packets are unencrypted. `NEWKEYS` activates the negotiated protection. The base packet structure is:

```
uint32  packet_length
byte    padding_length
byte[]  payload
byte[]  random padding (>= 4)
byte[]  MAC (or AEAD tag)
```

In the base RFC 4253 format, packet length including its four-byte length field but excluding the message authentication code is aligned to the cipher block size or 8 bytes, whichever is larger. Negotiated AEAD/Encrypt-then-MAC formats alter some framing and authentication details. Padding provides limited length hiding. Modern ciphers such as `chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com` and AES-GCM are AEADs, so integrity comes from the cipher's tag. Each direction tracks an implicit **SSH sequence number**. Base RFC 4253 MACs and some negotiated modes use that counter; SSH AES-GCM instead uses its IV-based invocation counter (RFC 5647). Integrity protection normally detects invalid packet manipulation, but the handshake interaction below exposed an exception for affected modes.

> [!warning] Terrapin (2023)
> Sequence numbers were not reset after the handshake. With affected encryption modes (notably ChaCha20-Poly1305 or CBC with Encrypt-then-MAC), an on-path attacker could inject a message during the unencrypted phase and delete one afterwards, keeping the counts consistent, and so silently strip extension negotiation. The fix, "strict KEX", resets sequence numbers at NEWKEYS and forbids stray messages during the handshake; both client and server must support it.

### User authentication

Within the encrypted transport, the client requests the `ssh-userauth` service and tries methods: **publickey**, password, keyboard-interactive (for OTPs). For publickey, the client signs a blob containing the **SSH session ID**, so a captured signature can't be replayed on another connection. A server talking to an attacker in the middle would have a different session ID, so the signature would not verify.

**Agent forwarding** (`ssh -A`) lets a remote host ask your local agent to sign for you. A privileged attacker on that host can request signatures through an unconstrained forwarded agent while it remains accessible. Confirmation, destination and hardware constraints can limit use; forwarding does not normally reveal the private key itself. `ProxyJump` (`ssh -J`) is safer for hopping through bastions: the end-to-end session is negotiated from your laptop.

## Key takeaways
- SSH establishes a protected transport, authenticates users and then multiplexes useful channels.
- Host-key trust and session-bound public-key authentication solve different impersonation and replay problems.

## Further reading
- [RFC 5647: SSH AES-GCM](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5647)
- [RFC 4253](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4253)
- [RFC 4252](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4252)
- [OpenSSH 10.0 release](https://www.openssh.com/txt/release-10.0)
- [Terrapin original research](https://terrapin-attack.com/)

questions.prompt: Assuming sound key exchange and signature algorithms, SSH public-key authentication signs data including the session ID. Which signature-reuse attacks does this resist? Select all that apply.

options.text: Replaying a captured signature on a new connection
options.explanation: Correct. Each connection has a different session ID, so an old signature is invalid.

options.text: Reusing the captured signature across a man-in-the-middle's two separately negotiated SSH sessions
options.explanation: Correct. The MITM has separate key exchanges with each side, so the two session IDs differ and the relayed signature fails on the server.

options.text: An attacker who already has your private key logging in
options.explanation: With the key they can sign any session ID. Binding to the session does not help.

options.text: The server learning your public key
options.explanation: The public key is presented for verification and is not secret. Authorisation may use authorized_keys, certificates or another configured source.

questions.workedExample: The first key-exchange hash ties the authentication signature to this session. A different session has a different exchange hash with overwhelming probability, so simply replaying that signature or relaying it across two separately negotiated sessions fails. Host-key verification still matters: trusting an attacker as the server exposes commands/data sent to that endpoint. That alone does not give the attacker authentication to the real server; agent forwarding or stolen credentials would be additional capabilities.

link.title: RFC 4253: The SSH Transport Layer Protocol — IETF

questions.prompt: For connections using affected encryption modes, what did the Terrapin attack (2023) exploit in SSH?

options.text: A weakness in curve25519 that leaked session keys
options.explanation: No cryptographic primitive was broken. The issue was in how sequence numbers interact with the handshake.

options.text: Weak random padding allowing plaintext recovery
options.explanation: Padding was not the issue; Terrapin manipulated which messages were received, not their content.

options.text: Sequence numbers that continued from the unencrypted handshake, letting an attacker inject a message before encryption and delete one after without detection
options.explanation: Correct. The counts stayed consistent, so integrity checks passed, while messages such as extension negotiation were removed. Strict KEX resets sequence numbers at NEWKEYS.

options.text: Clients accepting unknown host keys on first use
options.explanation: TOFU is a separate trade-off. Terrapin works even with a correctly verified host key.

questions.workedExample:
1. SSH message authentication codes (MACs) include an implicit per-direction sequence number that counts every packet from the start, including unencrypted handshake packets.
2. The attacker (on path) injects an ignorable message during the plaintext handshake: the receiver's counter goes up by 1.
3. After encryption starts, the attacker deletes the first encrypted message (e.g. EXT_INFO): the counter is now back in step.
4. With vulnerable modes such as ChaCha20-Poly1305, the later integrity checks can verify; the peer never learns that extension negotiation happened.
5. Fix: strict KEX resets counters after NEWKEYS and rejects unexpected messages during key exchange. Both sides must support it. This is not a claim that every SSH cipher construction permits the attack.

lessons.title: SSH channel credit and pipelined SFTP
lessons.summary: SSH channels have separate credit but still share one ordered TCP transport.
lessons.body:
SSH runs an encrypted transport, authenticates a user and multiplexes channels inside that transport. A session channel can run a command or a subsystem; port forwarding uses other channel/request types.

### Connection layer: channels

Everything useful happens in **SSH channels** multiplexed over one transport:

- `session` channels run a shell, a command (`exec`) or an **SSH subsystem** such as `sftp`.
- `direct-tcpip` channels carry `ssh -L` local port forwards.
- `tcpip-forward` global requests set up `ssh -R` remote forwards.

Each channel has its own **channel window**, adjusted with `CHANNEL_WINDOW_ADJUST`, just like HTTP/2 streams. A small channel window caps throughput at the window divided by the round-trip time (the same window-over-round-trip ceiling as HTTP/2 flow control), which is why bulk transfers over high-latency SSH links can be slow even on fast networks (HPN-SSH exists to raise these limits). Ordinary SSH port forwarding relays application bytes between separate TCP connections; it does not encapsulate complete inner TCP packets. Loss on the shared SSH TCP connection can nevertheless stall delivery for every multiplexed channel.

## SFTP: not FTP

SFTP is **not** FTP over SSH. It is a separate binary protocol (draft-ietf-secsh-filexfer; OpenSSH implements version 3) that runs as the `sftp` subsystem inside one SSH session channel. Since OpenSSH 9.0, the `scp` command uses the SFTP protocol by default too.

It works like a remote file system API:

```
C: SSH_FXP_OPEN  id=1 "/data/a.bin"
S: SSH_FXP_HANDLE id=1 h="\x00\x01"
C: SSH_FXP_READ id=2 h off=0     len=32768
C: SSH_FXP_READ id=3 h off=32768 len=32768
C: SSH_FXP_READ id=4 h off=65536 len=32768
S: SSH_FXP_DATA id=2 ...
S: SSH_FXP_DATA id=3 ...
C: SSH_FXP_CLOSE id=9 h
```

(Simplified; the real messages are binary.) File-operation requests carry an **SFTP request ID** (the INIT/VERSION negotiation is an exception), so a client can have many READs outstanding at once. That **pipelining** is what makes SFTP fast: OpenSSH's client keeps up to 64 requests in flight by default. A naive client that issues one 32 KiB read and waits for the reply gets at most one block per round trip. Over a 100 ms round trip that is about 2.6 Mbit/s, however fast the link; keeping 64 reads outstanding raises the ceiling 64-fold, until bandwidth, channel windows or the server become the limit. It is the same one-window-per-round-trip ceiling as HTTP/2 flow control:

```formula reference
T ≤ (k × b) / RTT
where
T: the best possible transfer rate, in bytes per second (B/s)
k: the number of read requests kept outstanding at once; 1 for a naive client, up to 64 for OpenSSH's sftp by default
b: the size of each read, in bytes (B); 32 KiB = 32,768 B is common
RTT: the round-trip time, in seconds (s)
≤: is at most
B: bytes
KiB: kibibyte, 1,024 bytes
s: seconds
In words: a client can receive at most the data it has asked for in each round trip, so more outstanding reads or bigger reads raise the ceiling, and a longer round trip lowers it.
```

## Key takeaways
- SSH channels have separate credit but still share one ordered TCP transport.
- SFTP is a separate binary file-operation protocol; request IDs permit pipelined reads.

## Further reading
- [RFC 4254](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4254)
- [SFTP v3 protocol draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-secsh-filexfer-02)
- [OpenSSH SFTP manual](https://man.openbsd.org/sftp.1)

lessons.summary: A native gRPC call uses an HTTP/2 stream containing length-prefixed messages; this example uses protobuf.
lessons.body:
## gRPC on the wire

This section describes native gRPC over **HTTP/2**. Each call is one HTTP/2 stream. Knowing the framing helps you debug it with ordinary HTTP tools.

### The request

```
HEADERS (stream 1)
  :method POST
  :scheme https
  :path /shop.Catalog/GetItem
  :authority api.shop.example
  content-type application/grpc
  te trailers
  grpc-timeout 250m
DATA (stream 1, END_STREAM)
  <length-prefixed message>
```

- The **path** is `/package.Service/Method`, which is how proxies route and authorise per method.
- `te: trailers` tells proxies the client understands trailers, which gRPC needs.
- `grpc-timeout` carries the **gRPC deadline**: `250m` means 250 milliseconds (units are H, M, S, m, u, n). Applications should propagate the remaining budget downstream; automatic support and configuration differ by language/library.

### Message framing

The gRPC framing is independent of its message encoding; protobuf is the usual default, rather than a requirement of this wire protocol. Inside DATA frames, each encoded message is prefixed with **5 bytes**: a 1-byte compressed flag and a 4-byte big-endian length. Take this message:

```
message GetItemRequest {
  int32 id = 1;
  string name = 2;
}
```

Protobuf encodes each field as a **protobuf tag** followed by the value. The tag packs the field number and the wire type into one varint: the field number is shifted left by 3 bits (`<< 3` in code, the same as multiplying by 8), leaving the low 3 bits for the wire type. So field 1 as a varint (wire type 0) has tag `08`, and field 2 as a length-delimited string (wire type 2) has tag `12`, hexadecimal for 18.

```python
import struct

def pb_varint(n):
    # Unsigned uint64 helper only.
    if (type(n) is not int
            or not 0 <= n < 2**64):
        raise ValueError("expected uint64")
    out = bytearray()
    while True:
        # Extract the low seven value bits.
        b = n & 0x7F
        n >>= 7
        if n:
            # Signal another group follows.
            out.append(b | 0x80)
        else:
            out.append(b)
            return bytes(out)

# id=150, name="hi"
msg = (b"\x08" + pb_varint(150)
       + b"\x12\x02hi")
# Prefix: uncompressed flag and length.
frame = struct.pack("!BI", 0,
                    len(msg)) + msg
print(frame.hex(" "))
# 00 00 00 00 07 08 96 01 12 02 68 69
```

- `08` = field 1, varint. `96 01` = 150. Each varint byte carries 7 bits of the number, least significant group first, and its top bit means "more bytes follow". `96` has that bit set and carries 22; `01` is the last byte and carries 1 lot of 128. 22 + 128 = 150.
- `12` = field 2, length-delimited. `02` = 2 bytes. `68 69` = "hi".
- The 5-byte prefix `00 00 00 00 07`: not compressed, 7 bytes.

This helper demonstrates nonnegative values; signed `int32` negatives use sign-extended varints, while `sint32` uses ZigZag encoding.

The message boundaries are independent of DATA frame boundaries: one message can span many DATA frames, and one DATA frame can carry several messages. **Streaming RPCs** simply send more length-prefixed messages on the same stream.

## Key takeaways
- A native gRPC call uses an HTTP/2 stream containing length-prefixed messages; this example uses protobuf.
- A message has a five-byte gRPC prefix, independent of HTTP/2 DATA frame boundaries.

## Further reading
- [gRPC HTTP/2 protocol](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/PROTOCOL-HTTP2.md)
- [Protobuf encoding](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/encoding/)

The prefix is always 5 bytes: 1 for the flag and 4 for the length.

options.explanation: A DATA frame's length is not a message boundary; messages can span DATA frames or share them, so gRPC adds its own framing.
Correct. 1 byte compressed flag (0), then a 4-byte big-endian length (3).

3. Length as uint32 big-endian: `00 00 00 03`.
4. Prefix: `00` + `00 00 00 03`.

Whole payload: `00 00 00 00 03 08 96 01`, 8 bytes.

lessons.title: gRPC trailers, deadlines and connection balancing
lessons.summary: HTTP success and RPC success are separate; grpc-status in trailers gives the RPC outcome.
lessons.body:
A native gRPC call is one HTTP/2 stream. Requests carry a method path, a content type and optionally grpc-timeout; 250m means a 250-millisecond remaining budget. Messages have a one-byte compression flag and four-byte length before each encoded body; these examples use protobuf. The final call result is separate from those bytes.

### The response and trailers

```
HEADERS  :status 200
         content-type application/grpc
DATA     <length-prefixed messages>
HEADERS  (END_STREAM)  trailers:
         grpc-status 0
         grpc-message ""
```

The **status is in the trailers**, because a streaming server only knows whether the call succeeded at the end. A conforming gRPC response uses HTTP status 200 even for a gRPC error; HTTP intermediaries and protocol errors can produce other HTTP statuses. A call that fails immediately can send a single "Trailers-Only" HEADERS frame.

Common codes:

| Code | Name | Retry? |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | OK | n/a |
| 3 | INVALID_ARGUMENT | No |
| 4 | DEADLINE_EXCEEDED | Maybe |
| 5 | NOT_FOUND | No |
| 8 | RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED | Depends on quota/resource cause |
| 13 | INTERNAL | Rarely |
| 14 | UNAVAILABLE | Consider retry if safe and budget permits |

Retry decisions need method semantics, duplicate-effect protection, retry policy and remaining deadline. A timeout can occur after a server has committed a change.

### Deadlines and cancellation

Pass the remaining deadline budget to downstream calls, reserving any time needed to finish the current response. Starting with 300 ms and spending 50 ms leaves about 250 ms; giving every downstream hop a fresh 300 ms timeout can keep work running after the caller has stopped waiting. Deadline propagation support differs between language libraries and configuration.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A delivery promise passed to subcontractors
> A restaurant promises a customer dinner within 30 minutes. The kitchen takes 10, so it tells the driver "you have 20 minutes", not "you have 30". If the customer cancels, a sensible restaurant tells the driver to turn back instead of delivering to an empty house.
>
> **How it maps:** The customer's promise is the caller's deadline, the kitchen is service A, and the driver is downstream service B. Passing on "20 minutes" is propagating the remaining budget in `grpc-timeout`. Telling the driver to turn back is cancellation.
>
> **Where it stops:** A driver hears "turn back" at once; a cancelled RPC reaches downstream servers after network delay, and only stops work if the handler checks for it. Nothing un-cooks a meal: a change the server has already committed stays committed.

When a client deadline expires, it can report DEADLINE_EXCEEDED and signal cancellation. Server handlers must cooperate by checking cancellation and stopping unnecessary work; cancellation is not an instantaneous distributed stop and cannot roll back an already committed side effect.

### Operational consequences

- **Browsers** can't read HTTP/2 trailers or control framing through `fetch`, so browsers use **gRPC-Web**, which moves trailers into the body and needs a proxy (or server support) to translate.
- **Load balancing.** A client using one long-lived HTTP/2 connection sends its streams to the backend chosen for that connection by a connection-oriented layer-4 balancer. A channel can also use multiple connections; the backend assignment lasts for that connection. Use a layer-7 (HTTP/2-aware) proxy such as Envoy, or client-side balancing across several connections.
- **gRPC keepalives** are HTTP/2 PING frames. Pinging more often than the server allows gets a GOAWAY with `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM` and the debug data `too_many_pings`.
- **Message size.** Receive limits are configurable and implementation-specific; exceeding an enforced limit can produce RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED. Defaults differ between language implementations, so check your library's documentation.

## Key takeaways
- HTTP success and RPC success are separate; grpc-status in trailers gives the RPC outcome.
- Retry safety and deadline propagation depend on effects and remaining budget, not just a status name.

## Further reading
- [gRPC HTTP/2 protocol](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/PROTOCOL-HTTP2.md)
- [gRPC deadlines](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/deadlines/)
- [gRPC load balancing](https://grpc.io/blog/grpc-load-balancing/)
- [gRPC keepalive](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/keepalive/)

lessons.title: BitTorrent metadata, bencoding and peer discovery
lessons.summary: BitTorrent v1 hashes the bencoded info dictionary, which commits to piece hashes rather than publisher identity.
lessons.body:
## BitTorrent

### The metainfo file and the info-hash

For **BitTorrent v1**, a `.torrent` file is a **bencoded** dictionary. Bencoding has four types:

| Type | Example | Encodes |
|---|---|---|
| Integer | `i42e` | 42 |
| String | `4:spam` | "spam" |
| List | `l4:spami42ee` | ["spam", 42] |
| Dict | `d3:cow3:mooe` | {"cow": "moo"} |

Dictionary keys are byte strings and must be **sorted by raw bytes**. Canonical integer and string-length encodings also matter; hash the original encoded `info` substring or fully validate input before re-encoding. That matters because of the `info` dictionary:

- `name`, `length` (or a list of files),
- `piece length`, chosen when the torrent is created (256 KiB is one example),
- `pieces`: the **SHA-1 hashes** of every piece, 20 bytes each, concatenated.

The **info-hash** is the SHA-1 of the bencoded `info` dictionary. It identifies the torrent everywhere: to trackers, in the DHT, in the peer handshake and in magnet links (`magnet:?xt=urn:btih:<info-hash>`). It ties the metadata to the piece hashes, subject to SHA-1's security limitations. An info-hash is not a publisher identity or proof that downloaded content is safe.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A packing list with a fingerprint for every box
> Someone ships a flat-pack wardrobe in many boxes, which you may collect from different strangers. The packing list gives a unique fingerprint for each box, and the whole list has its own fingerprint, which a friend you trust read out to you.
>
> **How it maps:** The packing list is the `info` dictionary, each box fingerprint is a piece hash, and the fingerprint of the whole list is the info-hash. Knowing the info-hash lets you check a list fetched from strangers, and the list then lets you check every box.
>
> **Where it stops:** The fingerprints prove the boxes match the list, not that the wardrobe is safe or who designed it. And because the list's fingerprint is taken over its exact bytes, everyone must write the list identically, which is why bencoding sorts dictionary keys.

```python
import hashlib

def bencode(x):
    if type(x) is int:
        return b"i%de" % x
    if isinstance(x, str):
        x = x.encode()
    if isinstance(x, bytes):
        return b"%d:%s" % (len(x), x)
    if isinstance(x, list):
        return (b"l" + b"".join(
            map(bencode, x)) + b"e")
    if isinstance(x, dict):
        pairs = []
        for k, v in x.items():
            if isinstance(k, str):
                k = k.encode("utf-8")
            if not isinstance(k, bytes):
                raise TypeError("key type")
            pairs.append((k, v))
        keys = [k for k, _ in pairs]
        # Reject str/bytes key collisions.
        if len(set(keys)) != len(keys):
            raise ValueError("same key")
        # Canonical order uses key bytes.
        pairs.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[0])
        return b"d" + b"".join(
            bencode(k) + bencode(v)
            for k, v in pairs) + b"e"
    raise TypeError("unsupported type")

# The output is sorted: cow, then spam.
print(bencode({"spam": ["a", 42],
               "cow": "moo"}))
# b'd3:cow3:moo4:spaml1:ai42eee'
```

BitTorrent v2 (BEP 52) replaces SHA-1 with **SHA-256 Merkle trees** per file, with 16 KiB leaves (the final block can be shorter). With the necessary hashes/proofs, blocks can be verified against the per-file root; identical file contents share that root. The v2 info-hash is SHA-256, with protocol-specific truncation where a 20-byte identifier is required.

### Finding peers

A client finds others through a **BitTorrent tracker** (an HTTP or UDP server returning peer lists for an info-hash), the **DHT** (below) or **peer exchange** with already-connected peers. A magnet link can carry an info-hash and optional parameters such as tracker URLs or a display name; the client fetches the `info` dictionary itself from peers (BEP 9) and verifies it against the hash.

## Key takeaways
- BitTorrent v1 hashes the bencoded info dictionary, which commits to piece hashes rather than publisher identity.
- Trackers, DHT lookups and peer exchange discover suppliers; magnet metadata must match its hash.

## Further reading
- [BEP 3](https://www.bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0003.html)
- [BEP 9](https://www.bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0009.html)
- [BEP 52](https://www.bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0052.html)

lessons.title: BitTorrent wire messages, verification and choking
lessons.summary: BitTorrent peers handshake, pipeline block requests and verify completed pieces against trusted metadata.
lessons.body:
A BitTorrent v1 torrent identifies pieces through SHA-1 hashes in trusted metainfo. Peers advertise what they have and trade blocks; the wire protocol and selection policies perform different jobs.

### The peer wire protocol

Peers talk over TCP (or uTP, a UDP-based protocol with delay-based congestion control designed to yield to other traffic). The connection starts with a **68-byte handshake**:

```
1   pstrlen = 19
19  "BitTorrent protocol"
8   reserved (extension bits)
20  info_hash
20  peer_id
```

The fixed length lets a receiver read exactly 68 bytes, then check that the info-hash names a torrent it is serving before going further.

After that, every message except the zero-length keep-alive carries a 4-byte big-endian length, a 1-byte ID and a payload:

| ID | Message | Payload |
|---|---|---|
| 0 / 1 | choke / unchoke | none |
| 2 / 3 | interested / not interested | none |
| 4 | have | piece index |
| 5 | bitfield | pieces I have |
| 6 | request | index, offset, length |
| 7 | piece | index, offset, block |
| 8 | cancel | as request |

A length of 0 is a keep-alive. Ordinary request blocks are **16 KiB blocks**, with shorter blocks where a piece ends, and clients keep several requests outstanding per peer (pipelining again, for the same window/RTT reason as SFTP).

Each completed piece is hashed and compared with the metainfo. A mismatch means the piece is discarded and re-downloaded, and the peers that supplied it may be banned. This detects mismatching content without trusting each supplier, but still depends on trusted metadata and hash assumptions. A mixed-source bad piece does not identify which contributor supplied a bad block.

### Piece selection and choking

Two policies make swarms work:

- **Rarest first.** Download the pieces that the fewest of your peers have. This promotes availability of scarce pieces but cannot guarantee that every piece remains online and makes you useful to others sooner.
- **Tit-for-tat choking.** You upload only to a few peers at a time. BEP 3 describes decisions on a 10-second cadence and rotation of an optimistic slot every 30 seconds. The optimistic interested peer counts within the four allowed interested downloaders, rather than being an unconditional fifth slot; new connections receive selection bias. Seeders use upload performance rather than download reciprocation. Client policies can differ.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A swap shop with a free-sample table
> At a swap shop, regulars trade mostly with the people who have recently given them the most. To give newcomers a chance, each trader also hands a free item to one stranger at a time, rotating every so often. A newcomer who receives something can start trading.
>
> **How it maps:** Trading with your best recent partners is tit-for-tat choking; the free item is the optimistic unchoke. Rarest first is choosing to pick up the items few people have, so you have something others want and the item survives if its owner leaves.
>
> **Where it stops:** BitTorrent's partners are judged on measured transfer rates and re-evaluated on a regular cadence (every ten seconds in BEP 3's description), not on goodwill. Seeders, which want nothing back, simply favour peers they can upload to well.

Near the end, **endgame mode** requests the last few blocks from every peer that has them and cancels duplicates on arrival, so one slow peer doesn't hold up completion.

## Key takeaways
- BitTorrent peers handshake, pipeline block requests and verify completed pieces against trusted metadata.
- Rarest-first and optimistic unchoking improve exchange without guaranteeing piece availability.

## Further reading
- [BEP 3](https://www.bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0003.html)
- [BEP 29](https://www.bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0029.html)

questions.prompt: A BitTorrent v1 client with trusted metainfo finishes downloading piece 812, hashes it, and the SHA-1 does not match the metainfo. What should it do?

options.text: Keep the piece, since TCP guarantees integrity
options.explanation: TCP's checksum only catches transmission errors, not a peer deliberately (or buggily) sending wrong data.

options.text: Ask the tracker for the correct hash
options.explanation: Given the trusted metainfo in the prompt, a tracker is not a replacement source of piece hashes. A mismatch means these bytes cannot be accepted as the expected piece.

options.text: Discard the piece, re-download it (possibly from other peers), and consider banning peers that contributed bad blocks
options.explanation: Correct. Piece hashes make peers untrusted: bad data is detected and replaced.

options.text: Abort the whole torrent
options.explanation: One bad piece is routine (deliberately corrupted pieces, buggy peers). Only that piece needs redoing.

questions.workedExample:
1. `pieces` in the info dict has 20 bytes per piece; take bytes 812 × 20 to 812 × 20 + 19.
2. Compare with SHA-1 of the downloaded piece. Mismatch.
3. Throw away all blocks of piece 812.
4. Re-request them, preferring other peers.
5. Apply a cautious peer-reputation policy. A mixed-source piece mismatch alone cannot identify the bad contributor; even a sole supplier does not prove deliberate malice.
6. Only after a good hash do you send `have 812` to peers.

questions.prompt: A new BitTorrent peer joins a swarm with no pieces. Under strict tit-for-tat, nobody would upload to it because it has nothing to offer. Which mechanism gets it started?

options.text: Rarest-first piece selection
options.explanation: Rarest first decides *which* piece to fetch, not whether anyone will send it.

options.text: Endgame mode
options.explanation: Endgame applies near the *end* of a download, requesting remaining blocks from everyone.

options.text: The tracker uploads the first piece
options.explanation: The tracker role supplies peer lists, rather than the initial data piece. A machine could separately run a seeding service.

options.text: Optimistic unchoking gives a peer an upload opportunity without requiring a prior contribution
options.explanation: In the classic BEP 3 policy an optimistic slot rotates on a 30-second cadence, with bias towards new connections. This creates an opportunity, not a guarantee of rapid completion.

questions.workedExample: BEP 3 describes changing choking decisions every ten seconds and rotating an optimistic unchoke every thirty. If that optimistic peer is interested, it counts within the four allowed interested downloaders. New connections are favoured in selection. This lets a newcomer obtain something to trade; seeders and modern client policies may behave differently.

lessons.title: Kademlia XOR distance and bounded routing buckets
lessons.summary: Kademlia ranks node and key IDs by XOR distance in one shared identifier space.
lessons.body:
## Kademlia: the XOR metric

A **distributed hash table** (DHT) maps keys to values with no central server. BitTorrent's **Mainline DHT** (BEP 5) is based on **Kademlia** (Maymounkov and Mazières, 2002) and stores "which peers have info-hash X".

Nodes and keys share a 160-bit ID space (info-hashes are 160 bits, so they fit). The distance between two IDs is their **XOR** (exclusive or: compare the IDs bit by bit, writing 1 where they differ and 0 where they match), read as an integer. With 4-bit IDs:

```formula essential
d(a, b) = a ⊕ b
d(0110, 0011) = 0101 = 5
where
d(a, b): the Kademlia distance between IDs a and b, a whole number
a, b: two node or key IDs, written here in binary (base 2); 160 bits long in Mainline DHT
⊕: XOR, exclusive or: each result bit is 1 if the two input bits differ and 0 if they are the same
In words: two IDs are as far apart as the binary number marking where their bits differ; 0110 and 0011 differ in the second and fourth bits, giving 0101, which is 5.
```

In Python the XOR operator is `^`, so `0b0110 ^ 0b0011` gives 5. A difference in a high bit outweighs all the lower bits together, so IDs that share a longer leading prefix are always closer. That gives a quick rule: to find the closest ID, look for the longest shared prefix.

XOR distance behaves like ordinary distance (it is a true metric): every ID is at distance zero from itself, the distance from a to b equals the distance from b to a, and going via a third ID is never shorter than going direct.

Crucially, **for any point and any distance there is exactly one ID at that distance**, so all nodes can consistently rank IDs for a target. Completing a lookup also requires adequate live routing information. Original Kademlia replicates each value on a small, fixed number of the closest nodes (the contact/replication parameter k); Mainline DHT stores peer contact information associated with the hash.

### k-buckets

Each node keeps a DHT routing table made of **k-buckets**. In the basic distance-bucket model, each bucket covers a band of distances twice as wide as the one before. Put another way, bucket i holds contacts whose IDs first differ from ours at the same bit position: the nearest bucket holds contacts that share all but the last bit with us, and the farthest holds contacts that differ in the very first bit, which is half of the whole ID space.

Each bucket holds a fixed maximum number of contacts, the contact-capacity parameter k: 20 as the original paper's example, and **8 in Mainline DHT**.

The capacity per bucket is bounded by k; contact **density** falls across exponentially larger distance regions. Mainline DHT uses a splitting routing-table implementation rather than a literal permanently allocated array of 160 buckets.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: An address book that thins out with distance
> Your address book holds almost every neighbour on your street, a handful of people elsewhere in your town, a few in other cities and one or two in each distant country. Each region gets only a few slots, however many people live there.
>
> **How it maps:** Regions further away are the higher buckets, which cover exponentially larger stretches of the ID space but still hold at most k contacts. Close to your own ID you know almost everyone; far away you know a few people, which is enough to ask for directions.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real distance is geographic. Kademlia "nearness" is only XOR closeness of random IDs, which says nothing about where the computers are or how fast they respond.

When a bucket is full and a new contact appears, Kademlia **pings the least recently seen** contact and drops the newcomer if the old one answers. The paper's analysis of Gnutella traces motivated favouring older responsive contacts; current networks need not have the same uptime distribution. This impedes an attacker simply displacing old contacts with a flood of new IDs, but does not eliminate Sybil or eclipse attacks.

## Key takeaways
- Kademlia ranks node and key IDs by XOR distance in one shared identifier space.
- Bounded k-buckets retain contacts across distance scales; Mainline DHT uses a splitting table.

## Further reading
- [BEP 5](https://www.bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0005.html)
- [Original Kademlia paper](https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/~petar/papers/maymounkov-kademlia-lncs.pdf)

questions.prompt: In a 4-bit Kademlia ID space, which node is closest to key `1011`: `1000`, `0011` or `1110`?

options.text: `0011`, because it shares the last three bits
options.explanation: XOR distance weights the **high** bits most. Differing in the top bit makes the distance at least 8.
1011 XOR 1110 = 0101 = 5, further than 1000's distance of 3.

options.text: They're all equally close
options.explanation: XOR gives three different distances; exactly one node is at each distance from the key.
Correct. 1011 XOR 1000 = 0011 = 3, the smallest of 3, 8 and 5.

questions.workedExample:
Compare the IDs from the left and find where each first differs from the key `1011`:

```
key   1011
1000  10.. shares 2 leading bits
1110  1... shares 1 leading bit
0011  .... differs in the top bit
```

1. The longest shared prefix wins, because the first differing bit outweighs all later bits together.
2. `1000` shares `10` with the key, so it is closest. As a check, 1011 XOR 1000 = 0011 = 3.
3. `1110` differs from the second bit: 1011 XOR 1110 = 0101 = 5.
4. `0011` differs in the top bit, so its distance is at least 8: 1011 XOR 0011 = 1000 = 8.

The closest is `1000`. Matching the last three bits, as `0011` does, counts for little.

lessons.title: Kademlia lookup progress and hostile identities
lessons.summary: A lookup queries progressively closer candidates and completes its closest responsive candidate set.
lessons.body:
Kademlia gives each node and key an identifier, using XOR as distance. A node retains bounded contact lists called k-buckets across distance scales. Mainline BitTorrent DHT uses 160-bit IDs and a contact-capacity parameter of eight.

### Lookup

To find the nodes closest to a target identifier (called T in the API examples):

1. Pick the few closest contacts you know (the paper calls this concurrency parameter α, alpha, with 3 as its example) and send each `find_node(T)` (or `get_peers(T)` in BitTorrent) in parallel.
2. Each reply contains the k closest contacts *it* knows.
3. Query the closest ones you haven't asked yet.
4. If a round finds no closer contact, query the remaining unqueried contacts among the k closest seen. Complete when the closest responsive candidates have been checked; handle failed contacts/timeouts rather than stopping after the first non-improving round.

With populated, maintained routing buckets and the model's ID-distribution assumptions, prefix progress supports **O(log n)** lookup scaling, where n is the number of nodes in the network. Big O notation describes how a cost grows as n grows, ignoring constant factors; log n is the logarithm of n, which grows very slowly. Roughly, each round fixes at least one more bit of shared prefix, and the number of bits needed to single out the closest nodes among n is about the base-2 logarithm of n: how many times you can halve n before reaching 1, about 20 for a million nodes. It is not a guarantee that every response halves numeric XOR distance or that an unavailable key will be found. Churn, timeouts, sparse tables and adversaries matter, so real lookups can take more rounds than the model suggests.

XOR distance is symmetric: a query sender can also be a useful routing contact for its receiver. Subject to routing-table admission and maintenance rules, learning from incoming messages improves coverage without contacting every node. This is an opportunity to learn a contact, not evidence that the sender is honest.

Mainline DHT messages are bencoded dictionaries over UDP (KRPC): `ping`, `find_node`, `get_peers` (returns peers, or closer nodes) and `announce_peer`. To stop arbitrary IPs being announced, `get_peers` replies include an IP-bound **announce token** that the requester must return to the issuing node when announcing. It limits announcement of other IP addresses; it does not prove the announcing peer actually has the content.

> [!warning] Sybil attacks
> Anyone can choose a node ID. An attacker who creates many IDs close to a target info-hash can hide or censor it ("eclipse"). Mitigations include tying IDs to IP addresses (BEP 42) and querying several disjoint paths.

## Key takeaways
- A lookup queries progressively closer candidates and completes its closest responsive candidate set.
- Logarithmic scaling needs routing/distribution assumptions; Sybil and eclipse attacks remain risks.

## Further reading
- [BEP 5](https://www.bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0005.html)
- [BEP 42](https://www.bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0042.html)
- [Original Kademlia paper](https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/~petar/papers/maymounkov-kademlia-lncs.pdf)

questions.prompt: Which properties make Kademlia lookups efficient and robust? Select all that apply.

options.text: XOR distance is symmetric, so nodes learn useful contacts from the queries they receive
options.explanation: Correct. If A is close to B, B is equally close to A, so incoming queries populate the right buckets.

options.text: Exponentially sized distance buckets support logarithmic lookup scaling when routing and ID-distribution assumptions hold
options.explanation: The model supports progress through ID prefixes. This is not a promise that every response halves numeric XOR distance or that failed nodes and adversaries cannot disrupt a lookup.

options.text: Parallel queries reduce dependence on one slow or dead contact
options.explanation: Concurrency, such as the paper's example α=3, can overlap delays. It does not eliminate all timeouts or guarantee a result.

options.text: Full buckets replace old contacts with new ones, keeping the table fresh
options.explanation: The opposite: original Kademlia retains responsive old contacts and drops newcomers. Its historical trace analysis motivated the uptime preference; the rule also impedes simple newcomer flooding without eliminating Sybil attacks.

options.text: A central bootstrap server answers every lookup
options.explanation: Bootstrap nodes only help a new node join; lookups are fully distributed.

questions.workedExample: XOR symmetry allows incoming messages to teach useful contacts. Maintained distance buckets support prefix progress under the model's assumptions. Parallel queries overlap delays, while responsive old contacts are retained rather than automatically replaced by newcomers. If a round finds no closer node, original Kademlia still queries remaining closest candidates before terminating. Actual latency, success and churn behaviour depend on the network; no current typical round count is assumed.
