lessons.title: WebRTC signalling, candidate checks and TURN
lessons.summary: WebRTC leaves signalling transport to the application while ICE tests candidate-pair reachability.
lessons.body:
## WebRTC: browsers talking directly

WebRTC lets two browsers exchange audio, video and data directly. The hard part isn't the media; it's getting a packet from one to the other when both are behind NATs.

### Signalling is your problem

WebRTC deliberately **does not specify signalling**. Peers exchange **SDP** offers and answers (session descriptions: codecs, ICE credentials, DTLS fingerprints) through any channel you like, usually a WebSocket to your server. The browser peer-connection API follows JSEP's offer/answer processing. The following fragment is illustrative and wrapped for display: candidate attributes are single lines on the wire, and the fingerprint/password here are abbreviated placeholders.

```
a=ice-ufrag:F7gI
a=ice-pwd:x9cml/YzichV2+XlhiMu8g
a=fingerprint:sha-256 4A:AD:B9:...
a=candidate:1 1 udp 2122260223
  192.168.1.20 54400 typ host
a=candidate:2 1 udp 1686052607
  203.0.113.5 61234 typ srflx
  raddr 192.168.1.20 rport 54400
```

### ICE, STUN and TURN

**ICE** (Interactive Connectivity Establishment, [RFC 8445](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8445)) gathers **ICE candidates**, addresses where a peer might be reachable:

- **Host candidates**: the device's own interface addresses.
- **Server-reflexive (srflx) candidates**: the externally observed address and port a NAT has mapped, learned by asking a **STUN** server "what address do you see me as?".
- **Relayed candidates**: an address on a **TURN** server that forwards packets for you.

Each side sends its candidates to the other (with **trickle ICE**, as they're found rather than all at once). ICE forms compatible candidate pairs and checks them in a prioritised process using authenticated STUN requests. Type/local preferences and both candidate priorities matter; peer-reflexive candidates may be discovered during checks. The controlling agent nominates a valid pair, rather than every first-success pair being automatically selected.

Why this works through NATs: when A sends a check to B's srflx address, A's NAT creates an outbound mapping. When B's check arrives at A's srflx address, the relevant mapping and filtering state may permit it. Success depends on both NATs' mapping and filtering behaviour; a STUN-observed mapping is not guaranteed to apply to every destination. This is **UDP hole punching**.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Two gated estates arranging a visit
> Two friends live on gated estates whose guards only let in visitors a resident has asked for. They swap notes through a mutual friend: "my gate is on Elm Road, and here is the password my guard will ask for". Each asks a passer-by outside "which gate do you see me at?", and both tell their guards to expect the other at the same time. If the guards still refuse, they meet at a café in town instead.
>
> **How it maps:** The mutual friend is the signalling server carrying SDP. The passer-by is a STUN server revealing your server-reflexive address, and telling the guards to expect the other is the outbound check that opens a NAT mapping, which is hole punching. The guard's password is the ICE username and password that authenticate checks. The café is a TURN relay.
>
> **Where it stops:** Guards are people; NATs are rules about addresses and ports, and some create a different outside mapping for each destination, so the address the passer-by saw may not work for your friend. ICE does not guess: it tests candidate pairs and uses one that actually works.

STUN messages are tiny: a 20-byte header with the **magic cookie** `0x2112A442` and a 96-bit transaction ID, plus attributes. The server reports your address in **XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS**: it XORs the port with the cookie's top 16 bits and an IPv4 address with the whole cookie, and the client applies the same XOR again to recover them. The point is that the real address never appears literally in the packet, because some NATs "helpfully" rewrote IP addresses they spotted inside packet payloads. For an IPv6 address, the XOR key also includes the message's 96-bit transaction identifier.

Endpoint-dependent NAT mappings (often called **symmetric NAT**) and restrictive filtering can defeat direct UDP hole punching, but NAT labels alone do not prove that every direct path fails. TURN provides a relay path when one is reachable and permitted. A 1 Mbit/s stream relayed once accounts for about 1 Mbit/s ingress and 1 Mbit/s egress, excluding overhead; provider charging varies. Client-to-TURN transport can use TCP or TLS, including a configured port 443, but this does not guarantee firewall traversal. How often calls need TURN depends heavily on the networks involved.

## Key takeaways
- WebRTC leaves signalling transport to the application while ICE tests candidate-pair reachability.
- STUN discovers or checks addresses, and TURN offers a relay when a permitted direct path fails.

## Further reading
- [RFC 8445](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8445)
- [RFC 8489](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8489)
- [RFC 8656](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8656)
- [RFC 9429](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9429)

questions.prompt: Two WebRTC peers are on different private networks with endpoint-dependent NAT mappings. ICE direct host and server-reflexive checks have failed, but a valid TURN relay path succeeds. Which candidate pair can be selected?

options.text: A pair involving a TURN relay candidate
options.explanation: The stated successful relay path supplies connectivity after these direct checks failed. TURN is not guaranteed to work on every network.

options.text: host to host, because it has the highest priority
options.explanation: Priority cannot make a failed path usable; this prompt explicitly says the direct host checks failed.

options.text: srflx to srflx via hole punching
options.explanation: The prompt says those checks failed. Endpoint-dependent mappings can make a STUN-observed address unsuitable for another destination, but NAT labels alone do not prove universal failure.

options.text: No pair; WebRTC cannot work behind symmetric NATs
options.explanation: TURN exists precisely for this case.

questions.workedExample: ICE evaluates actual reachability. In this scenario, direct checks fail and a relay-involving pair succeeds, so the controlling agent can nominate that valid pair. Depending on the selected pair, one or both peers use a TURN allocation. Relay transport must itself be allowed by the network; media traffic consumes relay bandwidth.

lessons.title: WebRTC security and group-call bandwidth
lessons.summary: WebRTC protects media and data using DTLS-derived keys, SRTP and SCTP channels.
lessons.body:
After ICE has checked candidates and nominated a path, WebRTC establishes protected media/data transport. The signalling exchange includes DTLS certificate fingerprints; the trustworthiness of that exchange is part of the security model.

### Security: DTLS-SRTP and SCTP

Encryption is **mandatory** in WebRTC:

- After ICE, peers run a **DTLS** handshake (TLS for UDP) over the chosen path. Each checks that the other's certificate matches the `a=fingerprint` received over signalling. So the signalling channel must be trustworthy; whoever controls it can swap fingerprints and sit in the middle.
- Media keys are exported from DTLS into **SRTP** (DTLS-SRTP, RFC 5764).
- **Data channels** run **SCTP over DTLS over UDP** (RFC 8831), giving multiple streams with reliable or unreliable, ordered or unordered delivery per channel.

With BUNDLE and RTP/RTCP multiplexing, several protocols share an ICE transport. First-byte ranges distinguish outer STUN, DTLS and RTP/RTCP packets; SCTP is inside DTLS, not a separate outer packet type. Connectivity-check headers and ordinary RTP headers are not all encrypted. TURN/TCP paths add their own transport framing.

### Group calls

A two-party call is naturally peer-to-peer. With more people:

| Topology | Each client uploads | Server work |
|---|---|---|
| Mesh | One per other participant | No media forwarding if paths are direct |
| SFU | 1 (or a few) | Forward packets |
| MCU | 1 | Decode, mix, encode |

In a mesh, each client sends its own copy of its stream to every other participant, so each extra person adds another full stream to everyone's upload. With five people at 1.5 Mbit/s video, a **full mesh** needs each client to upload four copies, 6 Mbit/s, before protocol overhead; whether an uplink supports this is deployment-specific. An **SFU** (selective forwarding unit) takes one upload per client and forwards copies, and with **simulcast** each client sends, say, three resolutions so the SFU can give each receiver the one that suits its bandwidth. An SFU reduces client upload replication at the cost of server forwarding. With ordinary per-hop DTLS-SRTP, the SFU holds media keys; an additional mechanism such as SFrame is needed to hide media content from it.

## Key takeaways
- WebRTC protects media and data using DTLS-derived keys, SRTP and SCTP channels.
- Mesh upload grows with other participants; SFUs reduce replication but ordinary per-hop media keys expose content.

## Further reading
- [RFC 8827](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8827)
- [RFC 8831](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8831)
- [RFC 5764](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5764)
- [RFC 9605](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9605)

questions.prompt: A small team's video calls use a full **mesh**: every participant sends its 1.2 Mbit/s stream directly to each other participant. Calls of three people work well. When a sixth person joins, several people on home connections with about 5 Mbit/s of upload report that their own video freezes for everyone, while incoming video still looks fine. What best explains this, and what fixes it?

options.text: Download is the bottleneck, because mesh receivers must decode five streams; switching to an SFU would cut each person's download
options.explanation: Incoming video is fine, so download is not the problem. Without selective forwarding, an SFU still delivers the same five incoming streams.

options.text: Each person now uploads five copies, about 6 Mbit/s, exceeding a 5 Mbit/s uplink; an SFU lets each client upload one copy (or a few simulcast layers) that the server forwards
options.explanation: Correct. Mesh upload grows with the number of other participants. An SFU moves the copying to the server, so each client's upload stays about one stream regardless of call size.

options.text: Route every peer through a TURN relay, which removes the need to upload separate copies
options.explanation: TURN relays each peer connection's packets, but each mesh peer connection still carries its own copy of the stream. Relaying does not combine them.

options.text: DTLS-SRTP encryption doubles the bit rate in a mesh; disable encryption for large calls
options.explanation: Encryption adds only small per-packet overhead, and WebRTC does not allow unencrypted media anyway.

questions.workedExample:
1. The symptom is outgoing video failing while incoming video is fine, so look at upload.
2. In a mesh each participant sends one copy of its stream to every other participant: with six people, five copies.
3. Five copies of 1.2 Mbit/s is about 6 Mbit/s before overhead, more than a 5 Mbit/s uplink. With three people it was two copies, about 2.4 Mbit/s, which fitted.
4. An SFU receives one upload from each client and forwards copies to the others, so each client's upload stays about one stream (or a few simulcast resolutions) as the call grows.
5. Download is roughly five incoming streams in either design unless the SFU forwards lower resolutions; that is not what is failing here.

The cost of the fix is server forwarding capacity, and with ordinary per-hop DTLS-SRTP the SFU can see the media unless something like SFrame is added.

questions.prompt: Which statements about WebRTC security are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Media is always encrypted with SRTP, keyed via a DTLS handshake
options.explanation: Correct. Unencrypted RTP is not allowed in WebRTC.

options.text: Each peer checks the DTLS certificate against the fingerprint received in SDP
options.explanation: Correct. That's how the peers authenticate each other without a CA.

options.text: Because media is encrypted end to end, a compromised signalling server cannot intercept calls
options.explanation: Whoever controls signalling can substitute their own fingerprints and relay the call as a man in the middle.

options.text: Data channels run over SCTP inside DTLS
options.explanation: Correct. SCTP gives multiple streams with configurable reliability, encrypted by DTLS.

options.text: Ordinary per-hop DTLS-SRTP alone prevents an SFU that terminates those sessions from reading the media content
options.explanation: False. That SFU has the per-hop media keys. Additional end-to-end content encryption such as SFrame can keep payload content hidden from it.

questions.workedExample:
1. DTLS handshake over the ICE path; the certificate may be self-signed.
2. Its hash must equal `a=fingerprint` in the SDP from the other side.
3. Without independent identity verification, substituted signalling fingerprints can enable an active intermediary; a passive TURN relay does not automatically obtain the media keys.
4. With an SFU, each client's DTLS-SRTP session terminates at the SFU, which decrypts and re-encrypts (or at least has the keys). End-to-end needs SFrame-style encryption on top.

lessons.title: RTP packet fields and media-clock timestamps
lessons.summary: RTP sequence numbers count packets while timestamps follow payload-specific media clocks.
lessons.body:
## RTP: real-time media packets

Media in WebRTC (and VoIP, IPTV and many broadcast systems) rides on **RTP** ([RFC 3550](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3550)) over UDP. UDP allows late media to be discarded without transport head-of-line blocking. RTP can also use other transports; TCP-based fallback can be useful on restrictive networks despite its latency tradeoffs. Whether a late packet is useful depends on the playout deadline.

The fixed header is **12 bytes**:

```
+-+-+-+----+-+-------+----------+
|V|P|X| CC |M|  PT   | Seq (16) |
+-+-+-+----+-+-------+----------+
|        Timestamp (32)         |
+-------------------------------+
|           SSRC (32)           |
+-------------------------------+
|  CSRC list (0-15 x 32 bits)   |
+-------------------------------+
V = version (2 bits), P = padding,
X = extension, CC = CSRC count
```

- **Payload type** (PT, 7 bits) says which codec, mapped in SDP (`a=rtpmap:111 opus/48000/2`).
- **RTP sequence number** (16 bits) increases by 1 per packet: detects loss and reordering.
- **Timestamp** (32 bits) is in **media clock** units, not wall time: **48,000 Hz for Opus** audio and **90,000 Hz for common video payload formats such as H.264**. It advances by the clock rate times the media time a packet covers, so a 20 ms Opus packet moves it on by 960 (Opus uses the 48 kHz RTP clock whatever sampling rate the audio itself uses) and each picture of 30-frames-per-second video by 3,000. Packet timestamp and marker rules are defined by the payload format.
- **Marker bit** (M) typically flags the last packet of a video frame.
- **SSRC** identifies the stream source; **CSRC** lists contributing sources when a mixer combined streams.

The two counters answer different questions. The sequence number says how many packets were sent, so a gap in it means loss or reordering. The timestamp says how much media time has passed, so it can jump without any loss: an Opus sender using discontinuous transmission (DTX) sends nothing during silence, and the next packet's timestamp leaps ahead while its sequence number is the next one in line. Several packets of one video frame share the same timestamp.

```python
import struct

pkt = bytes.fromhex(
    "806f1a2b000003c0deadbeef")
# Read only the twelve-byte fixed header.
b0, b1, seq, ts, ssrc = struct.unpack(
    "!BBHII", pkt[:12])
# Isolate version and payload-type bits.
print(b0 >> 6, b1 & 0x7F, seq, ts)
# 2 111 6699 960
```

This header fixture decodes as version 2, PT 111, sequence 6699 and timestamp 960. The top two bits of the first byte are the version, and the second byte holds the marker bit on top of a 7-bit payload type, so a parser must mask the marker off. PT 111 means Opus only if SDP negotiated that mapping. With an illustrative initial timestamp of zero and one 20 ms Opus frame per packet, 960 is the second frame; real initial timestamps and sequence numbers are randomised. This snippet parses only the fixed header, not a complete validated RTP packet.

## Key takeaways
- RTP sequence numbers count packets while timestamps follow payload-specific media clocks.
- A fixed-header parser illustrates fields but does not validate a complete RTP packet.

## Further reading
- [RFC 3550](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3550)
- [RFC 7587](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7587)
- [RFC 6184](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6184)

questions.prompt: A receiver logs an Opus RTP stream negotiated at the usual 48 kHz RTP clock with 20 ms packets. Sequence numbers run 1000, 1001, 1002, 1003 with no gaps, and the timestamps rise by 960 each time, except that packet 1003's timestamp is 1,920 above packet 1002's. What happened?

options.text: A packet between 1002 and 1003 was lost in the network
options.explanation: Loss shows up as a gap in sequence numbers. 1002 and 1003 are consecutive, so no sent packet is missing.

options.text: Packet 1003 arrived 20 ms late, so its timestamp was increased
options.explanation: The sender stamps the media time when it builds the packet. Arrival delay never changes the timestamp; it shows up as jitter.

options.text: The sender switched to a 96 kHz clock for that packet
options.explanation: The clock rate is fixed by the negotiated payload format; Opus over RTP always uses 48,000 Hz.

options.text: Nothing was lost: the sender sent no packet for one 20 ms interval, for example silence under discontinuous transmission, so media time advanced by 40 ms while the packet count advanced by one
options.explanation: Correct. Sequence numbers count packets sent; timestamps count media time. A timestamp jump with consecutive sequence numbers means the sender skipped media, not that the network lost a packet.

questions.workedExample:
1. At the 48 kHz Opus RTP clock, a 20 ms packet advances the timestamp by 960 ticks.
2. Sequence numbers rise by exactly one per packet sent, so 1000 to 1003 with no gaps means every sent packet arrived.
3. The jump of 1,920 ticks is 40 ms of media time between consecutive packets: one 20 ms interval had no packet at all.
4. That is what Opus discontinuous transmission (DTX) does during silence; RFC 7587 notes that a receiver tells DTX from loss by looking for sequence-number gaps.
5. The decoder fills the skipped interval with comfort noise or concealment rather than treating it as a loss.

questions.prompt: Your RTP parser reports payload type 96 for most packets of an H.264 video stream, but payload type 224 for others. SDP maps only PT 96, and the PT 224 packets are always the last packet of a video frame. What is wrong?

options.text: The sender is mixing in a second codec on PT 224 for keyframes
options.explanation: Payload types are only 7 bits, 0 to 127, so 224 cannot be a valid payload type at all; the parser is misreading the byte.

options.text: The parser reads the second header byte in little-endian order
options.explanation: Byte order affects multi-byte fields such as the sequence number and timestamp. The payload type sits within a single byte.

options.text: The parser treats the whole second byte as the payload type, so the marker bit, set on a frame's last packet, adds 128
options.explanation: Correct. The second byte holds the marker bit followed by a 7-bit payload type. 96 + 128 = 224. Mask with 0x7F to get the payload type and read the top bit as the marker.

options.text: Those packets are RTCP packets that arrived on the same port
options.explanation: RTCP reports are sent on their own schedule, not in step with the video, and their packet types (such as 200 for a sender report) are not 224.

questions.workedExample:
1. In the RTP fixed header the second byte is one marker bit (M) followed by a 7-bit payload type (PT), so PT can only be 0 to 127.
2. For H.264 the marker bit is set on the last packet of each video access unit, the coded data for one picture.
3. A parser that reads the whole byte as PT gets 96 normally and 96 + 128 = 224 whenever the marker is set.
4. Fix: `pt = byte1 & 0x7F` and `marker = byte1 >> 7`.

The lesson's parser does this with `b1 & 0x7F`. Big-endian order matters for the 16-bit sequence number and 32-bit timestamp, not for a field inside one byte.

lessons.title: RTCP reports, jitter and round-trip timing
lessons.summary: RTCP sender reports relate independent media clocks to wall time for synchronisation.
lessons.body:
RTP carries a packet sequence number, media-clock timestamp and source identifier. RTCP is its companion control protocol. RTP clock rates depend on the payload format: Opus uses 48,000 ticks per second, while common video formats use 90,000.

### RTCP: feedback

RTP's companion, **RTCP**, sends periodic reports:

- **Sender reports** map the RTP timestamp to wall-clock (NTP format) time, which is how receivers **lip-sync** audio and video streams that have unrelated RTP clocks.
- **Receiver reports** give fraction lost, cumulative loss and **interarrival jitter**, a running estimate of how much packet transit times vary.
- **Round-trip time**: a receiver report echoes the timestamp of the last sender report it received (LSR) and says how long it held that report before replying (DLSR, delay since last sender report). The sender subtracts its own send time and the receiver's holding time from the moment the report arrives; what remains is time on the network. Both the send and arrival times come from the sender's clock, so the two machines' clocks need not agree. On the wire these are compact fixed-point values, so the subtraction must handle the counters wrapping round.

The jitter estimate compares each packet's spacing on arrival with its spacing in RTP timestamps, and moves one sixteenth of the way towards the latest difference, so one-off spikes are smoothed:

```formula reference
D = (R_j − R_i) − (S_j − S_i)
J_new = J + (|D| − J) / 16
where
D: the change in transit time between two consecutively received packets i and j (which may arrive out of sequence): how much later or earlier packet j arrived than its timestamp predicts
R_i, R_j: the arrival times of packets i and j, measured in RTP timestamp units
S_i, S_j: the RTP timestamps carried in packets i and j
J: the previous jitter estimate, in RTP timestamp units
J_new: the updated estimate, in RTP timestamp units
|D|: the size of D, ignoring its sign
In words: if packets keep arriving with uneven spacing, J climbs towards the typical unevenness; dividing by 16 smooths out one-off spikes.
```

WebRTC adds RTCP feedback messages: **NACK** (please resend packet 6702, if there's time), **PLI** (picture loss indication, allowing an encoder to respond with recovery information such as an intra picture) and transport-wide congestion feedback, which drives Google Congestion Control in adjusting the encoder's bitrate.

On the receiving side, a **jitter buffer** holds packets briefly to reorder them and smooth out variable delay. It is a direct trade: a bigger buffer survives more jitter but adds latency. How much delay is acceptable depends on the application; interactive calls tolerate far less than one-way streaming.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A water tank between an uneven pipe and a steady tap
> Water arrives at a tank in irregular spurts, but the tap below it runs smoothly. A bigger tank rides out longer gaps in the supply, but each drop spends longer in the tank before it reaches the tap.
>
> **How it maps:** The spurts are packets arriving with jitter, the steady tap is playout at the media clock's pace, and the tank's size is the jitter buffer's added delay. RTCP's jitter figure tells both ends how uneven the supply is.
>
> **Where it stops:** Water is interchangeable, but packets are not: the buffer must also put packets back in order, and a packet that arrives after its playout time is useless and is discarded or concealed. Adaptive buffers also resize themselves as conditions change.

## Key takeaways
- RTCP sender reports relate independent media clocks to wall time for synchronisation.
- Receiver reports describe loss, jitter and timing; a jitter buffer trades added latency for tolerance.

## Further reading
- [RFC 3550](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3550)
- [RFC 4585](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4585)

questions.prompt: A monitoring tool computes RTCP round-trip time as (time the receiver report arrives) minus (echoed LSR timestamp), but ignores the DLSR field. Most receivers reply to a sender report within a few milliseconds, but receivers in one region batch their reports and hold each for about 200 ms. Network paths to every region are similar. What will the dashboard show?

options.text: Correct round-trip times everywhere, because LSR already includes the receiver's holding time
options.explanation: LSR is just the echoed timestamp of the sender report. The holding time is reported separately in DLSR, which the tool ignores.

options.text: Round-trip times about 200 ms too high for the batching region, and roughly right elsewhere
options.explanation: Correct. Arrival minus LSR is the whole interval from sending the report to getting the reply. Without subtracting DLSR, the receiver's 200 ms holding time is counted as network delay.

options.text: Meaningless values everywhere, because the sender's and receivers' clocks are not synchronised
options.explanation: The arrival time and LSR both come from the sender's clock, and DLSR is a duration measured by the receiver, so no clock synchronisation is needed.

options.text: Round-trip times about 200 ms too low for the batching region
options.explanation: Ignoring a holding time can only add it to the result, never subtract it.

questions.workedExample:
1. The sender report leaves at time T by the sender's clock, and the receiver echoes T as LSR.
2. The receiver holds the report for DLSR before replying, then the reply crosses the network back.
3. The reply arrives at A, again by the sender's clock. A − LSR is network time out, plus holding time, plus network time back.
4. The correct round trip is A − LSR − DLSR. Dropping DLSR adds each receiver's holding time to its reported RTT.
5. Receivers that reply within milliseconds look almost right; the batching region looks about 200 ms worse than it is, although its network is no slower.

On the wire, LSR and A use compact 1/65,536-second fixed-point values, and the subtraction must allow for the values wrapping round.
